items.text: Guess what, I finally finished the bookshelf! It took me a whole month of sanding, staining, and way too many trips to the hardware store, but it's done and it looks great. Come over this weekend and help me fill it up with books. I'll even supply the snacks!

I've called and emailed him like five times and keep getting "we're looking into it." I'm honestly about two seconds from buying a space heater and sending him the bill. Can I come over and use your hot water this weekend?

Hey! Want to do a board game night next Friday? I was thinking we could order some pizza and pull out a few games, maybe Catan or Codenames. Let me know if you're free and I'll round up a couple of other people too!

Hey! I was just thinking about the reunion and wondering if you're planning to go. It'd be so much fun to catch up with everyone, and it would be even better if you were there. Let me know what you're thinking, and maybe we can coordinate plans!

Subject: Handing over the Atlas project before my leave

Hi Sam,

Thank you again for agreeing to take over the Atlas project while I am on parental leave. I will be out from Monday, December 1st, and I expect to be back in early June. I wanted to put everything you need in one place so the handover is as smooth as possible.

The project is in good shape. The data migration is about 70 percent complete, and the remaining work is mostly the final two regional datasets and the validation pass afterwards. The main milestone ahead is the stakeholder review in late January, where we will need to present the migrated data and the updated reporting dashboard. I have set aside a draft of the presentation in the shared project folder, so you will not be starting from scratch.

There are a few things worth knowing that are not obvious from the documents. The vendor contact, Priya Raman, is very responsive but prefers a short call to a long email thread when something is unclear. The finance team needs the monthly budget update by the fifth of each month, and Daniel in finance will chase you if it is late, so it is easiest to send it a day early. The one risk I am watching closely is the schedule for the second regional dataset, which depends on a team outside our group and has slipped twice already. I would check in with them every couple of weeks rather than waiting for them to flag a delay.

All of the project documentation, including the plan, risk log, meeting notes and budget tracker, is in the shared Atlas folder. I have written a short handover note at the top of the risk log that summarises open decisions and who owns what. Please feel free to reorganise anything that does not suit the way you work.

I would like to walk you through all of this properly before I leave. Could we book an hour next week, and then a shorter follow-up the week after to cover any questions that come up once you have had time to read through everything? I will be fully offline once my leave begins, so I have asked Maria to be your point of escalation for anything that needs a decision above project level.

Thank you for taking this on. I am confident the project is in very capable hands, and I am grateful for your support.

Best wishes,
Alex

Subject: Urgent: Leaking Ceiling in Office Kitchen

Dear [Landlord's Name],

I am writing to report a leak in the ceiling of the kitchen at our office, located at [Property Address]. We first noticed water dripping from the ceiling on [date], and the problem appears to be getting worse. There is now a visible water stain spreading across the ceiling tiles, and water is collecting on the floor below.

We have placed a bucket under the leak and put up a wet floor sign to reduce the risk of anyone slipping. We have also moved nearby equipment and supplies away from the affected area to keep them from being damaged. As the kitchen is used daily by our staff, we are concerned about both the safety hazard and the potential for mold or further structural damage if the leak is not dealt with promptly.

Could you please arrange for a plumber or maintenance contractor to inspect the ceiling and identify the source of the leak as soon as possible? It may be coming from a pipe in the unit above or from the roof, so we would appreciate your help in tracing it. If it would be useful, I am happy to send photos of the damage or to arrange access for the contractor at a time that suits them.

Please let me know when you expect someone to visit, and confirm receipt of this message. I can be reached by reply to this email or by phone at [phone number].

Subject: Re: Request for comment – product recall

Hi Dana,

Thanks for reaching out. Here's where things stand.

We issued the recall on Monday after our quality team found that a small number of units from one production run had a faulty seal. We've had 14 reports of the problem so far, and none involved injuries. We'd rather pull the product and be wrong than leave it on shelves and be right.

If you have one of the affected units, please stop using it and check the lot number on the bottom of the package against the list on our website. Anyone with a matching number can get a full refund or a replacement. No receipt needed.

We're still working out exactly how the seal issue got past our checks. I don't want to guess in print before we know, but I can tell you we've paused that production line until we do. I'm happy to update you once the review wraps up.

You're welcome to quote me on the above. If you need anything else before your deadline, call me directly at the number below and I'll pick up.

I learned at 31 after years of hunt-and-peck, and honestly it took about a month before I stopped hating it.

What worked for me: pick one tutor and stick with it. I used Keybr for a while and then Monkeytype. Keybr is good early because it drip-feeds letters and focuses on whatever you're slow at. Do 15 to 20 minutes a day rather than one long weekend session. Short and daily beats long and occasional.

The hard part is accuracy over speed. Go painfully slow at first and don't look at the keyboard, even when you really want to. Put a cloth over your hands if you have to. If you make a mistake, resist the urge to peek. Speed comes on its own once your fingers know where things are.

Expect to be slower than your old method for a couple of weeks. That dip is normal, and it's where most people quit. Push through it. For me the crossover came around week three or four.

Also, use it for real stuff as soon as you can, like emails and chat, even if it's slow. Practice drills only get you so far.

I'm at about 80 wpm now, up from maybe 35.

Yellow leaves at the bottom of tomato plants are very common, and the cause is usually one of a few things:

**1. Natural aging.** As the plant grows, it sheds its oldest, lowest leaves because they're shaded and no longer productive. If the yellowing is limited to a few lower leaves and the rest of the plant looks healthy, this is normal.

**2. Nitrogen deficiency.** Nitrogen is mobile, so the plant pulls it from old leaves to feed new growth. Lower leaves turn uniformly pale yellow, and growth may be slow. Feed with a balanced fertilizer or compost.

**3. Watering problems.** Overwatering (soggy soil, poor drainage) and underwatering both cause yellowing. Water deeply but less often, aiming for consistently moist, not wet, soil. Mulch helps keep moisture even.

**4. Fungal disease.** If leaves have brown spots, rings, or yellow patches that spread upward, it may be early blight or septoria leaf spot. Remove affected leaves, avoid overhead watering, space plants for airflow, and rotate crops yearly.

**What to do:** Prune the yellow leaves, mulch to prevent soil splash, water at the base, and check your soil's nutrients. If the yellowing climbs quickly, the leaves have spots, or the plant wilts, disease is more likely.

No, it's not rude. Managing your health is more important than etiquette, and most hosts would much rather you eat safely than risk a reaction.

A few things make it go more smoothly:

**Tell the host ahead of time.** A quick message like "I have a severe allergy to X, so I'll bring a dish I can eat safely" avoids surprises and lets the host plan around you. They may even ask for tips on making something safe.

**Bring something to share.** If you can, make a dish that others can enjoy too, and that also happens to be safe for you. It feels more like participating than opting out, and people often appreciate the chance to try something new.

**Don't make it a big deal.** You don't need to over-explain or apologize. A simple "I'm playing it safe with my allergy" is plenty.

**Be careful with cross-contact.** Even if you bring your own food, shared serving utensils and nearby dishes can be a risk. Take your portion first, or use your own utensils.

If anyone takes offense, that's about their assumptions, not your behavior. A good host cares more that you're safe and included than what's on your plate.

Not rude at all. Honestly, it's the smart move.

A potluck is about sharing a meal and being together, not about everyone eating every dish. If you've got a serious allergy, nobody sensible expects you to gamble on a casserole whose ingredients you can't verify. Most hosts would much rather you show up with something safe than skip the event or end up in the ER.

My cousin has a severe nut allergy, and she's been bringing her own main dish to family gatherings for years. Nobody's ever blinked. If anything, people ask for her recipe.

A few things make it smoother:

- **Tell the host ahead of time.** A quick text like "I've got a food allergy, so I'll bring a dish I can eat" removes any awkwardness.
- **Bring something to share, too.** If it's safe for you and tastes good, put it out with the other dishes. It feels more like participating.
- **Don't over-explain.** A short "allergies, so I'm covered!" is plenty.

Anyone who takes offense at you protecting your health is the one being rude, not you.

Motorway anxiety is very common, and it responds well to gradual exposure. Here's an approach that works for many people:

**Start small.** Begin with dual carriageways or the quietest motorway stretch you can find, at off-peak times like a Sunday morning. Aim for just one junction at first, then extend to two or three as you feel comfortable.

**Bring support.** Have a calm, experienced friend sit beside you at first. Later, try driving alone but on a route you've already done with company.

**Plan ahead.** Study the route beforehand, know your exit, and use satnav so you aren't worrying about navigation. Unexpected decisions fuel panic.

**Stay in the left lane.** You don't have to overtake. Settle at a comfortable speed and leave a generous gap ahead.

**Manage your body.** Breathe slowly (in for four, out for six), relax your grip on the wheel, and keep your shoulders down. If you feel overwhelmed, it's fine to exit at the next junction or services. Knowing you can leave reduces the pressure.

**Consider a refresher lesson.** Many instructors offer motorway-specific sessions, such as Pass Plus in the UK. A professional can build your skills and confidence quickly.

**Be patient.** Each successful trip weakens the fear. If anxiety is severe, CBT can help.

You'll get there. Small, repeated steps are what work.

Mushy rice almost always comes down to three things: too much water, too much starch, or too much heat and stirring.

**1. Measure your water.** For most long-grain white rice, use about 1.5 cups of water per 1 cup of rice. Jasmine and basmati often need even less. The "1:2" ratio printed on many packages tends to produce soft, wet rice, especially in a tightly sealed pot.

**2. Rinse the rice.** Surface starch turns gluey when cooked. Swish the rice in a bowl or strainer under cold water until it runs mostly clear, usually 3 to 4 rinses.

**3. Don't stir.** Stirring releases starch and makes the rice sticky. Stir once when it comes to a boil, then leave it alone.

**4. Keep the heat low.** Bring the water to a boil, cover, then turn the heat to the lowest setting. A rolling boil breaks the grains apart.

**5. Rest it.** After about 15 minutes, turn off the heat and leave the lid on for 10 minutes. Then fluff with a fork. This lets excess moisture redistribute.

Also, make sure you're using the right rice. Short-grain and sushi rice are naturally stickier than long-grain varieties.

Try the ratio and rinsing first. They fix the problem most of the time.

Scratching is a natural, necessary behavior for cats. It stretches their muscles, marks territory, and maintains their claws. So the goal is to redirect it, not stop it.

**Provide better options.** Get a sturdy scratching post that's tall enough for a full stretch. Cats often prefer sisal rope or cardboard. Place it right next to the sofa, since cats scratch in prominent, social spots. Try both vertical and horizontal scratchers to see which your cat likes.

**Make the sofa less appealing.** Cover the scratched areas with double-sided sticky tape, a throw blanket, or plastic guards. Cats dislike sticky textures. Once the cat uses the new post consistently, you can gradually remove these.

**Encourage the right spot.** Rub catnip on the post, dangle a toy near it, and praise or treat your cat when it scratches there. Avoid punishment, which causes stress and doesn't teach what to do instead.

**Keep claws trimmed.** Trimming every two to three weeks reduces damage. Soft nail caps are another option.

**Consider pheromone sprays.** Products like Feliway can reduce stress-related scratching.

Avoid declawing. It's a painful amputation that can cause lasting behavioral and physical problems.

With patience and consistency, most cats switch within a few weeks.

Thesis procrastination usually comes from the task feeling too big and too vague. Here's what helps:

**Shrink the task.** "Work on thesis" is not a task. "Write three paragraphs of the methods section" is. Define a piece small enough that you can finish it in one sitting.

**Set a minimum.** Commit to just 25 minutes, or 200 words. Starting is the hardest part, and once you've begun you'll often keep going.

**Protect a regular time.** Pick the same daily slot, ideally when your energy is highest, and treat it like a class you can't skip. Routine beats motivation.

**Write badly first.** Perfectionism fuels avoidance. Give yourself permission to produce a rough draft you'll fix later. Editing is far easier than staring at a blank page.

**Remove friction.** Put your phone in another room, block distracting sites, and leave your document open with a note on where to begin tomorrow.

**Make it accountable.** Tell your advisor you'll send a few pages each week, or join a writing group or find a writing buddy. External deadlines work.

**Look at the real fear.** Often it's fear of judgment or of not being good enough. Naming that makes it less powerful.

Progress, not perfection, gets theses finished. Start small today.

There are a few reliable ways to check whether an egg is still good:

**1. The float test**
Place the egg in a bowl of cold water.
- Sinks and lies flat on its side: very fresh.
- Sinks but stands upright on the bottom: older, but still safe to eat. Use it soon.
- Floats: it's old. Air has seeped in through the shell over time. Discard it to be safe.

**2. Check the date**
Look at the "sell-by" or "best-by" date on the carton. Eggs are usually fine for 3-5 weeks past the pack date if refrigerated constantly.

**3. Crack it open**
- A fresh egg has a firm, rounded yolk and thick white that doesn't spread much.
- Older eggs have a flatter yolk and runnier white, but are still fine if they smell normal.
- Any sulfurous or rotten smell means throw it out immediately. Also discard eggs with pink, green, or iridescent discoloration.

**4. Inspect the shell**
Discard eggs with cracks, slimy texture, or powdery spots (possible mold).

**Storage tip:** Keep eggs in the main part of the fridge, not the door, at 40°F (4°C) or below. Cook eggs thoroughly to reduce any risk of illness.

When in doubt, throw it out.

Not necessarily. Plenty of people learn two languages at once successfully, and the research doesn't show that it harms either one. What matters is how you set it up.

**It works best when:**
- The languages are different enough that they don't blur together. Spanish and Japanese are easier to keep apart than Spanish and Portuguese.
- You give each one its own routine: different times of day, different apps, or different notebooks.
- You're realistic about time. If you only have 30 minutes a day, splitting it in two means slower progress in each.

**It gets harder when:**
- The languages are closely related. Vocabulary and grammar interference is common, such as mixing up Spanish and Italian words.
- You're a complete beginner at language learning. Building study habits is hard enough with one language.
- You're easily discouraged. Two languages mean two plateaus.

**A good compromise:** Start one language, get it to a comfortable beginner level (a few months), then add the second. You get the benefit of an established habit without waiting years.

Ultimately, motivation matters more than strategy. If you're excited about both, that enthusiasm will carry you further than any rule about "the right way" to study. Try it for a month, and if one language starts to suffer, adjust.

Stop trying to get them to talk, and focus on being someone worth talking to.

**Go where they already are.** Teens often open up side by side rather than face to face: in the car, on a walk, while cooking, or playing a game together. Eye contact and "we need to talk" feel like interrogation.

**Ask less, listen more.** Replace "How was school?" with something specific and low-pressure: "Did anything funny happen at lunch?" Then tolerate silence. They often fill it.

**Don't react big.** If your teen shares something awkward or upsetting and gets a lecture, they'll learn not to share. Stay calm, say "thanks for telling me," and save advice until they ask for it.

**Share a little of yourself.** Mention your own day, including frustrations or mistakes. It makes conversation feel two-way.

**Take their interests seriously.** Watch the show, listen to the song, ask what they like about it, and be curious rather than critical.

**Be available at odd hours.** Many teens open up late at night. If you can stay up for those moments, they'll happen more often.

**Be patient.** Pulling away is a normal part of development. Consistent, nonjudgmental presence builds trust over months, not days.

If silence is paired with big changes in mood, sleep, or friendships, consider reaching out to a counselor.

For most people, running every day is not bad, but it depends on how you do it. Many people run daily for years without trouble, and the habit can be great for heart health, mood, and consistency. The risk comes from doing too much, too soon, or at the same intensity every day.

Your muscles, tendons, and bones adapt to stress during recovery, not during the run itself. If every run is hard, you give your body little chance to rebuild, and overuse injuries like shin splints, stress fractures, and runner's knee become more likely. Beginners are especially vulnerable because their cardiovascular fitness improves faster than their connective tissue does.

If you want to run daily, keep most runs easy, at a pace where you could hold a conversation. Make one or two days short and gentle, and save harder efforts for only a couple of days a week. Increase weekly mileage gradually, by roughly 10 percent at a time. Good shoes and some strength work for your legs and core also help.

Watch for warning signs such as persistent soreness in one spot, unusual fatigue, poor sleep, or a rising resting heart rate. If they appear, take a rest day or two. If pain lingers, see a doctor or physical therapist.

A process is a running program with its own private chunk of memory. A thread is a unit of execution that lives inside a process. Every process has at least one thread, and it can have many.

The practical difference comes down to memory. Two processes can't see each other's variables unless you set up something explicit, like pipes, sockets, or shared memory. Threads in the same process share the heap and globals, so they can read and write the same data directly. Each thread still gets its own stack and its own set of registers, so local variables stay separate.

That sharing is the tradeoff:

- **Threads** are cheaper to create and switch between, and passing data around is easy. But because they share memory, you can get race conditions and deadlocks, and a bug in one thread can take down the whole process.
- **Processes** are heavier, and communication takes more effort. But they're isolated, so if one crashes, the others usually keep going. That's why browsers often give each tab its own process.

A rough rule of thumb: use threads when the work needs to share a lot of state and be fast, and use processes when you want isolation or safety.

One caveat: some languages complicate this. Python's GIL, for example, means threads don't run Python code in parallel, so people reach for multiprocessing for CPU-bound work.

Git says your branch has "diverged" when your local branch and the remote branch it tracks each contain commits that the other doesn't have. In other words, history split at some common ancestor, and both sides moved forward independently.

This typically happens when you commit locally while someone else (or you, from another machine) pushes different commits to the same remote branch. It can also happen after you rewrite local history with a rebase, an amend, or a reset, because the rewritten commits are new commits with different IDs, even though their content looks similar.

Git can't simply fast-forward either side, so it asks you to decide how to reconcile them. Your main options:

1. **Merge**: Pull with merge behavior. Git creates a merge commit that joins both lines of history. This is safe and preserves everything as it happened.

2. **Rebase**: Replay your local commits on top of the remote ones. This gives a cleaner, linear history, but it rewrites your local commits, so avoid it if others have based work on them.

3. **Force push**: If you intentionally rewrote history and want the remote to match your local branch, push with `--force-with-lease`. Only do this on branches you own, since it discards remote commits.

Before choosing, run `git fetch` and then `git log --oneline --graph --all` to see exactly where the histories split. That tells you which commits are unique to each side and helps you pick the right fix.

It's a trade-off rather than an outright mistake, but localStorage is generally the weaker choice for sensitive tokens.

**The core problem is XSS.** Anything in localStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on your page. If an attacker injects a script, whether through a vulnerable dependency, a compromised third-party script, or an unescaped user input, they can read the token and send it to their own server. The token can then be used from anywhere until it expires.

**The alternative: HttpOnly cookies.** A cookie flagged `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite` can't be read by JavaScript at all. An XSS attack can still make requests *as the user* while the page is open, but it can't steal the token and use it elsewhere. The cost is that you must handle CSRF, though `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` plus CSRF tokens covers most cases.

**Mitigations if you do use localStorage:**
- Keep access tokens short-lived (minutes, not days).
- Use refresh token rotation, and keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.
- Set a strict Content Security Policy.
- Minimize third-party scripts and audit dependencies.

**Bottom line:** For anything involving user accounts, money, or personal data, prefer HttpOnly cookies. localStorage is tolerable for low-risk apps with short-lived tokens and good XSS hygiene, but it makes a single XSS bug much more damaging.

Nine times out of ten this is the environment. When you run the script by hand, you're using your login shell, with your PATH, your variables, your home directory as the working directory, and everything your .bashrc or .profile set up. Cron gives the job almost nothing. PATH is usually just /usr/bin:/bin, so anything installed elsewhere (node, python from a virtualenv, homebrew stuff, anything in ~/.local/bin) simply isn't found.

Things to check, roughly in order:

1. Use absolute paths for everything: the interpreter, the script, any files it reads or writes. Don't rely on relative paths, because cron's working directory probably isn't what you think.
2. Capture the output. Cron swallows errors unless you redirect them, so tack `>> /tmp/job.log 2>&1` onto the end of the line. Nine times out of ten the error message tells you exactly what's wrong.
3. Check that the script is executable and has a proper shebang line, or call it explicitly through the interpreter.
4. Look at the syslog (grep CRON in /var/log/syslog, or `journalctl -u cron`) to confirm it's even firing.
5. Remember that `%` has special meaning in crontab lines. If you have a `date +%Y-%m-%d` in there, escape each percent sign with a backslash.

Also, make sure you edited the right user's crontab. A job in root's crontab behaves differently from one in yours.

Start with the log redirect. It'll save you a lot of guessing.

Eventual consistency means that if you stop writing to a piece of data, all the copies of it across your system will eventually agree, but at any given moment they might not. It is a trade you make in distributed systems: instead of making every write wait until all replicas have confirmed it, you accept the write on one node, return success, and let the change spread in the background.

In practice, this shows up as stale reads. You update your profile photo, refresh the page, and still see the old one because your request hit a replica that has not received the change yet. A few hundred milliseconds later (sometimes seconds, occasionally longer during outages) it shows the new photo. Shopping cart counts, like counters, DNS records, and social media feeds all behave this way.

The cost is that your application has to tolerate temporary disagreement. Two users might see different values, and concurrent writes to the same item on different nodes can conflict, so the system needs a resolution rule such as last write wins or merging the changes.

The benefit is availability and speed. Nodes keep serving requests even when the network between them is broken, and writes are fast because they do not wait on distant machines.

Use it where brief staleness is harmless. Avoid it for things like account balances or inventory that must never oversell, where you want strong consistency.

This error (EMFILE, or ENFILE at the system level) means a process tried to open a file descriptor but hit a limit on how many it's allowed to have.

**Important: "files" means file descriptors, not just files on disk.** Sockets, pipes, epoll/inotify instances, and device handles all count toward the limit.

**Common causes**

1. **Descriptor leaks.** The code opens files or sockets and never closes them, often on error paths or when exceptions skip the cleanup. The count creeps up until the limit is hit.
2. **Low per-process limit.** The default soft limit (`ulimit -n`) is often 1024, which a busy server can exhaust legitimately. Many concurrent connections each use a descriptor.
3. **Too many inotify watches or instances.** File watchers, IDEs, and dev servers can trigger a similar error tied to `fs.inotify.max_user_instances` or `max_user_watches`.
4. **System-wide exhaustion.** Rarely, the kernel-wide cap (`fs.file-max`) is reached.
5. **Service manager limits.** A systemd service ignores your shell's `ulimit`; it uses `LimitNOFILE`.

**How to diagnose**

- Check the process's limit: `cat /proc/<pid>/limits`
- Count its open descriptors: `ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l`
- See what they are: `lsof -p <pid>`. A long list of the same file or connection points to a leak.

**Fixes**

- Fix leaks first: close resources reliably using `with`, `defer`, `try/finally`, or RAII, and reuse connections via pooling.
- If usage is legitimate, raise the limit in `/etc/security/limits.conf`, or `LimitNOFILE` for systemd services.
- Raising limits without fixing a leak only delays the failure.

Because computers store numbers in binary, and some simple decimal fractions can't be represented exactly in binary.

Think of 1/3 in decimal: it becomes 0.3333… forever, and you have to cut it off somewhere. Binary has the same problem with different fractions. 0.1 is 1/10, and in binary it becomes a repeating pattern (0.0001100110011…) that never ends. Floating point stores only a fixed number of bits (53 bits of precision in a standard 64-bit double), so the value is rounded to the nearest representable number.

So what's actually stored for 0.1 is slightly *more* than 0.1, and 0.2 is also slightly off. When you add them, those tiny errors combine, and the result lands on a neighboring binary value that is not the same one you get when you store 0.3 directly. The difference is around 5×10⁻¹⁷, so printing the sum with enough digits shows something like 0.30000000000000004.

This isn't a bug in your language. It's how IEEE 754 arithmetic works, and you'll see the same result in Python, JavaScript, Java, C, and most others.

**What to do about it:**

- Never compare floats with `==`. Check whether they are within a small tolerance of each other (e.g., `abs(a - b) < 1e-9`, or a built-in like `math.isclose`).
- For money or exact decimal math, use a decimal type (such as Python's `decimal` or Java's `BigDecimal`) or store integer cents.
- When displaying, round to a sensible number of digits.

Probably yes, at least to start. With three small services, the overhead of separate repos usually costs more than it saves.

What you get with one repo: a single PR when a change touches two services (like an API change and its consumer), one place to search, shared config for linting and CI, and no fiddling with versioning internal libraries just to share a few helpers. If you're a small team, or one person, that adds up fast.

The usual objections are mostly about scale. Slow CI? You won't feel it with three small services, and path filters fix most of it later anyway. Access control per service? Only matters if different teams need different permissions. Independent deploys? A monorepo doesn't prevent that. You can still build and deploy each service on its own.

When I'd split them up: the services are owned by different teams, they use totally different stacks with nothing shared, or there are real security or compliance reasons to separate access.

One tip: keep clear boundaries inside the repo. Separate directories, separate dependency files, and no importing straight across services. If you do that, splitting one out later is an afternoon of work, not a project.

So start with one repo, and revisit it only if something actually starts hurting.

A database stores state; a message queue moves work. You can bolt a queue onto a database (a "jobs" table polled by workers), and for small systems that's often the right call. But a dedicated queue earns its place once you need things a database isn't designed for.

**Decoupling.** Producers hand off a message and move on. They don't need to know who consumes it, how many consumers exist, or whether they're online right now. Traffic spikes get absorbed in the queue instead of overwhelming downstream services.

**Delivery semantics.** Queues give you built-in acknowledgments, retries, visibility timeouts, dead-letter queues, and backoff. With a table, you have to build and debug all of that yourself, including the tricky part: making sure two workers don't grab the same row.

**Efficiency.** Polling a table is wasteful and adds latency. Queues push messages to consumers, and they handle high-throughput, short-lived records without the bloat, locking, and vacuum overhead that constant insert-and-delete patterns cause in a database.

**Fan-out and scaling.** Publishing one event to many subscribers, or scaling consumers horizontally, is native to brokers.

**Rule of thumb:** if you have low volume and one consumer, a database table (or Postgres with `SKIP LOCKED`) is fine. Reach for a real queue when you need multiple consumers, high throughput, reliable retries, or service decoupling.

Most of the time, "fine on my machine, broken on mobile" comes down to a handful of causes. Work through them in this order.

**1. Missing viewport meta tag.** Without `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` in your `<head>`, mobile browsers pretend the screen is about 980px wide and shrink everything. Your media queries then never fire.

**2. Testing only at desktop size.** Open your browser's dev tools and use device mode, or just drag the window narrow. This reproduces most layout bugs without needing a phone. Remember that it's an approximation, so still check a real device.

**3. Fixed widths and overflow.** Elements with pixel widths, wide images, or long unbroken text can push the page wider than the screen. Look for horizontal scrolling and use `max-width: 100%` on images.

**4. Viewport units.** `100vh` on mobile includes the area behind the address bar, so content gets cut off. Try `100dvh` instead.

**5. Hover-dependent UI.** Menus or tooltips that need hover don't work on touch screens.

**6. Caching or deployment differences.** If it's broken only on the live site, you may be seeing stale CSS or a build that differs from local. Hard refresh or clear the cache.

**7. Browser differences.** iOS Safari in particular lags on some CSS features. Check caniuse.com.

If none of this helps, remote debugging (Chrome's inspect for Android, Safari's Web Inspector for iOS) lets you see the real errors on the device.

Start top-down: find which filesystem is full, then drill into the biggest directories until you reach the culprit.

**1. Confirm which filesystem is full.** Run `df -h`. This shows usage per mount point. Also run `df -i`, because running out of inodes (millions of tiny files) looks the same as a full disk.

**2. Drill down with `du`.** Start at the root of the full filesystem and check one level deep, sorted by size: `du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h`. The `-x` flag keeps it on one filesystem so it doesn't wander into other mounts. Repeat on the largest directory, descending until the offender stands out.

**3. Use an interactive tool.** `ncdu` is much faster for this. It scans once, then lets you browse and delete from a terminal UI. Install it from your package manager.

**4. Common suspects.**
- `/var/log` (unrotated or runaway logs)
- Docker data in `/var/lib/docker` (old images, volumes, build cache; `docker system df` helps)
- Package caches, old kernels, and journal logs (`journalctl --disk-usage`)
- Database files, backups, and core dumps
- `/tmp` and user home directories

**5. Deleted but still held open.** If `df` says the disk is full but `du` totals are much smaller, a process may be holding a deleted file open. Run `lsof +L1` to find it, then restart that process to release the space.

**6. Prevent a repeat.** Set up log rotation, monitoring and alerts at around 80% usage, and cleanup jobs for caches and temp files.

Default to a hash map unless you have a reason not to. If all you do is insert, delete, and look things up by exact key, a hash map gives you O(1) on average, and a sorted array gives you O(log n) lookups but O(n) inserts because everything has to shift over.

Reach for a sorted array when:

- **You need ordered operations.** Range queries ("everything between 50 and 100"), nearest neighbor, min/max, predecessor/successor, iterating in order. Hash maps are useless here unless you sort first.
- **The data is mostly static.** Build once, query many times. Sorting is a one-time cost, and then binary search is fast and simple.
- **Memory layout matters.** Arrays are contiguous, so they're cache-friendly and have no per-entry overhead. For small or mid-sized collections, a sorted array can actually beat a hash map in practice, even though the big-O says otherwise.
- **You want deterministic behavior.** Hash maps have bad worst cases with poor hash functions, and resizing causes occasional latency spikes.

If you need both fast updates and ordering, neither is ideal. Look at a balanced tree (like C++'s std::map or Java's TreeMap) or a skip list.

Quick rule of thumb: exact lookups on changing data means hash map. Ordering or ranges, or read-only data, means sorted array.

That error means V8 hit its heap size limit and couldn't allocate more. Node caps the old-generation heap by default (depends on your version and how much RAM the machine has, but often somewhere around 2-4 GB), so once your process tries to hold more live objects than that, it dies.

There are really two different situations:

**1. You genuinely need more memory.** Processing a huge file, building a giant array, loading a big dataset all at once. You can raise the limit with `node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js` (value in MB). That's a fine fix if the workload is legitimately large, but better is to stream the data instead of loading it all up front.

**2. You have a leak.** Memory climbs steadily over hours or days and never comes back down. Usual suspects: caches or maps that only ever grow, event listeners added on every request and never removed, timers or closures holding references to big objects, global arrays you keep pushing to.

To tell which one you're in, watch `process.memoryUsage()` over time, or run with `--inspect` and take heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools at two different points. Compare them and see what's growing. Raising the limit on a leak just delays the crash.

Also check whether you're in a container with a low memory limit, since that can kill things earlier.

Yes, for many people it's worth it, though it depends on what you want out of it.

**Why it's worth it:** Go and Rust solve overlapping problems but from opposite philosophies. Go prioritizes simplicity and fast iteration, with a garbage collector handling memory. Rust gives you control over memory without a GC, enforced by the ownership and borrowing system. Learning it will change how you think about lifetimes, aliasing, and data races, and that carries back into your Go code. You'll write more careful concurrent code even in a language that doesn't force you to.

**Where Rust shines over Go:** systems programming, embedded work, WebAssembly, game engines, latency-sensitive services where GC pauses matter, and anywhere you want the compiler to rule out whole categories of bugs. Its type system (enums with data, pattern matching, traits) is also much more expressive.

**The costs:** The learning curve is steeper. Expect a few weeks of fighting the borrow checker. Compile times are longer, and the ecosystem for typical backend work, while strong, is less uniform than Go's batteries-included approach.

**My suggestion:** If you mostly build web services and CLI tools, Go may already be enough, and Rust would be an enrichment rather than a necessity. If you're curious about low-level work or want stronger correctness guarantees, start now. Build a small CLI tool first, and skim the official Rust Book alongside it.

A browser is one of the heaviest everyday programs you run, so the fan kicking in usually means the CPU is working harder than you'd expect. Common causes:

**1. Heavy pages and tabs.** Modern sites run a lot of JavaScript, autoplay video, animations, and ads. Each tab (and often each iframe or extension) runs as its own process, so the load adds up quickly.

**2. Extensions.** Ad blockers, coupon tools, and password managers inject code into every page. A misbehaving one can keep the CPU busy constantly.

**3. Startup work.** When the browser opens, it restores your previous tabs, syncs data, checks for updates, and rebuilds caches. This burst is often what triggers the fan.

**4. Hardware acceleration issues.** If the GPU driver is flaky, video and rendering fall back to the CPU or thrash the GPU. Toggling "use hardware acceleration" in settings can help either way.

**5. Poor cooling.** Dust-clogged vents or old thermal paste make the fan react to loads that wouldn't normally bother it.

**How to diagnose:**
- Open the browser's built-in task manager (Shift+Esc in Chrome, or "about:processes" in Firefox) to see which tab or extension is using CPU.
- Restart with extensions disabled, or try a fresh profile.
- Set the browser to not restore many tabs at launch.
- Update the browser and your graphics drivers.

If the fan spins up even with a blank tab and no extensions, check the system monitor for other processes, and consider cleaning the vents.

## Add pagination to `GET /items` list endpoint

### Summary

This PR adds pagination to the `GET /items` endpoint. Previously, the endpoint returned all matching records in a single response, which caused slow response times and high memory usage as the dataset grew. The endpoint now returns results in pages, with metadata to help clients navigate them.

### Changes

- Added `page` and `page_size` query parameters to `GET /items`
  - `page`: 1-indexed page number (default: `1`)
  - `page_size`: number of items per page (default: `25`, max: `100`)
- Updated the response shape to wrap results with pagination metadata
- Added input validation; invalid values (e.g. `page=0`, `page_size=500`) return `400 Bad Request` with a descriptive error
- Added a stable default sort (`created_at DESC, id DESC`) so pages are deterministic
- Added a database index on `(created_at, id)` to keep paginated queries performant
- Updated API docs and OpenAPI spec
- Added unit and integration tests

### Response format

**Before**
```json
[
  { "id": 1, "name": "Item 1" },
  { "id": 2, "name": "Item 2" }
]
```

**After**
```json
{
  "data": [
    { "id": 1, "name": "Item 1" },
    { "id": 2, "name": "Item 2" }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "page": 1,
    "page_size": 25,
    "total_items": 142,
    "total_pages": 6,
    "has_next": true,
    "has_previous": false
  }
}
```

### Breaking change

The response body changes from a bare array to an object. Existing clients that parse the response as an array will need to read from `data` instead. Requests with no pagination parameters will still succeed, but they return only the first 25 items.

**Migration notes:**
- Update consumers to read `response.data` and, where needed, iterate through pages using `pagination.has_next`
- Internal consumers have been updated in this PR; external consumers should be notified before release

### Testing

- [x] Unit tests for parameter parsing and validation
- [x] Integration tests covering first page, middle page, last page, and out-of-range page (returns empty `data`)
- [x] Tests for default values and the `page_size` cap
- [x] Tests for ordering stability across pages
- [x] Manually verified against a local dataset of ~10k records

### Performance

Offset-based pagination is used for simplicity and to support jumping to arbitrary pages. For very deep pages, offset queries may slow down; if this becomes an issue, we can follow up with cursor-based pagination.

### Rollout

- Run the index migration before deploying (non-blocking, created concurrently)
- Communicate the response format change to API consumers
- No feature flag; the change is effective on deploy

### Checklist

- [x] Tests added and passing
- [x] Documentation updated
- [x] Migration included
- [x] Breaking change documented

This PR adds cursor-based pagination to the list endpoint so clients no longer receive the entire collection in a single response. Previously the endpoint returned every record, which caused slow responses and high memory usage as the dataset grew. It now accepts optional limit and cursor query parameters, with a default page size of 50 and a maximum of 200. Requests that exceed the maximum are clamped rather than rejected.

The response shape has changed to wrap results in an object containing the items along with a next cursor value. When there are no more results, the next cursor is null. Cursors are opaque base64 encoded tokens derived from the sort key and record id, which keeps ordering stable even when new records are inserted between requests. I chose cursor pagination over offset pagination to avoid skipped or duplicated rows under concurrent writes and to keep query performance consistent on deep pages.

The query now orders by created time and id, and I added a composite index on those columns so the lookup stays efficient. The migration is included and is safe to run online. Invalid or malformed cursors return a 400 with a clear error message.

Because the response format changed, this is a breaking change for existing consumers. To ease the transition, I updated the API documentation and the internal client library, and I added a note to the changelog. Callers that do not pass any parameters will still get results, but they will need to read from the new items field and follow the next cursor to retrieve everything.

For testing, I added unit tests for cursor encoding and decoding, and integration tests covering the first page, middle pages, the last page, an empty result set, limit clamping, and invalid cursors. I also verified manually against a local dataset of about a million rows, where response times stayed flat across pages. Reviewers may want to look closely at the cursor logic and the migration, and to confirm that the rollout plan for downstream consumers works for their teams.

Migrating from callbacks to promises is straightforward if you approach it one function at a time. Every asynchronous method that previously accepted a trailing `(err, result)` callback now returns a `Promise` that resolves with `result` or rejects with `err`, so replace nested callback chains with `.then()` and `.catch()`, or better yet, flatten them with `async`/`await` inside a `try`/`catch` block. For example, `lib.readConfig(path, (err, data) => { ... })` becomes `const data = await lib.readConfig(path)`. Errors that were previously passed as the first argument are now thrown as rejections, so make sure every call site either handles them or lets them propagate to a higher-level handler; unhandled rejections can terminate the process in modern Node.js versions. To ease the transition, version 2.x continues to accept an optional callback as the final argument and will invoke it instead of returning a promise, but this behavior is deprecated and will be removed in 3.0. Run your test suite after each converted call, watch for code that relied on callbacks being invoked multiple times (such as event-style APIs), which should be migrated to streams or async iterators rather than promises, and use `util.promisify` for any third-party callback-based functions you need to interoperate with during the migration.

# Git Branch Naming

Short version: `type/ticket-short-description`. Lowercase, hyphens, no spaces.

Examples:

- `feature/PAY-214-refund-button`
- `fix/PAY-231-null-currency-crash`
- `chore/bump-node-20`
- `docs/update-onboarding-readme`

## Why we bother

When you're scanning `git branch -r` at 5pm on a Friday trying to figure out what's safe to delete, a name like `johns-stuff-2` doesn't help anyone. Consistent names also make it easier to filter in the GitHub UI and let CI pick the right pipeline based on the prefix.

## The prefixes

Pick whichever fits best. If you're torn, go with `feature`.

- `feature/` – new behavior or anything users will notice
- `fix/` – bug fixes, including ones found in production
- `hotfix/` – urgent fixes that branch off `main` and ship ahead of the normal release. Tell someone in #eng before you open one.
- `chore/` – dependency bumps, config tweaks, cleanup, anything without a user-facing change
- `docs/` – documentation only
- `test/` – adding or fixing tests with no other code change
- `spike/` – throwaway experiments. These don't get merged, and we delete them after a couple of weeks.

## Ticket numbers

If there's a ticket, put it right after the prefix, in the same case as it appears in Jira (`PAY-214`, not `pay-214`). That's what lets Jira link the branch and PR automatically. If there's no ticket, skip it. Please don't make up a number.

## The description part

- Keep it to roughly 3–5 words.
- Say what the change does, not how you did it. `fix/PAY-231-null-currency-crash` is better than `fix/PAY-231-added-null-check`.
- Hyphens between words, no underscores, no camelCase.
- No your-name-in-the-branch unless it's a spike. The commit history already says who wrote it.

## Things to avoid

- `main`, `master`, `develop`, `release/*` are reserved. Don't create branches with those names or prefixes.
- Don't reuse a branch name after it's been merged. If you need to pick the work back up, start a new branch.
- Avoid very long names. Anything over about 50 characters gets cut off in a lot of tools.
- Slashes beyond the first one (`feature/payments/PAY-214-refund`) cause trouble with some of our scripts. Stick to one.

## Release branches

Release branches are cut by whoever is running the release and are named `release/YYYY-MM-DD`, for example `release/2026-12-02`. You shouldn't need to make these yourself.

## Cleaning up

Turn on "automatically delete head branches" in the repo settings if it isn't already, and delete your local branch after merging. Every few weeks someone will run a sweep of anything stale, so if you want to keep a branch around, say so in the channel.

## Questions

If your situation doesn't fit any of this, ask in #eng-dev. If the same question keeps coming up, we'll add it to this page.

# Git Branch Naming Conventions

**Owner:** Engineering
**Last updated:** 2026-11-18

## Purpose

Consistent branch names make it easier to find work, understand intent at a glance, link changes to tickets, and automate tooling (CI rules, release notes, cleanup scripts). This page describes how our team names git branches.

## Format

```
<type>/<ticket-id>-<short-description>
```

- **type**: the category of work (see below)
- **ticket-id**: the issue tracker ID, e.g. `PROJ-123`. If there is no ticket, omit this segment.
- **short-description**: 2–5 words summarizing the change

### Examples

```
feature/PROJ-482-add-sso-login
bugfix/PROJ-517-fix-null-user-profile
hotfix/PROJ-530-patch-payment-timeout
chore/PROJ-541-upgrade-node-20
docs/update-onboarding-guide
```

## Branch Types

| Type | Use for |
|------|---------|
| `feature` | New functionality or enhancements |
| `bugfix` | Non-urgent fixes for bugs found in development or QA |
| `hotfix` | Urgent fixes branched from production that need immediate release |
| `chore` | Maintenance: dependency bumps, config, tooling, cleanup |
| `refactor` | Code restructuring with no behavior change |
| `docs` | Documentation-only changes |
| `test` | Adding or improving tests |
| `experiment` | Throwaway spikes or prototypes not intended to merge as-is |
| `release` | Release preparation, named `release/vX.Y.Z` |

## Rules

1. **Use lowercase** for everything except the ticket ID (e.g. `PROJ-123`).
2. **Use hyphens** to separate words. No spaces, underscores, or camelCase.
3. **Use a single forward slash** after the type to group branches.
4. **Keep it short.** Aim for under 50 characters total.
5. **Be descriptive.** Prefer `fix-null-user-profile` over `fix-bug` or `stuff`.
6. **Avoid special characters** other than hyphens and the single slash.
7. **Don't include your name** in the branch name; authorship is already tracked by git.
8. **One purpose per branch.** If a branch grows to cover unrelated work, split it up.

## Long-Lived Branches

These branches are protected and should not be used for day-to-day work:

- `main`: always deployable; the source of truth for production
- `develop` (if used): integration branch for upcoming work

Direct pushes are disabled. All changes land through pull requests with at least one approval and passing CI.

## Workflow Tips

- Branch from an up-to-date `main` (or `develop`, if applicable):
  ```
  git checkout main
  git pull
  git checkout -b feature/PROJ-482-add-sso-login
  ```
- Hotfix branches start from `main` and are merged back promptly.
- Rename a branch if the scope changes:
  ```
  git branch -m <new-name>
  ```
- Delete branches after merging. Enable "automatically delete head branches" in the repository settings, and clean up local branches with:
  ```
  git branch -d <branch-name>
  ```

## Pull Request Titles

Match the PR title to the branch intent and include the ticket ID, for example:

```
[PROJ-482] Add SSO login
```

## Anti-Patterns

| Avoid | Why | Better |
|-------|-----|--------|
| `fix` | Too vague | `bugfix/PROJ-517-fix-null-user-profile` |
| `john-work` | Names the person, not the work | `feature/PROJ-482-add-sso-login` |
| `Feature/Add_SSO` | Wrong case and separators | `feature/add-sso-login` |
| `new-branch-final-v2` | Meaningless and unversioned | Describe the actual change |
| `feature/PROJ-482-add-single-sign-on-login-for-enterprise-customers-with-okta` | Too long | `feature/PROJ-482-add-okta-sso` |

## Questions

If a case isn't covered here, ask in the engineering channel and propose an update to this page.

Migrating from callbacks to promises starts with replacing the trailing callback argument in each public function with a returned promise, so that a call like readConfig(path, function (err, data) { ... }) becomes readConfig(path).then(function (data) { ... }).catch(function (err) { ... }) or, in modern code, const data = await readConfig(path) inside a try and catch block. Errors that were previously passed as the first callback argument are now delivered through promise rejection, so any code that checked if (err) should move its handling into a catch handler and should always throw or reject with real Error objects to preserve stack traces. If your callers still depend on the old style, keep a transitional layer by having each function accept an optional callback and, when one is provided, invoke it with the usual (err, result) signature while still returning the promise, which lets consumers upgrade one call site at a time. For code that fans out multiple operations, replace manual counters and nested callbacks with Promise.all for parallel work and sequential await statements for dependent steps, and wrap any remaining third-party callback APIs with util.promisify or a small helper that constructs a new Promise and resolves or rejects inside the original callback. Finally, update your tests to return or await the promises they exercise, add a rejection test for each error path, and document the change in your release notes as a breaking change or a deprecation, depending on whether you retain the callback compatibility layer.

# Design Doc Summary: Move Image Resizing to a Background Worker

## Summary
Image resizing currently runs synchronously in the request path during upload. This proposal moves resizing to an asynchronous background worker so uploads return quickly and resizing load is isolated from the web tier.

## Problem
- **Slow uploads:** Users wait for all variants (thumbnail, medium, large) to be generated before receiving a response. Large images can take several seconds.
- **Resource contention:** Resizing is CPU- and memory-intensive. Spikes in uploads degrade latency for unrelated requests on the same web processes.
- **Poor failure handling:** A resize failure or timeout fails the whole upload, with no retry path.
- **Scaling coupling:** Web capacity must be provisioned for peak resize load rather than request traffic.

## Proposal
1. On upload, the web service validates the file, stores the original in object storage, writes an image record with status `pending`, and enqueues a resize job.
2. The API returns immediately with the image ID and original URL.
3. A pool of background workers consumes jobs, generates the configured variants, writes them to storage, and updates the record to `ready` (or `failed`).
4. Clients display the original or a placeholder until variants are ready, learning of completion via polling or a webhook/event.

## Design Details
- **Queue:** Use the existing job queue infrastructure (or a managed queue such as SQS or Redis-backed) with at-least-once delivery.
- **Idempotency:** Jobs are keyed by image ID and variant spec; output paths are deterministic so retries safely overwrite.
- **Retries:** Exponential backoff with a capped attempt count; exhausted jobs move to a dead-letter queue and mark the image `failed`.
- **Worker isolation:** Dedicated worker pool with memory limits and per-job timeouts. Input dimension and pixel-count limits guard against decompression bombs.
- **Status API:** `GET /images/{id}` exposes `status` and available variant URLs.
- **Fallback URLs:** Variant URLs resolve to the original until the resized version exists, avoiding broken images.

## Rollout Plan
1. Ship the worker and queue behind a feature flag, with the synchronous path unchanged.
2. Enable for internal users, then a small percentage of traffic, comparing latency and failure rates.
3. Ramp to 100% and remove the synchronous code path.
4. Backfill: optionally re-enqueue existing images missing newer variants.

## Risks and Mitigations
- **Eventual consistency in the UI:** Mitigate with placeholders, original-as-fallback, and status polling.
- **Queue backlog during spikes:** Autoscale workers on queue depth; alert on age of oldest job.
- **Silent failures:** Dead-letter queue monitoring, failure-rate alerts, and a manual replay tool.
- **Duplicate processing:** Handled via idempotent jobs.

## Success Metrics
- p95 upload response time reduced significantly (target: under 500 ms).
- Web tier CPU and memory variance during upload spikes decreases.
- Time to variant availability: p95 under 10 seconds.
- Resize failure rate under 0.1% after retries.

## Open Questions
- Polling vs. push notifications for completion?
- Which variants must be ready before an image is considered "published" in user-facing flows?
- Queue technology choice and cost at projected volume?

This proposal moves image resizing out of the synchronous request path and into a dedicated background worker. Today, when a user uploads an image, the web server generates every required size before responding. This ties up request threads, inflates upload latency, and causes timeouts when large files or traffic spikes arrive. Because resizing is CPU and memory intensive, it also forces us to overprovision web servers just to survive peak load.

The proposed design has the upload endpoint store the original file in object storage, record an image entry with a pending status, and enqueue a resize job before returning immediately. A pool of workers consumes jobs from the queue, fetches the original, produces the configured variants, writes them back to storage, and marks the image as ready. Clients receive the original or a placeholder URL while processing is underway, then switch to the resized variants once a status check or push notification confirms completion. Jobs are idempotent and keyed by image ID and variant spec, so retries after a crash or timeout never create duplicates or corrupt output. Failed jobs retry with exponential backoff and land in a dead letter queue after a fixed number of attempts, with alerts on queue depth and failure rate.

The main benefits are faster and more predictable upload responses, isolation of heavy workloads from user-facing traffic, and the ability to scale workers independently based on queue depth. The tradeoffs are added operational complexity, a short window in which variants are unavailable, and the need to update clients to handle the pending state gracefully. We would mitigate these with a feature flag for gradual rollout, a fallback that resizes inline for small images during the migration, and dashboards covering job latency, throughput, and error rates.

Rollout would proceed in three phases. First, deploy the worker and queue alongside the existing inline path and run both in shadow mode to compare output. Second, enable the background path for a small percentage of uploads and monitor latency and failure metrics. Third, ramp to full traffic, remove the inline code, and downsize web server capacity. Success is measured by a significant drop in p95 upload latency, zero increase in missing or broken images, and a reduction in web tier resource usage.

## `--dry-run`

Preview the changes a command would make, without making them.

### Synopsis

```
tells [command] [options] --dry-run
```

### Description

When `--dry-run` is passed, the CLI runs the command normally up to the point where it would modify anything, then prints a description of each change it would have made and exits. No files are written, deleted, moved, or modified, and no network requests that change remote state are sent.

Use `--dry-run` to verify a command before running it for real, especially for operations that are destructive or hard to undo.

### Behavior

- **Read operations still run.** The CLI may read files, inspect configuration, and query remote state so it can compute accurate results.
- **Write operations are skipped.** Each skipped operation is reported instead of executed.
- **Validation still runs.** Invalid arguments, missing files, and permission problems are reported as they would be in a real run.
- **Exit code.** Returns `0` if the command would have succeeded, and a non-zero code if it would have failed.

### Output format

Each line describes one pending change and is prefixed with `[dry-run]`:

```
[dry-run] create   ./config/settings.json
[dry-run] modify   ./src/index.js (+12 -3)
[dry-run] delete   ./build/old-output.js
[dry-run] 3 changes would be made. No changes were applied.
```

If nothing would change:

```
[dry-run] No changes would be made.
```

### Examples

Preview a command:

```
tells sync --dry-run
```

Combine with other options:

```
tells sync --source ./src --target ./dist --dry-run
```

Once the preview looks correct, run the same command without the flag:

```
tells sync --source ./src --target ./dist
```

### Notes

- `--dry-run` is safe to use in scripts and CI to check what a command would do.
- The preview reflects the state at the time it runs. If files or remote resources change before the real run, the actual result may differ.
- If both `--dry-run` and `--force` are provided, `--dry-run` takes precedence and nothing is changed.

# Soft Deletes vs. Hard Deletes

## Overview

When a user or system "deletes" a record, there are two fundamentally different ways to handle it. A **hard delete** permanently removes the data. A **soft delete** marks the data as deleted but leaves it in place.

## Hard Delete

A hard delete physically removes the row (or document, file, etc.) from storage.

```sql
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 42;
```

**Pros**
- Data is truly gone, which simplifies compliance with privacy requests (e.g., GDPR "right to erasure").
- Tables stay smaller, so queries and indexes stay faster.
- Simple mental model: if it's deleted, it doesn't exist.
- No need to remember to filter out deleted records in every query.

**Cons**
- Irreversible without restoring from a backup.
- Can break references from other tables (foreign key violations or orphaned records).
- No built-in audit trail of what was removed or when.

## Soft Delete

A soft delete keeps the record but flags it as deleted, usually with a `deleted_at` timestamp or an `is_deleted` boolean.

```sql
UPDATE users SET deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = 42;
```

Queries must then exclude flagged records:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

**Pros**
- Easily reversible: clearing the flag restores the record.
- Preserves history for auditing, debugging, and analytics.
- Keeps relationships intact, since referenced rows still exist.
- Supports features like "trash" or "recently deleted."

**Cons**
- Easy to forget the `deleted_at IS NULL` filter, which can leak "deleted" data into the UI or reports.
- Tables grow over time, which can hurt performance.
- Unique constraints get tricky (e.g., a deleted user's email still occupies the unique slot).
- Data is not actually erased, which can conflict with privacy and retention requirements.

## Quick Comparison

| Aspect | Hard Delete | Soft Delete |
|---|---|---|
| Data remains in storage | No | Yes |
| Reversible | Only via backup | Yes, by clearing the flag |
| Audit trail | None by default | Preserved |
| Query complexity | Simple | Requires filtering |
| Storage growth | Minimal | Grows over time |
| Privacy/erasure compliance | Straightforward | Requires extra purge process |

## When to Use Which

**Use soft deletes when:**
- Users may want to undo a deletion.
- You need an audit history or must preserve relationships (orders, invoices, comments).
- Accidental deletion would be costly.

**Use hard deletes when:**
- Law or policy requires data to be erased (privacy requests, retention limits).
- The data is temporary or low-value (sessions, caches, tokens).
- Storage or performance is a concern and history isn't needed.

## Best Practices

- **Pick one convention per project** and document it, so everyone filters consistently.
- **Use `deleted_at` timestamps** rather than booleans; they tell you when, not just whether.
- **Centralize filtering** with default scopes, views, or ORM-level query hooks to avoid leaking deleted records.
- **Combine both approaches**: soft delete first, then hard delete after a retention period (e.g., 30 days) via a scheduled purge job.
- **Use partial unique indexes** (e.g., unique on `email` where `deleted_at IS NULL`) to avoid conflicts with deleted records.
- **Handle cascades deliberately**: decide what should happen to child records when a parent is soft deleted.

## Summary

Hard deletes are simple and final. Soft deletes are safe and recoverable but add complexity. Many teams use a hybrid: soft delete for day-to-day safety, followed by a scheduled hard delete to meet storage and compliance needs.

## Security

We take the security of this project seriously and appreciate the efforts of researchers and users who help keep it safe.

### Reporting a Vulnerability

**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues, discussions, or pull requests.**

Instead, report them privately using one of the following methods:

1. **GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting:** Go to the repository's **Security** tab and select **Report a vulnerability**.
2. **Email:** Send details to `security@example.com`. If you'd like to encrypt your message, request our PGP key in your first email.

### What to Include

To help us triage and resolve the issue quickly, please include as much of the following as you can:

- A description of the vulnerability and its potential impact
- The affected version(s), commit hash, or environment
- Step-by-step instructions to reproduce the issue
- Proof-of-concept code, logs, or screenshots, if available
- Any suggested mitigation or fix

### What to Expect

- **Acknowledgment:** We will acknowledge your report within **3 business days**.
- **Assessment:** We will investigate, confirm the issue, and keep you updated on progress at least every **7 days**.
- **Resolution:** We aim to release a fix for confirmed vulnerabilities within **90 days**, depending on severity and complexity.
- **Disclosure:** We will coordinate public disclosure with you once a fix is available. With your permission, we will credit you in the release notes.

### Supported Versions

Security updates are provided for the latest released version. Please upgrade to the most recent release before reporting, if possible.

| Version  | Supported |
| -------- | --------- |
| Latest   | ✅        |
| Older    | ❌        |

### Scope

This policy covers the code in this repository. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies should be reported to the respective maintainers, though we appreciate a heads-up if they affect this project.

### Safe Harbor

If you act in good faith, avoid privacy violations, data destruction, and service disruption, and give us reasonable time to respond before disclosing publicly, we will not pursue legal action against you for your research.

```
# Three tries, no more. Not a magic number, just where the data landed.
#
# When we looked at the failures in the logs, almost everything that was
# going to recover did so on the second attempt. A handful needed a third.
# After that it was basically never, and by then it's not a blip, the
```

I don't think remote work makes junior developers worse, but it does make bad onboarding much more costly. In an office, a lot of learning happens by accident: you overhear a senior debugging something, you catch a code review conversation, you get a quick correction before a bad habit sets in. Remote teams have to replace that on purpose, and many don't. When a junior struggles in a fully remote setup, it's usually because nobody made time to pair with them, not because working from home dulled their skills.

The fix is mostly about structure. Regular pairing sessions, code reviews that explain the why behind comments, and a team culture where asking a question in chat is normal rather than an interruption go a long way. Juniors who get that support often ramp up just as fast, and some do better because written communication leaves a searchable record they can learn from. The ones who get dropped into a ticket queue with no guidance would probably struggle in an office too, just a bit less visibly.

I get the frustration, but a blanket ban feels like a blunt fix for a problem that's mostly about enforcement and infrastructure. Scooters replace short car trips and fill the gap between public transit stops and the final destination, which is exactly what city centres need if they want less congestion and cleaner air. Banning them pushes some of those riders back into cars or taxis, which take up far more space and cause more pollution per trip.

The real issues, like pavement riding, reckless parking, and drunk riding, can be tackled directly. Designated parking bays, geofenced slow zones, speed limits, and proper fines for offenders have worked in plenty of cities. Add protected lanes and you improve things for cyclists and pedestrians as well. Regulate them well rather than throwing out a useful option because of the worst behaviour.

Oh man, this reminds me of a week I lost to a "random" test failure that only showed up in CI, never locally. The symptom was a service occasionally returning stale data after a write. I blamed the cache, then the database replica lag, then a race in our job queue. I added logging everywhere, and of course the bug vanished whenever the logging was verbose enough to change the timing. Classic Heisenbug.

The culprit turned out to be a timezone-dependent date comparison. Our CI runners were in UTC, and my laptop wasn't, so a "last modified" check was off by a few hours for certain timestamps, which made the code think fresh data was older than the cached copy. The fix was a one-line change to normalize everything to UTC before comparing. The lesson I took away: when a bug depends on environment and not on logic, diff the environments first (timezone, locale, env vars, library versions) before you start theorizing about concurrency. It would have saved me about six days.

I'd say no, at least not as a default. The research keeps pointing the same way: when you remove walls, face-to-face interaction doesn't rise the way people expect. It often drops, because people put on headphones and move conversations to chat so they don't disturb anyone. You end up paying for density and getting less collaboration, plus more noise, more distraction, and more sick days.

That said, I don't think the answer is a return to private offices for everyone either. The best setups I've seen give people a mix: quiet zones for focused work, a few small rooms for calls and conversations, and open areas for the times when a team really does need to work side by side. If a company is pushing open-plan mainly to save on square footage, it should be honest about that and not sell it as a culture benefit.

Public libraries might be the most quietly radical institution we have left. Where else can you walk in without spending a dime and get books, movies, music, museum passes, free Wi-Fi, a quiet place to work, tax-filing help, language classes, and a librarian who will happily help you find answers to questions you didn't know how to ask? Most people think of libraries as "a place for books," but that undersells it. Many now lend tools, seeds, telescopes, and even instruments, and with apps like Libby you can borrow e-books and audiobooks from your couch.

What I appreciate most is that libraries are one of the last true "third places," where you don't have to buy anything to belong. Kids, retirees, job seekers, students, and people who just need somewhere warm to sit all share the same space. That kind of open, no-strings community is rare and worth defending. If you haven't visited your local branch in a while, go get a card and poke around. You'll almost certainly find something you didn't know you were paying for with your taxes.

Ljubljana caught me completely off guard. I only added it to a trip as a cheap stopover between Vienna and Zagreb, expecting a forgettable day of ticking off a castle and moving on. Instead I ended up staying three nights. The center is almost entirely closed to cars, so you walk along the river with cafes spilling out onto the water, and everything feels calm in a way capital cities rarely do. I kept waiting for the crowds or the tourist traps to show up, and they never really did.

What sold me was how easy it was to eat well and get out of town. The Saturday market had incredible local cheese and honey, and a short bus ride took me to Lake Bled, which was beautiful even with a bit of drizzle. If you're planning a Central Europe route and treating Ljubljana as filler, I'd honestly give it more time than I did.

I think it depends a lot on the type of business. A four-day week is much easier for an office-based or project-driven shop where output matters more than hours on the clock. It's harder for a small restaurant, retail store, or repair business where customers expect you to be open five or six days. Even then, some owners manage it by staggering shifts so the doors stay open while each person still works four days, though that usually means hiring a bit more help, which isn't easy on thin margins.

That said, the trials I've seen suggest it's more realistic than people assume. Many small businesses reported steady revenue, lower turnover, and fewer sick days, and for a company that can't compete with bigger employers on salary, a shorter week can be a real recruiting edge. The key is to start small: try it for a few months, measure what actually changes, and be willing to roll it back if it doesn't work. It's not a fit for everyone, but dismissing it outright seems like a missed opportunity.

I started bread baking the winter after my dad passed, mostly because I couldn't sleep and the kitchen was the only room that felt useful at 3am. My first loaves were dense enough to prop open a door, but there was something steadying about feeding the starter every day. It didn't care how I was doing, it just needed flour and water and a bit of patience, and somehow that made it easier to show up for.

Almost two years later I still bake every Sunday, and I've started leaving loaves on neighbors' porches. It turned a lonely routine into a small way of staying connected to people. If anyone here is on the fence about trying it, start with a basic no-knead recipe and don't worry about the crumb. The first ugly loaf still tastes great warm with butter.

I think the evidence for homework in primary school is weaker than most people assume. Research consistently finds little to no academic benefit for younger children, while the benefits for older students are clearer. What homework can do at this age is build routines, give parents a window into what's being taught, and encourage habits like reading regularly. Those are real positives, but they don't require worksheets or hours of take-home tasks. Fifteen minutes of reading or a simple practice activity can achieve most of it.

On the other side, the costs are easy to overlook. After a full day at school, young kids need play, rest, and time with family, and homework can turn evenings into a battleground and breed resentment toward learning. It also widens inequality, since children with quiet spaces and engaged parents get far more out of it than those without. My view is that light, purposeful homework, mostly reading and the occasional short task, is a sensible middle ground. Anything beyond that probably costs more than it gives.

I think whiteboard puzzles measure the wrong thing. They mostly test how well someone performs under artificial pressure and how recently they've practiced similar problems, not how they'd actually work on a team. Real engineering involves reading existing code, debugging, talking through tradeoffs, and looking things up. None of that shows up when you're asked to invert a binary tree while a stranger watches you in silence.

That said, I don't think the underlying idea is worthless. Watching someone reason through an unfamiliar problem out loud can reveal how they communicate and handle ambiguity. The problem is that most companies use it as a pass/fail filter rather than a conversation. A collaborative session in a real editor, with a realistic task and the freedom to use docs, gives you most of the same signal with far less noise.

Honestly, a lot of it comes down to design philosophy. Old games were often built for arcades, where the goal was to eat your quarters, so they were intentionally punishing. Even when they moved to home consoles, cartridges had limited space, so developers stretched short games with brutal difficulty, limited lives, and no saves. You couldn't just quicksave or respawn at a checkpoint; if you died, you often went back to the start.

The other factor is that games didn't hold your hand. No tutorials, no objective markers, no hints. You figured out the rules by dying repeatedly, and that trial and error got mistaken for pure difficulty. Add in the fact that many of us were kids with only a few games and a lot of time, and beating one felt like a huge accomplishment. Modern games are arguably just as challenging in places, but they're far better at teaching you and respecting your time.

# A Year of Writing Things Down

Twelve months ago, I bought a cheap black notebook and promised myself I'd write in it every day. I didn't. But I wrote in it often enough that the notebook is now swollen and dog-eared, and I'm a slightly different person for it.

The first month was awkward. I didn't know who I was writing for. My entries read like stiff status reports: *Went to work. Ate lunch. Tired.* It took until February before I stopped performing and started actually talking to the page.

What surprised me most was how much I forget. Reading back through spring, I found whole weeks I had no memory of: a conversation with my sister that shifted how I thought about our family, a small win at work that I'd brushed off at the time. Without the notebook, those moments would have vanished.
