The journal also became a pressure valve. Some nights I wrote three angry pages, closed the cover, and felt the anger loosen its grip. By morning, the problem usually looked smaller, or at least more manageable.

I missed plenty of days. Once I skipped almost three weeks. I learned to stop apologizing to the notebook and just begin again, even if all I managed was a single sentence.

Rereading the whole year, I see patterns I couldn't see while living it: what drains me, what restores me, who I reach for when things get hard.

I'm starting a second notebook next week. This one is green.

# Coming Home Again

I swore I'd never move back. At eighteen, I counted the days until I could leave this town of one stoplight, two diners, and a water tower everyone used as a meeting point. Twelve years and three cities later, I'm writing this from my parents' old kitchen table, two streets from the house where I grew up.

The decision wasn't dramatic. It crept up on me. I was paying too much rent for a apartment where I knew none of my neighbors' names. My weekends had become a blur of errands and screens. Then one visit home, a woman at the grocery store asked about my mother's knee surgery, and I realized she'd known me since I was in diapers. Nobody in the city had ever asked after my family.

Of course, it's not the same place. The old movie theater is a pharmacy now. Half my friends moved away, and the ones who stayed have kids, mortgages, and gray hairs I'm still adjusting to. I've had to get used to being "Linda's kid" again, which is comforting and slightly maddening at once.

But there's a quiet here that I didn't know I'd been missing. I walk in the evenings now. I've learned the names of birds I used to ignore. Last Saturday, I helped a neighbor stack firewood, and we talked for two hours.

I don't know if I'll stay forever. Maybe home is less a place you return to than a place you're finally ready to see. For now, I'm grateful to be here, noticing everything I missed the first time around.

# Coming Home Again

I never planned to move back. When I left at eighteen, I told everyone I was done with this town, with its one stoplight and its Friday-night football obsession. I wanted traffic, noise, anonymity. For eleven years, I got all three.

Then last spring, my mom called to say the roof needed replacing, and somewhere between her explaining the quote and me pretending to understand shingles, I realized I was tired. Not just worn out, but tired of renting, of commuting ninety minutes for a job I could mostly do from my couch, of knowing my neighbors only by the sound of their vacuum cleaners.

So here I am. Three months in, and it's strange how much has stayed the same. The diner still burns the toast. The library still smells like carpet glue and old paper. But some things have shifted, too. My old best friend has two kids now. The hardware store became a coffee shop, which feels like a small betrayal, though I've already ordered a latte there more times than I'd like to admit.

My favorite discovery is this: the creek behind my parents' house, where I used to skip stones, is still there. Last Sunday, I found my old lucky flat rock wedged in the same crack in the bank. I put it in my pocket.

I don't know if I'll stay forever. But for now, it feels like the right kind of slow.

# Where the Tomatoes Learned to Grow

My grandmother's garden was never large, but as a child it felt endless. It sat behind her small house at the end of a gravel road, a rectangle of dark soil framed by chicken wire and held together by stubbornness and old tomato stakes.

She rose before the sun, always. By the time I stumbled out in my pajamas, she was already kneeling between the rows, her straw hat tilted against the early light, humming something tuneless and content. She never wore gloves. "You have to feel what the soil is telling you," she'd say, pressing a thumb into the dirt like a doctor checking a pulse.

I didn't understand then that she was teaching me. I thought I was just helping, which mostly meant carrying the watering can and getting in the way. She let me plant beans, though, and showed me how to poke each seed in with a knuckle's depth of earth. When the first green shoots appeared, I was convinced I had performed a miracle.

Her tomatoes were legendary on our street. Neighbors left empty baskets on her porch in July, and they always came back full. She never took credit. "The plants do the work," she said. "I just keep them company."

She's gone now, and the house belongs to strangers. But last spring I planted my own small plot, pressing seeds in with my knuckle, and I swear I heard her humming.

# 13.1 Miles of Humility

Six months ago, I could barely run two miles without wheezing like an old accordion. Last Sunday, I crossed my first half marathon finish line, and I'm still not sure how it happened.

The training was humbling. I followed a twelve-week plan taped to my fridge, and for the first few weeks I resented every line of it. Tuesday intervals felt like punishment. Long runs on Saturday mornings meant giving up sleeping in, which, if you know me, is a real sacrifice. But somewhere around week six, something shifted. I stopped dreading the runs and started needing them. The quiet streets, the steady rhythm of my feet, the podcasts I'd saved for just the right moment.

Race morning was cold and buzzing with nervous energy. I shuffled into my corral beside a man dressed as a banana, which oddly calmed me down. If he could do this in a costume, so could I.

The first eight miles flew by. Miles nine through eleven were a negotiation between my brain and my legs. Neither of us won. But around mile twelve, a stranger holding a hand-painted sign that read "You're doing great, random person!" made me laugh out loud, and that laugh carried me a surprising distance.

I finished in 2:19. Not fast, but mine.

What I learned is that showing up matters more than talent. Every long run was a small promise I kept to myself, and those promises added up to 13.1 miles.

Now, the real question: when's the next one?

# Finally Showing Up for Myself

For about three years, I told myself I was "fine." Busy, sure. Tired, occasionally. But fine. Then one Tuesday I cried in a grocery store because they were out of my usual oat milk, and I knew fine had stopped being true.

Booking the first appointment took me nearly a month. I opened the website, closed it, and opened it again. I told myself therapy was for people with bigger problems than mine. What I've learned since is that this is exactly what almost everyone tells themselves.

My first session was awkward. I didn't know where to sit, how much to say, or whether I was supposed to start talking or wait for a question. My therapist just smiled and said, "You can begin anywhere." So I began with the oat milk.

We laughed about it, and then we didn't. Somewhere between the joke and the silence that followed, I said something out loud that I hadn't admitted even to myself. I felt lighter walking out, though nothing had been solved.

That's the part I didn't expect. Therapy isn't a quick fix or a lecture. It's an hour where someone is paying attention to you without needing anything back.

I'm only a few weeks in, and some sessions are hard. But I'm learning to notice my feelings before they ambush me in the cereal aisle.

If you've been putting it off, consider this your nudge. You don't need a crisis to deserve support. You can begin anywhere.

**The Night the Cellos Won Me Over**

I used to think classical music was something you endured at weddings. My playlists were wall-to-wall indie rock and whatever the algorithm served me on Tuesday mornings. Then a friend handed me a spare ticket to a chamber orchestra show, and I only said yes because I felt guilty about canceling on her twice already.

The hall was small, with warm wood paneling and a ceiling that seemed to hold its breath. I expected to be bored by the second piece. Instead, somewhere in the middle of a Shostakovich string quartet arrangement, the cellos dropped into a low, grinding phrase that I felt in my sternum before I heard it. The whole room went still. I realized I was gripping the armrest.

What surprised me most was how *physical* it was. On a recording, music is polished and tidy. Live, I could see the bow hair fraying, a violinist's grimace during a hard passage, the cellist closing her eyes as if she were somewhere else entirely. It felt less like a performance and more like watching people think out loud.

I walked out into the cold air barely speaking. My friend just grinned at me.

These days my playlists are a stranger mix: Shostakovich next to Phoebe Bridgers, Arvo Pärt next to Radiohead. I still love guitars and loud choruses, but I've learned to listen for patience, for tension that takes its time. And I never cancel on that friend anymore.

# The Teacher Who Handed Back My Red Pen

In eighth grade, I was convinced I couldn't write. Mrs. Halvorsen changed that, though not in the way I expected.

She taught English in a portable classroom that smelled like dry-erase markers and old carpet. On the first day, she told us she wouldn't be correcting our papers in red. "Red is for alarms," she said. Instead, she wrote in pencil, soft and gray, and her comments were always questions. *What did you actually see here? Why does this matter to you? Where's the sentence you're proud of?*

That last one drove me crazy. I'd turn in an essay and get it back with a small star beside a single line, and nothing else praised. At first I thought it meant the rest was bad. Eventually I understood she was teaching me to hear my own voice, one sentence at a time.

One afternoon I stayed after class, embarrassed, holding a story about my grandfather's garage. I told her it wasn't any good. She read it standing up, then looked at me and said, "You noticed the smell of motor oil and peppermint. Nobody makes that up. Keep noticing."

I've thought about that sentence for twenty years. It's the reason I keep a notebook in my bag and the reason I'm writing this now.

Mrs. Halvorsen retired years ago, but I hope she knows that her pencil is still in my hand every time I write something true.

# The Rusty Schwinn in the Garage

Last month I finally did something I'd been promising myself for years: I dragged my dad's old Schwinn out of the garage and decided to bring it back to life.

It was a sorry sight. The chain had fused into a rusty orange rope, both tires were cracked and flat, and a family of spiders had claimed the frame as a summer home. I almost talked myself out of it right there.

But I started small. A bucket of soapy water and an old toothbrush took care of the grime. Then came the satisfying part: soaking the chain in degreaser and watching the black gunk melt away. Wire-brushing the rust spots revealed paint underneath that was still a lovely deep green, hiding there for decades.

The real challenges came next. The brake cables were seized, so I replaced them, which took three attempts and a lot of muttering. I watched an embarrassing number of videos about adjusting derailleurs. New tires and tubes went on without a fight, which felt like a small miracle after everything else.

What surprised me most was how much I enjoyed the slowness of it. Each evening I'd tackle one little problem, wipe my hands on a rag, and step back to look at the progress. There's something deeply calming about fixing a thing with your own hands.

Yesterday I took it for its first ride. The gears clicked a bit, the seat is still too stiff, and I wobbled at first. But rolling down the street with the autumn leaves crunching under the tires, I felt like I was borrowing a piece of my dad's past.

I think I'll keep it.

The 7:42 and Me

I've been taking the 7:42 train for almost three years now, and I'm still not sure whether I love it or just tolerate it. Probably both.

The platform at that hour has its own cast of characters. There's the man in the green parka who always stands exactly where the third door will open. There's the woman who does her makeup with the precision of a surgeon. Nobody talks. We just nod, sometimes, the way strangers do when they've shared a hundred silent mornings.

Once I'm on board, I grab a window seat if I can. The first twenty minutes are mine. I usually read, though lately I've been staring out the window instead, watching the backs of warehouses and the occasional heron standing in a drainage ditch like it pays rent there. I don't know why that heron makes me so happy. It just does.

Here's my small ritual: I buy a cinnamon roll from the kiosk at the station, and I save half for the ride home. Every single day. Some evenings it's the best part of my day, which is either sweet or a little sad. I haven't decided.

Of course, the train isn't perfect. Delays happen. The heating either roasts you or doesn't work at all. Last Tuesday we sat motionless for forty minutes outside the city, and someone's phone alarm went off twice.

Still, I'd miss it. There's something honest about a commute that gives you time to think, even when you didn't ask for it.

**Why Schools Should Assign Summer Projects**

Every September, teachers face the same frustrating reality: students return having forgotten much of what they learned the previous spring. Researchers call this "summer learning loss," and it affects students of all backgrounds. To fight it, schools should assign meaningful summer projects. Done well, these projects protect academic progress, build important life skills, and give students a chance to explore their own interests.

The strongest argument for summer projects is that they prevent learning loss. Studies have shown that students can lose a month or more of math and reading progress over a long break. Teachers then spend the first weeks of the new year reviewing old material instead of moving forward. A modest project, such as a reading journal or a small science investigation, keeps students' minds active. Even a few hours of work each week can make the transition back to school far smoother.

Summer projects also teach skills that regular homework rarely develops. During the school year, assignments are usually short and tightly directed. A summer project, by contrast, requires students to plan their time, set goals, and finish something on their own. These are habits of independence and responsibility that students will need in college and in their future careers. A student who builds a birdhouse, writes a short story, or interviews a grandparent about local history learns far more than how to follow instructions.

Critics argue that students deserve a real break, and they have a point. Rest matters, and summer should not feel like another school term. However, this concern can be solved through good design rather than by eliminating projects altogether. Assignments should be flexible, offer choices, and require reasonable effort. If students can pick topics they care about, the work feels like enjoyment instead of punishment. Schools can also provide support for families who lack resources, such as library access or loaned materials, so that the projects do not widen inequality.

In conclusion, summer projects offer benefits that outweigh their drawbacks. They reduce learning loss, strengthen independence, and encourage curiosity. With thoughtful planning and a focus on student choice, schools can keep summer relaxing while still making it a time of growth. Students who spend even a little of their break learning will return to class more confident and ready to succeed.

Summer projects should be a required part of every student's school experience. Critics argue that summer is a time for rest, and that assigning schoolwork during vacation robs young people of their freedom. However, a well-designed summer project offers benefits that outweigh these concerns, because it protects learning, builds responsibility, and encourages curiosity.

First, summer projects help prevent the learning loss that happens when students spend ten weeks away from the classroom. Researchers have long observed that students often return in September having forgotten part of what they learned the previous spring. Teachers then spend weeks reviewing old material instead of moving forward. A short project, such as reading a novel and writing a reflection, keeps the mind active and makes the transition back to school much smoother.

Second, summer projects teach responsibility and time management. During the school year, deadlines are set by teachers and reinforced by daily reminders. Over the summer, students must plan their own schedule and decide when to work. This is a skill they will need in college and in any career. A student who can finish a project without constant supervision has learned something no worksheet can teach.

Third, summer projects give students the chance to explore topics that interest them. Unlike regular homework, a project can be flexible. One student might build a birdhouse and research local wildlife, while another might interview grandparents for a family history. Because the work connects to personal interests, it feels less like a chore and more like discovery. This kind of learning often lasts longer than anything memorized for a test.

Opponents say that students need a true break, and they are right that rest matters. Yet a project does not have to consume the whole summer. If it takes only a few hours each week, students still have plenty of time for friends, family, sports, and relaxation. Schools can also keep the workload reasonable by offering choices and clear guidelines.

In conclusion, summer projects strengthen memory, develop independence, and spark curiosity. When they are kept manageable and meaningful, they do not take away from summer. They make it more valuable. Schools should embrace them as a simple and effective way to keep students growing all year long.

Schools should require every student to take part in at least one extracurricular activity. Critics say that students need free time and that forcing participation defeats the purpose of activities meant to be enjoyed. However, the benefits of a mandatory requirement far outweigh these concerns, because it gives all students access to growth that the classroom alone cannot provide.

First, extracurricular activities build skills that academic courses rarely teach well. Teamwork, leadership, time management, and public speaking are learned by doing, whether on a sports field, in a debate club, or backstage at a school play. Employers and colleges consistently value these qualities, yet students who never join anything miss the chance to develop them. A requirement ensures that no student graduates without this practical experience.

Second, a mandatory policy helps students who would otherwise be left out. Shy or uncertain students often avoid clubs because they fear rejection or assume they will not fit in. Others come from families that do not encourage involvement. Without a push, these students may spend their school years isolated. When participation is expected of everyone, joining no longer feels like a risky choice. It becomes normal, and friendships form naturally around shared interests.

Third, structured activities can improve student well-being and focus. Research has linked participation in clubs and sports to stronger school attendance, better grades, and lower rates of risky behavior. Students who spend afternoons in supervised, purposeful activities are less likely to drift into boredom or trouble. Belonging to a group also gives students a sense of identity and pride in their school.

Opponents worry about overburdening students, but a reasonable policy can address this. Schools could require only a few hours per week and offer a wide range of options, from robotics to music to volunteering, so that every student can find something that suits their interests and schedule. Students with jobs or family responsibilities could receive flexible alternatives, such as counting community service or caregiving toward the requirement.

In conclusion, mandatory extracurricular activities prepare students for adult life, include those who might be overlooked, and support healthier, more engaged school communities. With flexibility and choice built in, the requirement would not be a burden but an opportunity. Schools have a duty to educate the whole person, and this policy is a practical way to do so.

**Put the Phone Down: Why Handheld Device Use While Driving Must Be Strictly Banned**

Every day, millions of drivers glance at their phones, believing a quick text or notification check is harmless. It is not. Using a phone while driving is one of the most preventable causes of death on our roads, and stricter laws and stronger personal responsibility are needed to stop it.

First, phones cause a dangerous kind of distraction. Driving requires visual, manual, and cognitive attention at the same time, and texting takes all three away. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, reading or sending a text takes a driver's eyes off the road for about five seconds. At highway speed, that is long enough to travel the length of a football field blind. No message is worth that risk.

Second, some people argue that hands-free calling is a safe alternative. However, research suggests that the problem is not only where our hands are, but where our minds are. Studies from the University of Utah have found that drivers talking on a phone, even hands-free, miss important visual cues and react more slowly, sometimes comparable to drivers who are legally intoxicated. A conversation pulls attention away from the road, no matter how the call is made.

Others claim they are skilled enough to multitask. Yet the human brain does not truly multitask; it switches rapidly between tasks, and each switch costs reaction time. Confidence is not the same as ability, and many crash victims were certain they were in control right up until the moment they were not.

Finally, laws must be strong and enforced. Seat belt laws and drunk driving penalties have saved countless lives because they changed public behavior. Phone laws can do the same when they carry real fines, license penalties, and consistent enforcement. Technology can help too, through "do not disturb while driving" modes that silence notifications automatically.

Ultimately, a text can wait, but a life cannot be restored. Drivers who use phones behind the wheel put themselves, their passengers, and strangers in danger for no good reason. By supporting strict laws and choosing to put the phone away, we can make our roads safer for everyone. The safest call, text, or scroll is the one that happens after the car has stopped.

Car-Free Cities Are a Good Idea

Cars have been a big part of city life for a long time, but I think cities would be better off if they got rid of cars in the downtown areas. Some people think this is crazy, but there are a lot of good reasons why car-free cities make sense.

The first reason is pollution. Cars put out a lot of gas that is bad for the air we breathe. In big cities, the air can get so dirty that people with asthma have trouble going outside. If there were less cars, the air would be cleaner and people would be healthier. Also, cars add to climate change, which is something my science teacher talks about all the time. Getting rid of cars in cities would be one way to help with that.

Another reason is safety. Every year, a lot of people get hurt or killed in car accidents, and many of them are pedestrians or people riding bikes. If cars were not allowed in the middle of the city, there would be way less accidents. Kids could walk to school without their parents worrying so much. 

Car-free cities would also be quieter and nicer to live in. Right now, so much space is used up by roads and parking lots. If that space was turned into parks, bike lanes, and places to hang out, cities would be more fun. Some cities in Europe, like Copenhagen and parts of Oslo, have already done this and people there seem to like it a lot.

Some people say that car-free cities would be hard for people who are disabled or who live far away. This is a fair point, and I think it is important. But cities could still have buses, trains, and special services for people who need them. Public transportation can be really good if the city puts money into it. Also, instead of spending money on fixing roads all the time, cities could use that money for better transportation.

Others say it would hurt businesses because people wouldn't be able to drive to the stores. However, studies have shown that when streets become walking areas, stores often get more customers because more people walk by and see them.

In conclusion, car-free cities would be cleaner, safer, and more enjoyable. It might be hard to change at first, but I think it would be worth it in the long run. Cities should start by closing off some streets and see how it goes.

**The Face on Mars: Natural Landform, Not Alien Monument**

In 1976, NASA's Viking 1 orbiter photographed a region of Mars called Cydonia. One image showed a mesa that, in the shadows, looked remarkably like a human face staring up at the sky. The picture sparked decades of speculation that an ancient alien civilization had carved the formation. Although the idea is exciting, the evidence clearly shows that the Face on Mars is simply a natural landform, shaped by erosion and tricked into resemblance by lighting and human psychology.

The strongest argument against the alien theory comes from better photographs. The original Viking image was low resolution, and shadows created the illusion of eyes, a nose, and a mouth. When the Mars Global Surveyor photographed the site in 1998 and 2001 with far sharper cameras, the "face" looked like an ordinary eroded mesa. Later images from the European Space Agency's Mars Express and NASA's HiRISE camera confirmed this. No symmetrical features, no carved structures, and no signs of artificial construction appeared.

Furthermore, the human brain explains why the illusion seems so convincing. Psychologists call this tendency pareidolia, the habit of seeing familiar patterns, especially faces, in random shapes. People see faces in clouds, in burnt toast, and in the craters of the Moon. Our brains evolved to recognize faces quickly because doing so helped our ancestors survive. Seeing a face in a hill on Mars is therefore not evidence of aliens but a reflection of how our minds work.

Finally, Mars has many similar mesas, formed by wind and water wearing down surrounding rock over millions of years. Similar landforms exist on Earth, such as the buttes of the American Southwest. Scientists have no reason to treat one formation as special when natural processes easily explain it.

Some believers argue that NASA is hiding the truth. However, the later photographs were released publicly, and anyone can view them. A cover-up makes little sense when the evidence is available to the whole world.

In conclusion, the Face on Mars is a fascinating story, but it is not a monument. Improved imaging, the psychology of pareidolia, and basic geology all show that it is a natural hill. The real lesson is that careful science should always outweigh first impressions.

Why Community Service Should Be Required in High School

Community service should be required for all high school students. Some people think it is unfair to make students work for free when they already have homework, sports, and jobs. But I think the benefits are way bigger than the problems, and schools should make it a graduation requirement.

First of all, community service teaches students responsibility. When you have to show up at a food bank or a park cleanup, people are counting on you. You cant just say you dont feel like it. That is a good lesson for real life, because adults have to show up even when they are tired. Students who learn this early will probably be better workers later.

Another reason is that community service helps students see problems they would not notice otherwise. A lot of teenagers only pay attention to their own friends and school. When I helped at a canned food drive in middle school, I was surprised how many families in my own town needed help. Before that I honestly thought hunger was something that happened in other countries. Experiences like that make students more understanding and less selfish.

Also, community service can help students in their future. Colleges and employers like to see that someone has volunteered. Students can also try out different jobs, like working at an animal shelter or a hospital, and figure out what they might want to do later. This is useful because many teens have no idea what career they want.

Some people say that if service is required, then it is not really volunteering and students wont care. This is a fair point, and some students will probably just do the minimum. However, even if someone starts out only doing it for the hours, they still end up helping people. The food bank doesnt care why you showed up, the food still gets sorted. Also, a lot of students might keep going after they finish the requirement because they actually enjoyed it.

In conclusion, requiring community service in high school would help students learn responsibility, understand their community, and prepare for the future. It might be a little inconvenient, but the good it does for both students and the community is worth it. Schools should make it a requirement.

**The Electoral College Does Not Work**

The Electoral College was designed in 1787 as a compromise between electing the president by Congress and electing him by popular vote. More than two centuries later, the system no longer serves the democratic ideals it was meant to protect. The Electoral College does not work because it can override the will of the majority, distorts campaigning, and gives voters unequal power.

First, the system allows a candidate to win the presidency while losing the national popular vote. This has happened five times, including in 2000 and 2016. In a democracy, the person with the most support should win, yet the Electoral College makes it possible for millions more Americans to choose one candidate while another takes office. When the outcome contradicts the majority, public trust in elections suffers.

Second, the system distorts how campaigns are run. Because nearly every state awards all its electoral votes to the statewide winner, candidates focus almost entirely on a handful of "battleground" states. Voters in states like Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Arizona receive constant attention, while voters in safe states such as California, Texas, or Wyoming are largely ignored. A Republican in California or a Democrat in Alabama has little reason to vote, since their ballot will not change the result. A system that tells tens of millions of citizens their votes hardly matter is not working.

Third, the Electoral College gives voters unequal weight. Every state receives at least three electors regardless of population, so a voter in Wyoming has roughly three times the influence of a voter in a large state like California. This violates the principle of "one person, one vote" that American courts have upheld in nearly every other context.

Defenders argue that the system protects small states and forces candidates to build broad coalitions. However, candidates already ignore most small states, since they are not competitive, and a national popular vote would encourage campaigning in every region, including rural areas, because every vote would count equally. Defenders also claim the system provides stability, but the risk of faithless electors and contested results shows it can create chaos instead.

In conclusion, the Electoral College fails the basic test of a democratic institution: it does not reliably reflect the people's choice, it ignores most voters, and it values some votes more than others. Replacing it with a national popular vote would create a fairer system in which every citizen's voice carries equal weight.

The Electoral College was designed as a compromise, but today it fails the basic test of a democratic system: it does not reliably reflect the will of the people. While defenders point to its role in protecting federalism, the system distorts representation, narrows campaigns, and has repeatedly overridden the national popular vote. For these reasons, the Electoral College does not work.

The most serious flaw is that it can award the presidency to the candidate who received fewer votes. This happened in 2000 and again in 2016, when the winners lost the popular vote by hundreds of thousands and nearly three million votes respectively. In a country that values the idea of one person, one vote, this outcome is difficult to defend. A voter in Wyoming has roughly three times the influence in the Electoral College as a voter in California, because every state receives at least three electors regardless of population. Votes are not equal, and that undermines fairness.

The system also warps how campaigns are run. Because nearly every state awards all its electors to the statewide winner, candidates focus almost entirely on a handful of swing states. Millions of voters in reliably red or blue states are ignored, since their votes are unlikely to change the outcome. Candidates spend their time and money in places like Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Arizona, while the concerns of voters elsewhere receive little attention. A system that makes most citizens irrelevant to the campaign is not serving them well.

Supporters argue that the Electoral College forces candidates to build broad coalitions and protects smaller states from being overlooked. Yet the current system does not even achieve this. Small states like Wyoming and Vermont are ignored in practice because they are not competitive, while large swing states receive the most attention. The protection it claims to offer is largely an illusion.

Defenders also say it provides stability and clear results. However, a national popular vote would be just as clear, and a tight race could be settled by a runoff or a recount process applied consistently across the country rather than in a few decisive states.

Ultimately, a democracy should give every citizen an equal voice and let the majority choose its leader. The Electoral College fails at both. It is time to replace it with a system that counts every vote equally.

Distance Learning Is Not as Good as Going to School

Distance learning is when students do their classes online from home instead of going to a real school building. It became really popular during the pandemic and some people think it should stay. I disagree. I think distance learning is worse than regular school for most students because it makes it harder to focus, it hurts social skills, and it isn't fair for everyone.

First of all, its really hard to focus at home. When I did online classes in middle school, I was always distracted. My phone was right next to me, my bed was right there, and sometimes my little brother was being loud. In a classroom the teacher can see if you're not paying attention and make you get back on track. At home nobody does that, so a lot of students just turn off their camera and do something else. Studies and a lot of teachers have said that grades went down during online school, which shows it didn't work that well.

Another problem is that students dont get to talk to other people. School is not just about learning math and english, its also about making friends and learning how to work in a group. When your just looking at a screen all day you miss out on that. I felt kind of lonely and bored during that time, and I know other kids did too. Talking to people through a screen is just not the same as talking in person.

Finally, distance learning isn't fair. Not every family has fast wifi or a good computer. Some students had to share one laptop with their brothers and sisters, or do their work on a phone. Those students fell behind while others who had better stuff did fine. At school everyone has the same desks, books, and teachers, so its more equal.

Some people say distance learning is good because you can sleep in and learn at your own pace. That's true, and it might work for some students who are really responsible. But for most kids it causes more problems than it solves.

In conclusion, distance learning has too many problems. Students get distracted, miss out on friends, and some dont have the right technology. Because of this, I think regular school is the better choice.

**The Wisdom of Many Voices**

Every important decision, from choosing a medical treatment to deciding on a career, carries consequences. In such moments, the easiest path is to trust a single source and move forward. Yet the wiser path is to seek multiple opinions. Consulting several perspectives leads to better decisions, guards against bias, and encourages the open-mindedness that a thoughtful person needs.

First, multiple opinions improve the quality of decisions. No single person knows everything. A doctor may recommend surgery, while a second doctor may suggest a less invasive therapy that achieves the same result. Without the second opinion, the patient would never know the alternative existed. Studies of group judgment also show that averaging many independent estimates often produces answers more accurate than those of most individual experts. When people combine their knowledge, errors tend to cancel out and useful insights add up.

Second, seeking several viewpoints protects us from bias. Every advisor has a background, interests, and blind spots. A salesperson naturally recommends the product that earns a commission, and a friend may tell us only what we want to hear. By comparing answers from different sources, we can notice where they disagree and ask why. This process exposes hidden motives and weak reasoning. It also protects us from our own confirmation bias, the habit of favoring information that supports what we already believe.

Finally, listening to many opinions builds intellectual humility and understanding. When we engage with ideas that challenge our own, we learn to weigh evidence rather than simply react. Even if we end up keeping our original view, we hold it with more confidence because it has survived scrutiny.

Critics argue that too many opinions create confusion and delay. This is a fair concern, as endless consultation can paralyze action. Conflicting advice can also leave a person more uncertain than before. However, the solution is not to avoid additional views but to choose them carefully. Consulting a few reliable, knowledgeable sources is enough to gain the benefits without drowning in noise.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions leads to stronger decisions, reduces bias, and develops a humble and curious mind. In a world full of complex choices, relying on one voice is a risk that few of us should be willing to take.

Working in a team and working alone each have real strengths, but on balance, teamwork is usually the better choice, especially for complex tasks.

The strongest argument for teamwork is the variety of perspectives it brings. One person can only draw on their own experiences and knowledge, while a group combines many. When students work together on a science project, for example, one may be good at research, another at design, and another at presenting. Together they can produce something none of them could manage alone. Teams also catch mistakes more easily, because a fresh pair of eyes often spots a problem the original author has overlooked.

Teamwork also teaches valuable life skills. Communicating clearly, resolving disagreements, and sharing responsibility are abilities that employers and communities value. Working with others forces us to listen, compromise, and consider ideas we might have dismissed. These lessons are difficult to learn in isolation.

However, working alone has clear advantages. A person who works independently can move at their own pace, make decisions quickly, and avoid the frustration of coordinating schedules. Solitary work can also encourage deep concentration and creativity. Many writers, artists, and scientists have produced great work in quiet solitude. In addition, group projects can sometimes be unfair, with one or two members doing most of the work while others contribute little.

Despite these drawbacks, the problems of teamwork can usually be solved through clear roles, good communication, and mutual respect. The limits of working alone are harder to overcome, since no individual can possess every skill or see every flaw in their own thinking.

In the end, the best approach depends on the task. Simple, focused jobs may suit an individual, while large or complicated ones benefit from many minds. Still, because most important achievements in modern life, from building bridges to developing medicines, depend on cooperation, I believe teamwork is generally the better way to work. The ideal worker is someone who can do both: think independently, and collaborate well.

What Makes a Good Friend?

A good friend is someone who makes life feel lighter and more meaningful simply by being present in it. While people may value different qualities in their friends, three traits stand out above the rest: honesty, loyalty, and empathy.

Honesty is the foundation of any real friendship. A good friend tells us the truth, even when it is uncomfortable. Anyone can offer praise and agreement, but it takes care and courage to say, "I think you're making a mistake," or "That wasn't fair to her." Honest friends help us grow because they show us what we might not see ourselves. Importantly, their honesty comes with kindness. They are not trying to hurt us; they are trying to help us.

Loyalty is the second quality that defines a good friend. Friendships are easy when times are good, but true friends reveal themselves during hardship. A loyal friend shows up when we are sick, struggling in school, or dealing with a loss. They keep our secrets, defend us when we are not in the room, and stay with us through awkward phases and disagreements. Loyalty does not mean never arguing; it means choosing to repair the relationship rather than abandon it.

Finally, a good friend is empathetic. Empathy means listening carefully and trying to understand how another person feels, not just waiting for a turn to speak. When we are sad, an empathetic friend does not rush to fix everything or dismiss our feelings. Sometimes they simply sit beside us and listen. They also celebrate our successes without jealousy, which shows that they truly want us to be happy.

In the end, a good friend is not perfect. Good friends make mistakes, forget things, and sometimes disappoint us. What sets them apart is their willingness to be honest, to stay loyal, and to care deeply. Having even one such friend is a gift, and being one is among the best things we can do for others.

**What Makes a Good Friend?**

Friendship is one of the most important things in human life. Everybody needs someone to talk with, to laugh with, and to trust. In my opinion, a good friend is a person who is honest, loyal, and who really listen when you need help.

First of all, honesty is very important in a friendship. A good friend tells you the truth, even when it is not easy to hear. For example, if you are making a mistake, a real friend will say it to you politely instead of just agree with everything. Some people only say nice things because they want to be liked, but this is not real support. I think that honest words, said with kindness, show that the person really cares about you.

Another quality is loyalty. Life is not always easy, and everyone have bad moments. When I moved to a new country, I felt very alone and I did not know anybody. One of my old friends called me every week, only to ask how I was doing. This small thing meant a lot to me. A loyal friend stays with you in difficult times, not only when everything is going well and it is fun to be together.

Finally, a good friend knows how to listen. Many people want to give advice immediately, but sometimes we only need someone who hears us without judging. When a friend gives you his or her full attention, you feel that you are important and that your problems matter. Listening also means remembering the little details, like your birthday or the exam you were worried about.

Of course, nobody is perfect, and good friends make mistakes too. However, they say sorry and try to do better. In conclusion, I believe that a good friend is honest, loyal, and a good listener. If we have even one or two friends like this, we are very lucky, and we should also try to be this kind of person for others.

Yes, school should start later. I know that's what every tired teenager wants to hear, but there's real evidence behind it, and I've felt it myself.

My alarm goes off at 5:50, and for most of the first period I'm not really there. I'm sitting upright, my eyes are open, and I might even be taking notes, but my brain is still back in bed. By second period I start to wake up, and by third I'm finally useful. That's three hours of school where I'm barely learning anything, and I don't think I'm the only one.

The reason isn't laziness. During puberty, teenagers' body clocks shift later, so we get sleepy later at night and wake up later in the morning. Falling asleep at 9:00 p.m. isn't something most of us can just decide to do. Doctors recommend eight to ten hours of sleep for teens, but with early start times, plenty of students get six or less. Several schools that moved their start times back by an hour or so reported better attendance, fewer students falling asleep in class, and even fewer car accidents among teen drivers.

Of course, there are real problems. Later schedules mean sports practices run into the evening, bus routes have to be rearranged, and parents who leave for work early have to figure out what to do with their kids in the morning. Those are legitimate concerns, and I don't want to pretend they're small.

Still, they're logistical problems, and logistics can be solved. Teachers can't fix a sleep-deprived brain. If the goal of school is to help students learn, it makes little sense to hold class during the hours when our minds work worst. Pushing the first bell back an hour or two would cost some convenience, but it would give students something much more valuable: the chance to actually be awake for their education.

Is It Important to Have a Positive Attitude?

I think having a positive attitude is really important, because it affects how you deal with almost everything in life. It doesn't mean you have to be happy all the time, but it does mean trying to look at the good side of things when stuff gets hard.

One reason it matters is that it helps you keep going when something is difficult. For example, when I started learning guitar, my fingers hurt and I sounded terrible. If I had thought "I'm never going to be good at this," I probably would have quit after a week. Instead I told myself that everybody starts out bad, and I kept practicing. Now I can play a few songs. A positive attitude made me stick with it.

Another reason is that it changes how other people treat you. Nobody really wants to hang around someone who complains about everything. On my soccer team, there's a girl who always cheers people on, even when we are losing. Everybody likes her, and she makes the whole team feel better. When someone is positive, it kind of spreads to the people around them.

However, I also think people can take positivity too far. Sometimes bad things happen and it's okay to be sad or upset about it. If you just pretend everything is fine, that can make things worse later. I think a good attitude means being honest about your problems but still believing you can handle them.

Positive thinking also won't fix everything by itself. You still have to work hard and make good choices. If I think positively about a test but never study, I'm still going to fail. Attitude only helps when you also take action.

In conclusion, I believe a positive attitude is important because it helps you push through challenges and makes your relationships better. It's not magic, but it gives you a better chance at doing well. I think everyone should try to have one, even if it's hard sometimes.

The city at night is a different place wearing the same clothes. The streets I cross each morning with a coffee and a deadline become, after dark, something looser and more honest. Shopfronts shuttered, traffic thinned, the whole machinery of purpose winds down, and what remains is the architecture of the place itself, lit by sodium lamps and the occasional blue glow of a late pharmacy.

I walk at night to lose the version of myself that the day requires. In daylight a city asks things of you: keep to the right, mind the crossing, be somewhere by nine. At night those demands soften. No one expects anything of a person walking alone at midnight, and that absence of expectation is a rare kind of freedom. My pace changes. I notice the iron detail on a balcony I have passed a hundred times, the way a church tower catches light from below, the small private theatre of a lit window where someone is washing dishes or reading on a sofa.

Those windows are the strange intimacy of night walking. You glimpse lives without entering them, a borrowed closeness that asks nothing in return. A woman waters a plant. A man paces with a phone to his ear. I do not know them and never will, yet for a moment we share the same hour, and the city feels less like a crowd of strangers than a vast, quiet household where everyone is, in their own room, awake.

There is also fear, and it would be dishonest to leave it out. Night walking is not equally easy for everyone. Many people learn early to carry keys between their fingers, to cross the street, to glance behind them. The freedom I describe is real but unevenly distributed, and part of loving the nocturnal city is wishing it were safer for those who cannot take it for granted. The darkness is not the danger; the danger is what we have failed to fix.

Still, the walk rewards attention. Sounds sharpen: a distant siren, footsteps echoing under a bridge, the hum of a refrigerated truck idling behind a restaurant. The air smells of rain on asphalt, of bread from a bakery already at work for the morning. The city never fully sleeps; it only changes shifts.

By the time I turn toward home, something in me has settled. The day's noise has drained away, and I carry back a little of the night's stillness. Behind me the streets continue, patient and luminous, keeping their own counsel until the light returns.

The Pleasure of Reading Slowly

There is a particular kind of hunger that modern life cultivates in us: the hunger to finish. We count pages remaining, track reading goals, and speak of books as things to be "gotten through." Somewhere along the way, reading became a task with a completion date rather than a place to linger. Yet the deepest pleasure I have found in books arrives only when I stop trying to arrive anywhere.

Reading slowly begins with a small act of permission. I allow myself to stay with a sentence that has caught me, to read it a second time simply because it was beautiful. A well-made sentence has a weight and a rhythm that speed flattens. Taken quickly, it delivers information; taken slowly, it delivers itself, with its hesitations, its choice of one word over a near neighbor, its music. Slowing down turns the reader from a consumer of content into a listener.

There is also the matter of what slowness lets in. When I read quickly, the book stays largely on the page, a series of events I follow from outside. When I read slowly, the book begins to mingle with my own thoughts. A description of a kitchen in winter summons my grandmother's kitchen. A character's small cruelty makes me wince, then wonder about my own. I put the book down, stare out the window, and let the passage settle. These pauses are not interruptions of the reading but part of it, the way silence belongs to music.

Slow reading is also a form of respect. Someone spent years, sometimes decades, arranging these words. To hurry through them is a little like walking through a gallery at a jog, technically present but missing the entire point. Attention is the only real gift a reader can give an author, and it cannot be given in a rush.

Perhaps most surprising is what slowness does for memory. The books I have read slowly are the ones that remain with me, their images and phrases intact years later, while the ones I devoured have blurred into a general impression. Speed gives the sensation of having read; slowness gives the thing itself.

I do not want to turn slowness into another virtue to be measured and achieved. The point is the opposite: to loosen the grip of productivity on one of life's few remaining private pleasures. A book read slowly is an afternoon made larger, a small refusal of the idea that time must always be spent efficiently. In that refusal, I find I am not losing time at all. I am finally inhabiting it.

I used to think that travelling alone was something people did because they had no one to go with. It took a train station in a town whose name I could barely pronounce to change my mind. I had missed a connection, my phone had died, and there was nobody to share the small panic with. So I sat on a bench, bought a bad coffee, and worked out what to do next. It was the first time I realised that I was perfectly capable of being my own company.

Solitary travel strips away the buffer that companionship provides. When you travel with someone, a great deal of energy goes into negotiation: where to eat, how long to linger, whether the museum is worth the afternoon. Alone, those questions vanish. You follow a street because it looks interesting. You leave a gallery after ten minutes or stay for three hours in front of a single painting. The freedom is almost embarrassing at first, like being handed a gift you do not feel entitled to.

But freedom has a flip side, and it arrives around dinner time. Eating alone in a restaurant in a foreign city can feel like being under a spotlight. I remember hovering outside a small place in Lisbon, convinced that everyone inside would pity me. When I finally went in, nobody cared. The waiter was kind, the fish was excellent, and I found that watching the room, really watching it, was a pleasure I would have missed if I had been busy talking. Loneliness, I learned, is often less a fact than a story we tell ourselves about how we look to others.

Travelling alone also makes you more open. Without a companion to turn to, you talk to strangers. A woman on a ferry told me about her late husband's village. A retired teacher in a hostel kitchen taught me how to make a simple lentil soup. These conversations were brief, but they had a clarity that long acquaintance sometimes lacks, because neither of us had anything to prove.

What I value most, though, is what happens afterwards. Coming home, I carry a quieter confidence. I know I can be lost and find my way, be uncomfortable and survive it, be alone and not be diminished. The trips themselves fade into a blur of light and weather, but that knowledge stays. It turns out that the person I was most unfamiliar with, and most glad to meet, was myself.

The town had one stoplight, and for most of my childhood it blinked yellow after nine o'clock, as though even the traffic signal had decided the day was done. I didn't think of this as small. Small is a judgment you make from somewhere else, and I had not yet been anywhere else. To me, the town was simply the world, complete and fully furnished.

What I remember first is how known everything was. The woman at the post office knew my handwriting. The man who ran the hardware store knew which of my uncles had borrowed his ladder and never returned it. If I skipped a Sunday service or scuffed my knee on the playground, the news traveled faster than I could walk home. As a child, I resented this. Privacy seemed like a luxury that other, luckier people enjoyed in cities I had only seen on television. I wanted to be unobserved, to try on versions of myself without an audience that remembered every previous version.

Only later did I understand the other side of that attention. When my father was laid off one winter, casseroles appeared on our porch without a note. When a classmate's house burned, the whole town seemed to show up with blankets and folding tables before the smoke had cleared. Being known meant being watched, yes, but it also meant being held. The same memory that kept me from reinventing myself also meant that no one could quietly disappear.

The town shaped my sense of time, too. Seasons mattered because they dictated everything: planting, the harvest festival, the high school football game under borrowed lights. Boredom was real and enormous, a long August afternoon with nothing in it, but boredom was also where I learned to invent things. I built forts, wrote terrible stories, and walked the gravel roads until I knew every culvert and fencepost. Nobody had scheduled my childhood, so I had to furnish it myself.

I left at eighteen, certain I was escaping. The city offered anonymity, and for a while I loved it. But anonymity has a hollow ring when you are sick with the flu and no one notices your absence. I began to realize that I carried the town with me: in how I greeted strangers, in my habit of lingering over conversations, in my instinct to bring food to a grieving neighbor.

I visit now and then. The stoplight has been replaced, and the hardware store is a coffee shop. Still, someone at the counter recognizes my face and asks about my mother. For a moment I am known again, and I am surprised by how much I have missed it.

# Learning to Fail

For most of my early life, I treated failure as a verdict. A bad grade, a missed shot, a rejected application: each one seemed to say something permanent about who I was. I arranged my choices accordingly, gravitating toward what I already did well and quietly avoiding anything that might expose a gap. It felt like prudence. In truth, it was fear dressed up as good judgment.

The shift came slowly, and not through any grand epiphany. It came through accumulation. I attempted things I was not ready for, and I failed at them, and the world did not end. A presentation fell flat. A project I had poured months into collapsed under its own ambition. A friendship strained because I was too proud to admit I had been wrong. Each failure stung, but the sting had a shorter half-life than I had expected. What lingered was not shame but information.

That was the first real lesson: failure is data before it is judgment. When something breaks, it shows you exactly where the weak joint was. Success often hides this. When things go well, I rarely ask why, and I can attribute to skill what was really luck. Failure forces the question and, if I am honest enough to answer it, supplies a more reliable teacher than praise ever did.

The second lesson was about speed. Learning to fail is largely learning to fail sooner and smaller. The person who tests an idea in a rough draft risks an afternoon; the person who waits for perfection risks years. I began to value the cheap experiment, the unpolished first attempt, the question asked out loud even when it exposed my ignorance. Embarrassment is a small price for avoiding a large mistake.

The third lesson, and the hardest, was separating the act from the self. "I failed" and "I am a failure" are different sentences, though they feel identical at midnight after a bad day. Practicing that distinction, again and again, loosened the grip failure once had on me. I could look at what happened with something closer to curiosity, even a little humor.

I do not enjoy failing, and I suspect no one truly does. But I no longer organize my life around avoiding it. The goal was never to stop falling; it was to stop being afraid of the ground. Having learned that I can get up, I am freer to reach for things that might actually be worth the fall.

Every time I sit down to a meal that includes meat, I am participating in a question I rarely stop to ask: what do I owe the animal on my plate? The discomfort of that question is, I suspect, part of why we avoid it. Eating is habitual, cultural, and pleasurable, and ethics tends to arrive as an unwelcome guest at the table.

The strongest argument against eating meat is also the simplest. Animals can suffer. Pigs, cattle, and chickens experience pain, fear, and something like distress, and modern industrial farming inflicts these on an enormous scale. Billions of animals live in confinement so that meat can be cheap and abundant. If I would be horrified to watch a dog treated this way, I must ask what justifies the difference. Often the honest answer is only convenience, and convenience is a thin defense against suffering.

Yet I hesitate to treat the matter as settled, because the counterarguments are not frivolous. Humans evolved as omnivores, and meat has been central to nearly every culture's food, ritual, and hospitality. For some people, including subsistence farmers, Indigenous communities, and those without access to varied diets, meat is not a luxury but a necessity. An ethics that ignores these realities risks becoming a moral stance available only to the wealthy and well supplied.

There is also a quieter question about what a good animal life looks like. A creature raised on pasture, free from fear and killed swiftly, seems morally different from one that never sees daylight. Some argue that such an animal has been given a life it would otherwise never have had. I find this argument partly persuasive and partly self-serving. It is convenient to conclude that the arrangement benefiting me also benefits the animal, and I notice how rarely this reasoning is applied to anything but food.

Environmental concerns complicate the picture further. Meat production, especially beef, contributes heavily to greenhouse gas emissions, land use, and water consumption. Even someone unmoved by animal suffering may find reason to eat less on behalf of other people and future generations.

Where does this leave me? Not at a clean verdict, but at a sense of proportion. The ethical weight seems to lie less in whether one ever eats meat than in how much, how often, and how thoughtfully. Eating less, choosing higher-welfare sources, and refusing to look away from where food comes from are modest steps, but they are real. Perhaps the deepest obligation is simply attention: to let the question remain uncomfortable, and to let that discomfort change what I do rather than merely what I feel.

**What We Owe Our Neighbours**

The word "neighbour" has grown strange in an age when we can know someone across the ocean better than the person whose wall we share. We nod at them on the stairs, learn their car before their name, and call this peaceful coexistence. But proximity creates a quiet claim on us, and it is worth asking what that claim amounts to.

The first debt is the plainest: consideration. Our lives overlap in small, unavoidable ways, through noise, rubbish, shared hedges, parking, and the smell of cooking drifting through a window. To live well beside others is to remember that our freedom ends somewhere inconvenient to us, usually at the edge of their sleep or peace. Most neighbourly virtue is this unglamorous restraint, practised daily and rarely noticed until it fails.

The second debt is attention. We need not be friends, but we owe each other the courtesy of noticing. An elderly man whose curtains stay drawn for three days, a child who is often alone, a light left burning all night: these are small signals, and only someone nearby can read them. Many a quiet disaster has been averted, or discovered too late, because of whether anyone was paying attention. To be a neighbour is to be, in a modest way, a witness to someone else's life, and sometimes its first responder.

The third debt is harder to define: willingness. When the storm takes down a fence, when a family brings home a new baby, when someone's car won't start in the cold, we owe a readiness to help that is proportionate and unforced. The old parable of the Samaritan endures because it refuses to let neighbourliness be a matter of kinship or tribe. The neighbour is whoever is placed in our path, and the obligation arrives uninvited.

Yet there are limits worth naming. We do not owe our neighbours agreement, intimacy, or the surrender of our privacy. Good neighbourliness respects boundaries as much as it crosses them. The best relationships are often those where help is freely offered and freely declined, without offence on either side.

What, then, do we get in return? Rarely a bargain. More often, a texture of trust that makes a street feel like a place rather than a row of addresses. A borrowed ladder, a watered garden during a holiday, a knock at the door when it matters. These are modest exchanges, but a society is built from them long before it is built from laws.

We owe our neighbours, in the end, what we would hope to find on the other side of the wall: patience, attention, and a door that can be knocked upon.

October 14th, 1917
Somewhere in Flanders

Dearest Mother,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cough has left you before the cold sets in. I think of you often, especially in the evenings when the light fades and the guns grow quiet for a while.

You asked in your last letter what it is like here. I will tell you only the gentler parts, for I know you worry enough. The men in my company are a good lot. Tom Hargreaves, the baker's son, has taught us all to make tea over a candle stub, and we drink it as though it were a feast. Someone found a battered mouth organ, and on Sunday we sang "Abide With Me" so loudly I believe they must have heard us in Blighty.

The rain has not stopped for nine days. The mud is beyond anything you could imagine, and we are forever damp. But I keep your woollen socks dry inside my coat, and they are the finest comfort a man could have. Please thank Aunt Edith for the scarf as well.

Do not trouble yourself on my account. I am well fed, mostly warm, and in good spirits. I carry Father's pocket watch, and it has not failed me yet.

Tell little Annie that I will bring her a proper French doll when I am home. Tell Jim to mind his schoolwork and look after the garden. I dream of the apple tree behind our house, and of your bread cooling on the sill.

Write soon. Your letters are dearer to me than I can say.

Your loving son,
William

October 14th, 1917

Dear Mother,

I got your parcel yesterday, and the socks came at the perfect moment. My old pair gave out last week, and I'd been walking about with a hole the size of a shilling in the left heel. Tom Hartley laughed at me for it. He's stopped laughing now that he's seen the new ones and wants to know if you've any more wool.

I'm well, so don't fret. The rain hasn't let up in nine days, though, and the mud here is something you'd have to see to believe. It gets into everything. My tea tastes of it. Still, we've had hot food most evenings, and the lads keep their spirits up better than you'd think. Someone found a mouth organ, and it's been passed around like a prize.

I can't say where we are or what we're doing. You know that. But I'll tell you I think of the kitchen often, the kettle on the hob and Father's chair by the window. I even miss Sunday sermons, which you'd never have expected from me.

Tell Annie I'm proud of her for the school prize. Tell Father his advice about keeping my feet dry was good, if impossible to follow.

I carry your last letter in my breast pocket, folded small. I've read it so many times the creases are going soft.

Write soon, Mother. Don't worry more than you must.

Your loving son,
Will

Dear Little One,

I don't know your name yet, or the color of your eyes, or whether you'll laugh loudly or quietly. But I'm writing to you anyway, because I want you to know you were wanted long before you arrived.

There are things I hope for you. I hope you grow up curious, asking "why" until the adults around you are tired and delighted at once. I hope you find something you love enough to be bad at for a long time. Skill comes slowly, and joy often comes first.

I hope you learn that kindness is not weakness. The strongest people I've known were gentle with others and honest with themselves. Be both when you can. When you can't, apologize quickly and mean it.

You will make mistakes. Some will be small and embarrassing, and some will feel enormous. Please remember that none of them will make me love you less. Love isn't something you earn by being perfect. It's simply yours.

Take time to look up: at the stars, at the trees, at the people you care about. The world moves fast, and you're allowed to move slowly through it.

Call your friends. Eat dinner at the table sometimes. Tell the truth, even when your voice shakes. Be brave in small ways, because that's how big bravery gets practiced.

And when you're unsure of the way, remember that you always have a home to come back to, and someone waiting there who is on your side.

I can't wait to meet you.

With all my love,
Your Parent

Dear little one,

I don't know your name yet, or whether you'll have my stubborn chin or your other parent's laugh. But I've been thinking about you lately, so I'm writing this down before the days get too busy to remember.

Here's what I want you to know. You don't have to be good at everything. I'm not, and I've survived. I once spent an entire winter trying to learn the guitar and ended up knowing exactly three chords, all of them badly. I still play them sometimes when no one's home. It makes me happy anyway.

Be curious. Ask the question that feels silly, because someone else in the room is wondering the same thing and too scared to say it. Be kind, especially when it costs you something. And when you mess up, which you will, tell the truth early. It's almost always easier than the alternative.

I hope you'll love books, or dirt, or numbers, or music. Honestly, I hope you'll love whatever you love without apologizing for it.

There will be hard days. Some of them will be mine, and you'll see me struggle. That's okay. Families are allowed to be human together.

I'll make you terrible pancakes on Sundays. I'll embarrass you in public. I'll probably cry at your first day of school.

But I'll always, always be on your side.

Until we meet,

Your future parent

Rome, the 14th of April, 1890

My dear Edmund,

I write to you from a small room near the Piazza di Spagna, with the window thrown open and the sound of a flower-seller's cries drifting up from the steps below. I scarcely know where to begin, for Rome has overwhelmed me entirely.

On Monday I walked through the Forum at dusk, when the broken columns turn the colour of honey and the whole place seems to hold its breath. I stood a long while beneath the Arch of Titus and tried to imagine the processions that once passed there. One feels very small, and yet strangely glad of it.

The Colosseum surpasses every engraving I ever studied. I climbed to the upper tier and saw the city spread out beneath a pale sky, domes and bell towers crowding together like old friends. St. Peter's is beyond my powers of description; I can only say that I entered talking and left silent.

The food is simple and excellent. Each evening I dine at a little trattoria where the owner, a stout fellow named Giacomo, insists on correcting my Italian and then pours me wine as compensation for my errors.

The Roman spring is mild, though the guides are relentless and the carriage drivers more so. I have been cheated twice already, and consider it a modest tuition.

I shall move on to Florence in a fortnight, but part of me will linger here. Do write and tell me how the garden fares, and whether your father's health has improved.

Ever your affectionate friend,

Arthur

To the Editor:

I was disheartened to learn that our neighborhood library will close its doors at the end of the year. As the council debates budget lines, I urge residents and decision-makers alike to consider what we stand to lose.

A library is not merely a building full of books. It is where children attend story time and fall in love with reading before they can even sound out words. It is where students without reliable internet complete homework, where job seekers polish résumés and submit applications, and where seniors find company, conversation, and help learning new technology. For many families in our community, it is the only place that offers all of this for free.

Supporters of the closure point to savings, and I understand that budgets are tight. But the true cost of closing a library never appears on a spreadsheet. It shows up in lower literacy, in fewer opportunities for those who can least afford them, and in the quiet erosion of a shared space where neighbors of every age and background meet as equals.

Digital services are often offered as a substitute, yet they depend on devices and connections that not everyone has. They cannot replace a patient librarian, a quiet table, or a child's wide-eyed discovery of a favorite series.

I call on the council to reconsider, to explore alternatives such as shared funding, volunteer partnerships, or reduced hours, and to hold a public hearing before any final vote. I also encourage fellow residents to attend the next council meeting and make their voices heard.

Once a library is gone, it rarely returns. Let us not trade a lasting community asset for a temporary line in the budget.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Neighbor

Dear Daniel,

I've started this letter more times than I can count. Each draft ended up in the bin, either too angry or too polite to be true. So I'll just say it plainly: I miss you.

It's been almost two years since we last spoke properly, and I've replayed that argument at Mum's kitchen table far too often. I said things I didn't mean, and some I did mean but should never have said the way I did. I'm sorry for that. I'm sorry for the way I walked out, and sorrier still that I let the silence stretch on because my pride was easier to live with than an apology.

I've had time to think about what we were really fighting over. It wasn't the money, or the house, or who did more for Mum. It was that we both felt unseen by the one person who had known us longest. I think that's still true for me, and I suspect it is for you.

I'm not asking you to forget what happened, or to agree with my side of it. I'd just like the chance to hear yours, properly this time, without raised voices or old scores.

Last week I drove past the fishing spot at Harlow Pond and nearly pulled over. I thought of Dad's terrible thermos coffee and how we'd laugh until we couldn't hold the rods.

If you're willing, I'd love to meet for coffee, wherever suits you. No agenda. If you're not ready, I understand, and I'll keep the door open.

Your brother,
Tom

Harlan had been up the tower twice already that night, once to trim the wick and once because the wind had changed and he didn't like the sound of it. The third time he went out onto the gallery for no reason at all, just to stand there with his tea going cold, and that was when he saw the shape below the west rocks, pale against the black and not moving the way kelp moves.

He took the lamp. He took the boathook too, though he couldn't have said why, and he went down the stairs faster than his knees liked.

The path to the west rocks was nothing but a suggestion, a line of worn places between the gorse and the drop. Rain came at him sideways. Twice he put a foot wrong and caught himself on his hand, and the second time he swore loudly, because there was nobody to hear it and he'd always thought that was one of the better things about the job.

The man lay wedged in a crack between two slabs, one arm over his head like someone shielding himself from a blow. He wore a good coat, far too good for these waters, and one shoe. His hair was plastered flat across his forehead. When Harlan crouched and held the lamp close, the man's eyes were open, and they moved to the light and then to Harlan's face with an expression of mild, tired annoyance.

"You took your time," the stranger said.

Harlan said nothing. Thirty-one years on the rock and he'd pulled out drowned sailors, a dead seal once, and a crate of lemons that had washed up whole. Nobody had ever complained about the service.

"Can you stand?" he asked finally.

"I haven't tried," said the man. "I was waiting to see who came."

The dryers at Suds & Duds had been tumbling the same pair of jeans for forty minutes when Marguerite realized they weren't hers.

She hadn't brought jeans. She'd brought sheets, a week of work shirts, and the gray wool blanket she'd been meaning to wash since her mother's funeral. But there they were, behind the round glass window of Dryer 6, flipping over and over in the fluorescent hum, a zipper clicking against the drum like a slow metronome.

It was 3:07 a.m. The wall clock said so, and the wall clock had been right about everything else tonight, including how long she'd been sitting here pretending to read a four-year-old issue of *Good Housekeeping*.

She looked around. The place was empty except for her and the attendant's chair, which was also empty, its vinyl seat split and patched with duct tape. Outside, the streetlight on Fennimore Avenue buzzed and flickered orange against the wet pavement. A bus went by with no one in it, lit up like an aquarium.

Marguerite stood, her knees cracking, and walked to Dryer 6. She pressed her palm to the glass. Warm. She watched the jeans tumble, and in the left back pocket, each time it came around, she caught a flash of something white. Paper. A receipt, maybe. Or a note.

The machine had eleven minutes left.

She told herself she wasn't going to open it. She told herself that the polite thing, the *normal* thing, was to wait until the cycle ended, fold the jeans, and leave them on the counter for whoever came back.

Then the dryer door clicked open on its own, the drum slowed, and the jeans fell still, and the white thing in the pocket was not a receipt.

It was an envelope, and it had her name on it.

Walter Brandt had been retired for eleven years, and in that time he had mastered exactly three things: crossword puzzles, the slow decline of his tomato plants, and the art of not answering the door.

So when the knocking started at half past seven on a gray Tuesday morning, he stayed in his chair and let his coffee go cold.

The knocking did not stop. It was patient, almost polite, the knock of someone who had already waited a long time and could wait longer.

"I know you're in there, Detective," said a woman's voice through the wood. "Your porch light's been on since Sunday, and you're the only man in Harlow Street who still believes in saving daylight."

Walter sighed, pushed himself up on knees that complained about it, and shuffled to the door. Through the frosted glass he could make out a small figure in a green raincoat, clutching something flat against her chest.

He opened the door three inches. "I'm not a detective anymore."
