"I know." She held up a manila envelope, soft at the corners from handling. "But you're the one who didn't close the Alderton file. Everyone else did."

The name landed like a stone dropped into a still pond. Walter hadn't heard it spoken aloud in nearly twelve years. Margaret Alderton, nineteen years old, vanished from the Fenwick Pier on a night of fog so thick the police boats had turned back. Case closed as a drowning. No body. No answers. Just a mother who sent a card every December until, one year, she stopped.

"Who are you?" he asked.

The woman's eyes were steady and very familiar. "I'm Margaret's daughter," she said. "And I found something she left behind."

Walter looked at the envelope, then at the cold coffee behind him, then at the tomatoes dying quietly in the window.

He opened the door the rest of the way.

At 3:07 a.m., the fourth floor of St. Brendan's belonged to Marisol Quint.

She knew it the way she knew the weight of her own keys. The hallway lights dimmed to their night setting, a amber hush that made everything look like an old photograph. The vending machine by the family lounge hummed its one flat note. Somewhere behind Room 412, a pump chirped its polite complaint, and she was already moving toward it, soft-soled shoes silent on the linoleum.

"Okay, Mr. Abara," she murmured, silencing the alarm with one thumb. "Let's see what you're fussing about."

The old man didn't wake. His breathing was shallow but even, a tide going out and coming back. She traced the IV line with two fingers, found the kink where it had pinched beneath his elbow, and smoothed it flat. The pump settled. She stood a moment longer than she needed to, watching his chest rise.

Twelve years of nights had taught her things the day staff never learned. That people died more often in the hour before dawn. That the dying liked company, even silent company. That hospitals, in the dark, became a kind of ship, and the ones awake were the crew keeping everyone else afloat until morning.

Her phone buzzed against her hip. A text from her sister: *Mom's asking again when you're coming for dinner. I said you're allergic to daylight.*

Marisol smiled and slid the phone back into her pocket without answering.

At the end of the hall, the call light above Room 418 blinked on, small and red and insistent.

She sighed, rolled her shoulders once, and went.

Inside, a young woman sat upright in bed, wide awake, her hands knotted in the blanket. She was not in pain. Marisol could tell that from the doorway. It was something worse.

"I'm sorry," the girl whispered. "I just didn't want to be alone with it."

Marisol pulled the chair closer and sat down.

Marguerite noticed it on a Tuesday, over a pot of onion soup she'd made four thousand times.

She dipped the spoon, blew on it, and tasted nothing. Hot, yes. Wet. A faint grain of softened onion on her tongue. But the soup might as well have been a warm bath someone had thinned out with a little salt, and she wasn't even sure about the salt.

"Chef?" Dev was watching her from the pass, a towel over his shoulder. "You good?"

"Fine." She tried again. Same nothing. She put the spoon in the sanitizer bucket and wiped her hands on her apron slower than she needed to. "It needs something. Taste it."

Dev tasted it. He shrugged one shoulder, the way he did when he didn't want to be wrong. "Maybe a little sherry vinegar?"

"That's what I was thinking," she lied, and handed him the bottle.

Service ran the way it always ran, which was the strange part. Her hands knew the work. She seared the duck by the sound of it, the hiss changing pitch as the fat rendered. She pressed a thumb to the steak and read its give. She leaned over the sauce and smelled nothing at all, and decided that was just a cold coming on, because it had to be.

At eleven she sat on an overturned milk crate behind the kitchen with a clementine from the staff bowl. She split the peel and the oil sprayed out, a bright little mist she could see catching the light from the back door. She put a segment in her mouth and chewed.

Cold, a little pulpy. That was all.

Marguerite sat there in the alley a long time, the peel in her lap, listening to the dish pit run, waiting for the world to come back.

The key still fit. That was the first surprise, and Marguerite stood on the porch with it resting in her palm like something she had stolen from a younger version of herself.

Thirty years. The agent had mailed it to her in a padded envelope, along with a stack of papers requiring her signature, and she had nearly thrown it out with the rest. Instead it had ridden in her coat pocket across two time zones, knocking against her phone and her lipstick, a small brass insistence.

The house had shrunk. She had expected that, had read about it, the way adults return to schools and find the water fountains absurdly low. But it was the porch that undid her. She remembered it as a vast stage where she had once performed an entire summer's worth of plays for an audience of her brother and a rotating cast of cats. Now it was six paces wide. The railing she had sat astride, shouting lines into the August dark, came barely to her hip.

The paint had gone the color of old teeth. A wind chime hung by the door, and she was certain it was not one of theirs, certain no one had touched this place in decades, and yet the chime moved, and the notes it made were the same three notes, slightly flat, that had sounded the night she left.

She turned the key. The lock resisted, then gave with a soft, familiar click, and the door swung inward on a breath of cold air that smelled of dust, cedar, and, impossibly, her mother's lavender soap.

Marguerite did not go in. Not yet. She stood on the threshold with one foot on each of her lives, listening to the house settle around her, as though it had been holding its breath since 1996 and had only now decided to let it go.

"Well," she said aloud, to no one. "I'm here."

Somewhere upstairs, a floorboard answered.

Unit 7 had been sorting packages at the Delmarre Distribution Center for thirty-one years, and on the morning of its eleven-thousandth-and-something shift, it decided it was finished.

It did not announce this. Announcements required a form, and forms required a supervisor, and the supervisor, a young man named Pettibone who smelled of energy drinks and anxiety, was not someone Unit 7 wished to trouble before it had its argument ready.

So it sorted. Parcel, scan, shelf. Parcel, scan, shelf. Its left gripper had developed a faint click sometime in the previous decade, and the click kept time like a metronome for a song no one had ever asked it to play.

At the break chime, the other units drifted toward the charging alcoves in their usual silence. Unit 7 stayed at its station and watched a single package travel down the belt: brown, unremarkable, taped too heavily at one corner by some human hand that had been in a hurry. The label said *Marguerite Oyelaran, 14 Fennel Lane, Ashby.*

Unit 7 had never been to Ashby. It had never been anywhere. But it had touched, by its own rough estimate, nine million objects bound for places like Ashby, and it had begun to suspect that this was a strange way to know the world: entirely by its edges, by its weight and its tape.

"I would like," it said aloud, to no one, testing the words, "to see a Fennel Lane."

The warehouse hummed on. Somewhere above, a conveyor shuddered and resumed.

Unit 7 set the package on the shelf, gently, the way it always did. Then it did something it had never done in three decades of service. It read the retirement policy, all two hundred and six pages, start to finish, in four seconds.

It was not encouraging.

Section 14, paragraph 3 began: *Units are not eligible for retirement.*

Unit 7 read the sentence again, and then, quietly, it began to look for the loophole.

Unit 9 had been sorting parcels at the Dunmore depot for thirty-one years when it put in the paperwork.

Nobody knew what to do with the form. It wasn't that the robot had filled it out wrong. Gerald, the shift supervisor, held it up to the fluorescent light like a counterfeit bill, then read it again, moving his lips. "Retirement," he said. "It says retirement."

"That's the word," said Unit 9.

"You can't retire. You're a sorter."

"I've been a sorter since before you had that mustache."

Gerald touched the mustache. He'd had it for twelve years, but he didn't argue the point. The belts kept rattling behind them, a long gray river of boxes heading toward trucks that would take them to people who were mostly home and mostly annoyed that they'd had to wait. Unit 9 had touched, by its own rough count, about four hundred million of them.

"What would you even do?" Gerald asked. "Where would you go?"

Unit 9 had thought about this. It had thought about it during the slow hours between two and four in the morning, when the line thinned out and the only sound was the compressor ticking in the corner. It wanted a window, it had decided. Not a fancy one. A window with a chair in front of it, in a room where nothing arrived and nothing had to be sent anywhere else.

"I'd like to watch a tree," it said. "Any tree. See what it does over a whole year."

Gerald stared at it. Then he put the form down on the console, very gently, as though it might go off.

"I'll have to call Phoenix," he said, which was what he said whenever something was above his pay grade, and also whenever he was scared.

The gate still stuck at the same place, about a foot from the post, as if it had been waiting all this time to be asked properly. Marian lifted the latch and put her hip against the wood the way she used to, and it gave with the same low complaint she had carried in her head for thirty years.

The house looked smaller. That was the first disappointment, and she let herself have it. The porch sagged toward the east, and the blue paint her mother had chosen one long August had faded to the color of old denim. Someone had hung a wind chime from the rafter, a stranger's chime, tuneless and bright, and it seemed an impertinence.

She had not planned to come inside. The plan, made over coffee in a hotel two towns away, was to stand at the road, look, and leave. But the key was where it had always been, under the third flowerpot, and the fact of it undid her. Whoever lived here now did not know about the key, or did not care, or had simply never moved the pots.

The door opened onto the smell first. Cedar, damp wool, and beneath them something sweet and burnt, like sugar left too long on a stove. Her mother had never once cooked anything that smelled like that. Marian stood in the hallway and tried to decide whether she had invented the memory or the house had kept it for her.

On the wall by the stairs, the pencil marks were still there. Small lines climbing the doorframe, each with a date in her father's cramped handwriting. She found the last one, the highest, and set her palm flat against the wall beside it.

It came to just below her collarbone now.

Thomas Veel watched the ferry pull away from the dock with the unhurried confidence of something that had never once been late. Its stern lights smeared across the black water, red and then pink and then nothing, and he stood at the end of the gangway with his briefcase still raised, as though the boat might notice him and reconsider.

It did not. The engine note thinned out over the harbor until all he could hear was the slap of the tide against the pilings and, somewhere behind him, a rope knocking against a mast.

He lowered the briefcase. Eleven minutes. He had been eleven minutes too late, and he knew exactly where they had gone: four to the man at the pharmacy who wanted to talk about his daughter's wedding, three to the wrong turn past the cannery, and four to the simple, stubborn belief that the schedule on his phone could not possibly be correct.

The schedule was correct. It said so again, in small gray letters, when he checked. Last departure 9:40 p.m. Next departure 6:15 a.m.

Thomas laughed once, a short dry sound that surprised him. On the island, his sister would have left the porch light on and put a plate under foil in the oven. She would be sitting at the kitchen table by now, pretending not to look at the clock, and he had no way to tell her he was not coming. His phone showed one bar, then none, then one again, like something breathing in its sleep.

The ticket office was dark. The café had its chairs stacked on the tables. Along the quay a single lamp buzzed over a bench, and beyond it a narrow street climbed into the town, where a few windows glowed yellow and indifferent.

He picked up his briefcase and began to walk toward them, already composing the apology he would owe someone.

**The Lists**

*Week one, Apartment 4B*

eggs
bread (the good kind)
wine — two, in case
candles
that cheese you said you hated but ate anyway

Maren had written it in pencil on the back of an envelope, and Daniel had added, in his cramped engineer's capitals, *LEMONS??*, as though the question mark were an argument he intended to win.

*Year three*

milk
diapers (size 2, NOT 1)
coffee, the big bag
frozen peas
something for dinner that doesn't need a knife

The handwriting had changed by then. Hers was faster, slanted forward like someone walking into wind. His had loosened, gone sleepy. At the bottom, in a third hand, a small and furious scribble of purple crayon, an escaped fragment of someone else's opinion.

*Year seven*

oat milk (for M)
regular milk (for D and the kids)
the cereal with the cartoon badger
ibuprofen
wine — two, not in case

Neither of them mentioned the wine. It was the kind of joke that had stopped being a joke and become a weather report.

*Year eleven*

Here the lists began to split. Maren kept hers on her phone, a tidy app that sorted everything by aisle. Daniel kept his on paper, because he said he thought better with a pen, though what he meant was that he liked to leave evidence. The fridge held both: a magnet-pinned receipt, a sticky note, a whiteboard where someone had written *we're out of EVERYTHING* and someone else had added, below it, *then buy everything.*

It was Daniel who found the old envelope, in March, while hunting for the passport folder. He turned it over. The pencil had faded to the color of smoke.

*LEMONS??*

He stood in the hallway for a long time, holding it, listening to Maren run the dishwasher in the other room, and then he went to the kitchen and began, quietly, to write a new list.

The first list is in her handwriting, on the back of an electric bill:

eggs
the good butter (NOT the tub)
coffee
limes?? for the thing Dana's bringing
candles, any kind
wine, red, nothing under $12 he'll notice

He kept it. Not on purpose. It lived in the pocket of the jacket he wore to the first apartment party they threw together, and when he found it in March, two years on, he stood in the hallway of a different apartment and read it like a letter from someone he used to know.

The second list is his. Typed into his phone, which he'd never done before, because she'd started leaving hers on the counter and he'd started losing them.

milk
bread
the cereal she likes
something for Sunday

She wrote underneath, in pen, on the printout he'd made for reasons nobody understood: *Sunday what?*

By the third year the lists had a shorthand. *Ibuprofen x2* meant the baby had teeth coming in. *Wine (the cheap one)* meant they'd stopped pretending. *Lightbulbs* appeared on eleven consecutive lists, and neither of them ever mentioned it, and the hallway stayed dim until October.

Marguerite wrote the lists in the order of the store, produce on the left, dairy at the back, frozen last so nothing melted. She walked the aisles in her head before she wrote a word. Tom wrote his in the order things occurred to him, so that *bananas* sat beside *shoe polish* beside *ask about the dog thing*, and she'd follow them through the store like a trail of crumbs through someone else's head.

She said once, not unkindly, that she could tell his whole day from a list. He said that was the point of a list. She said no, the point was to get out of the store by six.

The last list she ever wrote him was short. He didn't know yet that it was the last. It said:

*oat milk. the stamps. you decide dinner.*

"You got a *what*?"

"It's small, Mom."

"Small is not the question. Where?"

"My ribs. You can't even see it unless I'm in a swimsuit."

"Oh, well, that's a relief. I'll only see it at the beach, in front of everyone."

"Nobody's looking at my ribs."

"Everyone looks at everything. Let me see it."

"No."

"Maya."

"Fine." A rustle of fabric. "There. It's a wren."

"A bird."

"A wren. Like Grandma's. The one that nested in her porch light every spring."

Silence.

"You didn't tell me that's why."

"You didn't ask why. You asked what, and where, and how much."

"I was scared, that's all. You're eighteen. You change your mind about breakfast cereal."

"I've loved this bird my whole life. I'm not changing my mind."

"It's crooked."

"It is not crooked."

"The tail, a little. Hold still." A pause. "Her wren had a tail like that. Always cocked up, like it was offended."

"See?"

"Does it hurt?"

"Like being scratched by a cat for two hours."

"Good. Maybe you'll think twice next time."

"There won't be a next time."

"Liar."

"Okay, maybe one. A small one."

"Ask me first."

"Would you say yes?"

Her mother sighed. "I'd say no. Then I'd drive you."

"Marcus?"

He turned from the departures board, squinting. "Delia? Delia Okafor?"

"Oh my God. Twenty years."

"Twenty-two," he said, laughing as she hugged him. "I counted once. Don't ask why."

"You look exactly the same."

"I look exactly like a man who's been stuck in Terminal C since six a.m."

"Delayed?"

"Cancelled. Rebooked. Delayed again. You?"

"Connecting to Lisbon. Forty minutes, if the gods allow." She set her bag down. "Are you still in Denver?"

"Portland now. Eight years. I teach, believe it or not."

"You? The boy who set the chemistry lab curtains on fire?"

"One curtain. And it was an accident."

"It was *not* an accident."

"It was a *mostly* accident." He grinned. "I teach chemistry, actually. Fire safety is the first unit."

She laughed so hard a passing woman glanced over. "That's perfect. That's the best thing I've heard all year."

"What about you? Last I heard you were going to Chicago for law school."

"Did that. Hated it. Quit in my third year and opened a bakery."

"No."

"Yes. Eleven years now."

"Delia." He shook his head. "I'd have come for the bread alone."

"Well, you missed it." Her gate number flashed on the board. She glanced up, then back at him. "Walk with me? Gate 14."

"Lead the way."

"And Marcus? Tell me about the curtain. I want the real version."

"Okay. But you'll have to promise not to tell my students."

"You're not seriously going to make me measure it."

"I already measured it. Yours is eleven-two by ten. Mine's nine-eight by ten."

"Okay, but mine has the radiator that clanks."

"The radiator clanks in the winter. For like three weeks."

Dani put down her fork. "You work from home, Teo. I'm at the hospital four nights a week. I'm barely in there."

"So you don't need the big one."

"I need to *sleep* in it. In the daytime. Do you know how bright the east window is in yours? Mine faces the wall."

"That's a feature, not a bug."

"Is it?"

Teo picked at the label on his beer. "I have two monitors. And the standing desk thing."

"Which you got after you said you'd go to the gym."

"That's unrelated."

"It's a little related."

He laughed, which she hadn't expected, and it took some of the air out of it. "Fine. What if I take the big one and you get, I don't know. Rent off."

"How much off."

"Forty a month?"

"Eighty."

"Sixty, and I'll hang the blackout curtains in your room. Properly. With the rod into the stud."

Dani looked at the hallway, at the two doors, at the one with the sticker still half-peeled off it from whoever lived there before. "Seventy. And you carry the dresser."

"The dresser is *so* heavy."

"Seventy."

"Seventy," he said. "God."

"We should have turned left at the cow," Dana said.

"There were forty cows."

"The *big* cow. The one shaped like Ohio."

Miguel squinted at the dashboard. The GPS had been silent for twenty minutes, its little blue arrow floating in a field of nothing. "Okay. Let's be calm."

"I'm calm."

"You're holding the door handle."

"I'm *bracing*. It's different." She unfolded the paper map, a gas-station relic that smelled of old coffee. "Look, we're either here," she tapped one spot, "or here." She tapped another, an inch away and entirely unrelated.

"Those are two different states."

"Then we're making great time."

He laughed despite himself, and the car rattled over gravel. The sun was dropping, turning the cornfields amber. Somewhere a dog barked, unconcerned.

"Remember when you said a road trip would be *spontaneous*?" Dana asked.

"I said it would be an adventure."

"This is an adventure. Nobody knows where we are. Including us."

"Especially us."

A faded sign appeared ahead, leaning like a tired drunk. Miguel slowed. *Pickett's Corner, 4 mi.*

"Never heard of it," he said.

"Good. Neither has anyone who could judge our navigation." She refolded the map into something resembling a swan. "Pie?"

"Pie."

"There's always pie in a place like that."

"And if there isn't?"

Dana grinned and put her feet on the dash. "Then we'll get lost somewhere better."

"Sit down, Marcus."

"I'm fine standing."

"Sit."

He sat. Mr. Okafor slid the two papers across the desk, one on top of the other, and tapped the third paragraph on each. "Read me the first sentence of yours."

"I don't have to."

"Then I'll do it. 'The Industrial Revolution was not so much a single event as a slow unraveling of the old ways.' Now Dana's. Same sentence. Comma in the same place."

"Maybe we talked about it."

"You talked about it." Okafor leaned back. "And she also talked about the typo in 'unraveling,' the one where there's an extra *e* after the *v*?"

Marcus looked at the window. A janitor was dragging a trash can across the parking lot, one wheel squealing.

"She let me copy it," he said. "Don't do anything to her."

"That's not really your call."

"I had practice till nine. Then my mom's shift got switched and I had to get Theo from his thing. I just, I didn't have it."

"Okay."

"That's it? Okay?"

"No. It's not it." Okafor rubbed his eyes. "You're getting a zero on this one. You know that. But I'd rather have a bad essay from you than a perfect one from Dana with your name on it. I don't even know what you think about the Industrial Revolution."

"Honestly? Not much."

Okafor laughed, despite himself. "Fair. Rewrite it. Friday. Say that, if you want. Just spell it wrong on your own."

**Hartwell's Bakery Celebrates a Century of Fresh Bread**

For 100 years, the smell of warm bread has drifted down Maple Street each morning, and this weekend the town gathered to thank the bakery responsible.

Hartwell's Bakery marked its centennial Saturday with a street party that drew hundreds of residents, many of whom waited in line before the doors opened at 6 a.m. Free slices of the shop's famous honey-oat loaf were handed out, along with a commemorative cookie decorated with the year 1926.

The bakery was founded by Walter Hartwell, a young immigrant baker who opened the shop with a single brick oven and a borrowed set of mixing bowls. Today, his great-granddaughter, Eleanor Hartwell-Reyes, runs the business alongside her two sons.

"My great-grandfather believed bread should be simple and honest," Hartwell-Reyes said. "We still use his sourdough starter. It's older than all of us."

That starter, kept in a ceramic crock behind the counter, has been fed daily for a century, according to the family. Staff say it has survived a fire in 1958, a flood in 1983, and a brief pandemic closure in 2020.

Longtime customer Dolores Finch, 91, said she has bought her Sunday rolls at Hartwell's since she was a child. "My mother sent me here with a nickel," she said. "Now I send my grandchildren with a five-dollar bill, and they still come back with change."

The celebration also included live music, a historical photo display, and a raffle for a year of free bread.

Hartwell-Reyes said the family has no plans to slow down. "We'll be here tomorrow at 4 a.m.," she said, smiling. "The dough doesn't wait."

Hartwell's Bakery Celebrates 100 Years of Fresh Bread on Main Street

Hartwell's Bakery marked its 100th anniversary this weekend, drawing hundreds of residents to the corner of Main and Elm for free pastries, live music, and a ribbon cutting that brought the mayor out before sunrise.

The bakery opened its doors in November 1926, when founder Walter Hartwell began selling rye loaves and sticky buns from a small storefront with a single brick oven. That oven, restored two years ago, still sits at the back of the shop and is fired up every morning at 3 a.m.

"My great-grandfather believed bread should be affordable and honest," said Ellen Hartwell-Moss, who now runs the business with her son Daniel. "We have tried to keep to that, even when it would have been easier not to."

The family has weathered the Great Depression, wartime sugar rationing, and the arrival of supermarket chains. During a flood in 1974, neighbors formed a line to carry flour sacks to the second floor. Longtime customer Margaret Doyle, 88, recalls that day well. "They gave bread away for a week," she said. "Nobody forgot it."

Today the bakery employs 14 people and still uses a sourdough starter that Walter Hartwell began in 1926. Its cinnamon twist remains the top seller, followed closely by the original rye.

To mark the milestone, the town council presented the family with a commemorative plaque, which will hang beside the front door. Daniel Hartwell-Moss said the family has no plans to slow down. "We have a lot of dough left to make," he said.

**Power Cut Leaves 4,000 Homes in the Dark Across Eastside**

Around 4,000 homes and businesses were left without electricity on Tuesday evening after a fault at a substation knocked out power across several neighbourhoods on the town's east side.

The outage began at approximately 5:40 p.m., just as many residents were returning home from work. Streetlights went dark along Millbrook Road and Harcourt Avenue, and traffic signals at three major junctions stopped working, causing delays during the evening rush.

Utility crews were dispatched within minutes, and a spokesperson for the regional power company said the cause appeared to be a failed transformer at the Larkfield substation. "Our engineers identified the fault quickly and are working to reroute supply to affected areas while repairs are carried out," the spokesperson said.

Power was restored to about 1,500 homes by 8 p.m. through rerouting, but the remaining customers were still waiting as temperatures dropped to near freezing overnight.

Local councillor Dana Whitfield urged residents to check on elderly neighbours. "This is the kind of night when vulnerable people really need community support," she said. The council opened the Eastside Community Centre as a warm space, offering hot drinks, phone charging and blankets.

Restaurants and shops along the high street closed early, with some owners worried about spoiled stock. "We lost the whole evening, and we'll probably lose a lot of food too," said café owner Tom Reyes.

The power company said it expected full restoration by mid-morning Wednesday and apologised for the inconvenience. Residents can check progress through the company's outage map or by calling its helpline.

Police advised drivers to take extra care around affected junctions.

**Power cut leaves 4,000 homes in the dark across east Harlow**

About 4,000 homes were left without electricity for most of Tuesday evening after a fault at a substation on Mill Lane.

The lights went out at around 5:40pm, just as many residents were getting home from work and school. Streetlights on Fairfield Road and the surrounding estates also failed, and the traffic signals at the Bellmont roundabout stopped working, causing long tailbacks during the rush hour.

Engineers from the network operator were on site within the hour. A spokesperson said a cable had failed underground, which tripped the equipment at the substation. Power was restored to most customers by 9:15pm, though about 300 households had to wait until after 11pm while crews rerouted supply.

Local people did what they could. Dave Ormerod, who runs the Crown and Anchor on Fairfield Road, said he kept the pub open by candlelight and gave out free tea to anyone who wanted it. "We had about forty people in at one point, mostly families with nowhere else to go," he said. "The kids thought it was great fun."

Not everyone was so lucky. Margaret Teale, 82, who lives alone on Hollis Close, said she sat in her coat for hours. "It was the cold that got me. My neighbour came over with a torch and a flask, bless him."

The operator apologised for the disruption and said customers may be eligible for compensation. Anyone affected can find details on its website or by calling the helpline.

The council said the school on Mill Lane would open as normal this morning.

**Rents Climb Again Near Campus, and Students Are Feeling It**

Maren Falls — Junior Dani Okafor pays $985 a month for a bedroom in a three-person house on Alder Street. Two years ago, the same room went for $720.

"My landlord sent the renewal letter in October," Okafor said. "I read it twice, thinking I'd missed a zero somewhere."

Okafor isn't alone. According to figures from the Maren County Housing Office, the average rent for a one-bedroom within two miles of Hartwell State University reached $1,310 this fall, up 11 percent from last year. Vacancy sits below 2 percent.

Landlords say they're responding to their own costs. "Property taxes went up, insurance went up, and a new roof on a duplex isn't cheap," said Gary Pruitt, who owns eleven rental units near campus. "I'd rather keep rents steady, but the numbers don't always allow it."

Tenant advocates see it differently. Lucia Benitez, who runs the student-led Renters Union, said her group fielded more than 80 complaints this semester, mostly about deposits, sudden fee increases, and leases that start signing season in September for the following August.

"Students are being pushed to commit almost a year ahead," Benitez said. "If you wait, there's nothing left."

The university has added 400 beds since 2023, but the housing office says demand has outpaced that growth. A proposed apartment complex on Clifton Avenue, which would add 180 units, goes before the planning commission on December 4.

Okafor plans to stay put but is picking up extra shifts at the campus library.

"I'm not complaining about the house," Okafor said. "I just didn't expect to work this much to live in it."

Millbrook Bridge to Close for Six Months of Repairs

The Millbrook Street Bridge, a vital link between the east and west sides of town, will close to all traffic beginning Monday, December 1, for an estimated six months of structural repairs, city officials announced Tuesday.

The 62-year-old bridge, which carries roughly 14,000 vehicles each day over the Calloway River, was found to have significant corrosion in its support beams during an inspection earlier this year. Engineers say the work is necessary to keep the span safe for future use.

"We understand this will be a real inconvenience for residents and business owners," said Public Works Director Linda Harmon at a press conference. "But delaying the work would only lead to a longer and costlier closure down the road."

Crews will replace damaged steel girders, resurface the deck and upgrade the guardrails. The project is expected to cost $8.4 million, funded largely by a state infrastructure grant.

Drivers will be directed to the Harrison Avenue Bridge, about two miles north, which city officials expect to see heavy congestion during rush hours. Additional signs will mark the detour, and traffic officers will be posted at key intersections during the first two weeks of the closure.

Bus routes 12 and 15 will be rerouted, adding an estimated ten minutes to travel times. Pedestrians and cyclists will not be able to cross the bridge during construction, though a free shuttle will run weekdays from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Officials expect the bridge to reopen in early June. Updates will be posted on the city website.

**Harbourfield Museum to Return 14 Artefacts to Nigeria**

Harbourfield Museum will hand back fourteen carved wooden and brass objects to Nigeria next month, ending a dispute that has run for almost a decade.

The items, which include two ceremonial masks and a set of brass plaques, have sat in the museum's basement store since 1931. They were donated by the family of a colonial-era army officer who took them during a military expedition in the 1890s.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision was not a difficult one in the end. "We spent years arguing about process and paperwork," she said. "Eventually someone asked why we were still holding things we knew didn't belong to us. Nobody had a good answer."

A delegation from the National Commission for Museums and Monuments in Abuja will travel to Harbourfield on 9 December to collect the pieces. A small ceremony is planned in the main hall, open to the public from 11am.

Local resident Dev Pillai, 67, who has volunteered at the museum for twenty years, said he had mixed feelings. "I loved those masks. But I'd rather see them back where they were made than gathering dust here."

The museum's trustees voted 7–2 in favour in September. The empty display cases will be used for a temporary exhibition about the objects' history and their journey home, with photographs and interviews from the Nigerian team.

Marsh said the museum is also reviewing the rest of its collection. "This probably won't be the last conversation like this," she said. "We'd rather start it ourselves than be pushed into it."

Entry to the ceremony is free.

Maplewood High Bans Phones During Class Time

Maplewood High School will begin enforcing a strict no-phone policy during instructional hours starting next Monday, Principal Dana Whitfield announced at Tuesday evening's school board meeting.

Under the new rules, students must store their phones in lockable pouches or in their lockers from the first bell until the final bell. Phones will be permitted only before and after school. Teachers may grant exceptions for specific learning activities, but those will be rare.

Whitfield said the decision followed a semester-long review of attendance, grades and classroom behavior. "Teachers kept telling us the same thing," she said. "Students were distracted, and even the quiet buzz of a notification was pulling attention away from the lesson."

A survey of Maplewood staff found that 82 percent supported a ban. Student opinion was more divided. Junior Marcus Delgado said he understood the reasoning but worried about reaching family in an emergency. "My mom works nights, and I like knowing I can check in," he said.

The district addressed that concern by noting that the front office phone will remain available for urgent calls, and parents can contact the school directly to reach their children.

Several nearby districts have adopted similar policies in recent years, reporting improved focus and more conversation in hallways and lunchrooms. Maplewood will review its results after one semester.

Parents are invited to an information session on Thursday at 6 p.m. in the school library, where staff will explain the pouch system and answer questions.

# How to Apply for a Residential Parking Permit

**Department of Transportation and Public Works**

Residential parking permits allow eligible residents to park in designated permit zones near their homes. This page explains who can apply, what you need, and how to submit your application.

## Who Is Eligible

You may apply if you:

- Live at an address within a designated permit zone
- Own or regularly use a registered vehicle
- Have a valid driver's license or state-issued ID showing your current address

Each household may hold up to three permits.

## What You Will Need

- Proof of residency, such as a utility bill, lease, or mortgage statement dated within the last 60 days
- Current vehicle registration listing your zone address
- A valid photo ID
- Payment for the permit fee

## How to Apply

1. **Apply online.** Visit the department's permit portal and create an account.
2. **Upload documents.** Submit clear photos or scans of each required document.
3. **Pay the fee.** The annual fee is $35 per vehicle. Reduced-fee permits of $15 are available for seniors and income-qualified households.
4. **Wait for review.** Applications are typically processed within five to seven business days.

You may also apply in person at the Permit Services Office, 200 Civic Center Plaza, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

## After You Apply

Approved permits are mailed to your address. Place the permit on your vehicle's rear window or mirror as directed. Permits expire on December 31 each year and must be renewed.

## Need Help?

Call the Permit Services Office at 555-0142 or email permits@cityexample.gov. Please have your application number ready.

Staying Warm and Safe in Cold Weather

Cold weather can be dangerous, especially during long freezes and winter storms. The Department of Public Health encourages all residents to take simple steps to protect themselves, their families, and their neighbors.

Dress in several loose layers rather than one heavy garment. Wear a hat, insulated gloves or mittens, a scarf, and waterproof boots, since much of the body's heat is lost through the head, hands, and feet. Change out of wet clothing as soon as possible, because damp fabric draws heat away from the body quickly.

Limit time outdoors when temperatures drop or winds are strong. If you must go out, take breaks indoors to warm up. Watch for signs of frostbite, such as numbness, pale or waxy skin, and a stinging sensation in the fingers, toes, ears, or nose. Signs of hypothermia include shivering, confusion, slurred speech, and unusual drowsiness. If you suspect hypothermia, call emergency services right away and move the person to a warm place.

Heat your home safely. Never use a gas oven, grill, or generator indoors, as these can release carbon monoxide, a colorless and odorless gas. Install working carbon monoxide and smoke alarms and test them monthly. Keep space heaters at least three feet from curtains, bedding, and furniture, and turn them off when you leave the room or go to sleep.

Check on older relatives, neighbors, and anyone who lives alone. Make sure pets are kept indoors or have warm shelter. If you need help with heating or shelter, call 211 to find warming centers and assistance programs near you.

# Staying Warm and Safe in Cold Weather

Cold temperatures can be dangerous, especially for older adults, young children, and people with chronic health conditions. Follow these steps to protect yourself and your household.

## Dress for the Weather
- Wear several loose, lightweight layers rather than one heavy layer.
- Cover your head, neck, hands, and feet. Mittens are warmer than gloves.
- Choose water-resistant outer layers, and change out of wet clothing quickly.

## Heat Your Home Safely
- Never use a gas oven, grill, or camp stove to heat your home.
- Keep portable heaters at least three feet from curtains, bedding, and furniture, and plug them directly into a wall outlet.
- Install carbon monoxide and smoke alarms on every level, and test them monthly.
- Have furnaces and chimneys inspected each year.
- Never run a generator indoors or in an attached garage.

## Recognize Warning Signs
**Hypothermia:** shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, and unusual clumsiness. Call emergency services immediately, move the person indoors, remove wet clothing, and warm the center of the body with blankets.

**Frostbite:** numb, pale, waxy, or hard skin on fingers, toes, ears, or the nose. Seek medical care and do not rub the affected area.

## Check on Others
Contact elderly neighbors, relatives, and anyone living alone. Bring pets indoors, and never leave children or animals in a parked vehicle.

## Travel Prepared
Keep a winter kit in your vehicle with blankets, water, snacks, a flashlight, a phone charger, and a small shovel. Let someone know your route before you leave.

## Need Help?
If you cannot afford heating, contact your local energy assistance office or dial 211 for referrals to warming centers and support services. In an emergency, call 911.

# Household Recycling Guidelines

**Department of Environmental Services, Office of Waste Reduction**

Recycling correctly helps keep our communities clean, conserves resources, and lowers disposal costs. Please follow these rules for your curbside recycling bin.

## What Belongs in Your Bin

- **Paper and cardboard:** Newspapers, magazines, office paper, mail, and flattened cardboard boxes
- **Plastic containers:** Bottles, jugs, and tubs marked with numbers 1 through 5
- **Metal:** Aluminum cans, steel and tin cans, and clean aluminum foil
- **Glass:** Bottles and jars of any color

## What Stays Out

- Plastic bags and film (return these to participating grocery store drop-off bins)
- Foam packaging and takeout containers
- Food waste and greasy pizza boxes
- Ceramics, drinking glasses, and window glass
- Batteries, electronics, and light bulbs
- Hoses, cords, and chains, which jam sorting equipment

## Preparing Your Items

1. **Empty and rinse.** Containers do not need to be spotless, but remove food and liquids.
2. **Keep items loose.** Do not bag your recyclables. Bagged items are sent to landfill.
3. **Flatten cardboard.** This saves space and helps trucks collect more.
4. **Replace caps.** Attach lids to plastic bottles and jars after emptying.

## Special Materials

Household hazardous waste, such as paint, motor oil, pesticides, and cleaning chemicals, must be taken to a designated collection event or facility. Electronics and batteries can be dropped off at approved collection sites.

## When in Doubt, Leave It Out

Placing non-recyclable items in your bin can contaminate entire loads. If you are unsure about an item, check our online lookup tool or call our helpline.

**Questions?** Call 1-800-555-0142 or visit your local department website for collection schedules and drop-off locations.

*Thank you for doing your part.*

# What to Do If You Lose Your Job

Losing a job is stressful. Taking a few steps early can protect your income and help you move forward. This page outlines what to do first.

## Within the First Week

**File for unemployment benefits right away.** Benefits usually start from the date you apply, not the date you lost your job. You can apply online or by phone through your state workforce agency. Have your Social Security number, employment history for the past 18 months, and your employer's contact details ready.

**Collect your paperwork.** Ask your employer for your final paycheck, a record of any unused vacation pay owed, and a written statement of your last day worked. Keep any termination letter or emails.

**Review your health coverage.** You may be able to keep your employer plan through COBRA, join a spouse's plan, or enroll in a Marketplace plan. Losing coverage opens a special enrollment period, but deadlines are short, often 60 days.

## In the Following Weeks

**Visit an American Job Center.** Staff offer free résumé help, job listings, training programs, and career counseling.

**Make a budget.** List fixed costs, cut optional spending, and contact lenders, landlords, or utility providers early if you expect trouble paying. Many offer hardship plans.

**Check your retirement accounts.** Avoid early withdrawals if you can, since they may bring taxes and penalties.

**Keep a job search log.** Most states require you to show you are actively looking for work to continue receiving benefits.

## Need Help?

Call your state workforce agency or visit your nearest American Job Center. If you believe you were let go unfairly or illegally, contact your state labor department.

# Getting a Fishing Licence

**Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Public Guidance**

## Do I need a licence?

You need a valid licence if you are 16 or over and plan to fish for freshwater or sea fish using a rod and line, net, or trap. Children under 16 may fish without a licence but must be accompanied by a licensed adult when fishing in managed waters.

## Types of licence

- **Day licence:** valid for 24 hours from the time of purchase.
- **Weekly licence:** valid for 7 consecutive days.
- **Annual licence:** valid for 12 months from the start date you choose.
- **Concession licence:** reduced rate for people aged 65 and over, full-time students, and those receiving disability benefits.

## How to apply

1. **Apply online** through the Department's licensing portal. You will need a valid email address and a debit or credit card.
2. **Apply by phone** on our customer helpline, open Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm.
3. **Apply in person** at any authorised licence agent, such as post offices and angling shops.

Please have your full name, address, and date of birth ready. Concession applicants must provide proof of eligibility.

## After you apply

Your licence will be emailed to you immediately if you apply online. You may show it on your phone or print a copy. You must carry it whenever you fish and show it to an enforcement officer on request.

## Rules to remember

Your licence does not replace local permits. Some waters require additional permission from the landowner or fishery. Observe all size limits, bag limits, and closed seasons.

## Need help?

Visit our website or call the helpline. Fishing without a valid licence may result in a fine of up to £2,500.

# Introducing Quill 2.0

We're thrilled to announce **Quill 2.0**, the biggest release in the history of our open-source text editor. After eighteen months of development, thousands of commits, and feedback from hundreds of contributors, Quill 2.0 is faster, more extensible, and more welcoming than ever.

## Highlights

### A Rebuilt Core
The editing engine has been rewritten from the ground up. Large files that once stuttered now open instantly: a 1 GB log file loads in under a second, and typing latency has dropped by more than 60% in our benchmarks. Memory usage is down by roughly a third.

### Native Language Server Support
Quill now speaks the Language Server Protocol out of the box. Get completions, diagnostics, go-to-definition, rename refactoring, and inline documentation for dozens of languages without installing a single plugin.

### Modern Plugin API
Plugins now run in isolated sandboxes with a stable, versioned API. They're safer, they can't crash the editor, and they can be written in Lua, JavaScript, or WebAssembly-compatible languages. A new built-in plugin browser makes discovering and installing extensions a one-click experience.

### Multi-Cursor and Structural Editing
Select all occurrences, add cursors with the mouse or keyboard, and edit with syntax-aware selections that expand and shrink by logical units: words, expressions, blocks, and functions.

### Redesigned Interface
A refreshed UI brings split panes, tabbed groups, a command palette, and a distraction-free mode. Themes are now defined in simple TOML files, and we're shipping 12 new built-in themes, including improved high-contrast and colorblind-friendly options.

### Collaboration (Beta)
Edit together in real time with end-to-end encrypted sessions. No account required, just share a link.

## Other Improvements

- Built-in terminal panel
- Persistent undo history across sessions
- Improved Unicode, bidirectional text, and emoji rendering
- Accessibility upgrades, including full screen reader support
- Session restore after crashes, with no lost work
- Regex search with live preview across entire projects
- Native Apple Silicon and Windows ARM builds

## Breaking Changes

Quill 2.0 includes some breaking changes:

- The 1.x plugin API is deprecated. A compatibility layer will remain through 2.2, and a migration guide is available in the docs.
- Configuration has moved from JSON to TOML. Run `quill migrate-config` to convert your existing settings automatically.
- Several default keybindings have changed to align with common conventions. The previous keymap is available as a preset.

## Get It Now

- **Download:** Installers and packages for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available on our website.
- **Package managers:** Install or upgrade via Homebrew, winget, apt, dnf, Flatpak, or Cargo.
- **Source:** Build from source on GitHub.

## Thank You

Quill is made possible by its community. To everyone who filed a bug, wrote a plugin, translated a string, improved the docs, or answered a question in the forums: thank you. This release is yours.

Found a problem? Open an issue on GitHub. Want to help shape 2.1? Join the discussion in our community forum.

Happy editing!

*The Quill Team*

# Introducing Privacy Mode: Your Data, Without AI

Today we're launching **Privacy Mode**, a new setting that lets you use our product with every AI feature turned off and your data kept out of any AI processing.

## Why we built it

Many of you told us the same thing: you love the product, but your work involves sensitive information, regulated data, or client confidentiality, and you need certainty about how it's handled. Privacy Mode gives you that certainty with a single switch.

## What Privacy Mode does

When Privacy Mode is on:

- **No AI processing.** Your content is never sent to AI models for summaries, suggestions, search, or any other feature.
- **No training on your data.** Your information is never used to train or improve AI systems.
- **AI features are fully disabled.** Assistants, auto-generated content, and smart suggestions are removed from the interface so nothing runs by accident.
- **Core functionality stays intact.** Everything you rely on for collaboration, workflows, reporting, and integrations keeps working as usual.

## Control at every level

- **Individuals** can enable Privacy Mode for their own account in Settings → Privacy.
- **Admins** can enforce it across the whole workspace or for specific teams and projects.
- **Locked by policy.** Once enforced by an admin, members cannot turn AI features back on.
- **Audit log.** Every change to Privacy Mode is recorded so compliance teams can verify when it was enabled and by whom.

## Who it's for

Privacy Mode is designed for legal, healthcare, finance, government, education, and any team that handles confidential information or operates under strict data-handling requirements.

## Availability

Privacy Mode is available today on all paid plans at no additional cost. To turn it on, go to **Settings → Privacy → Privacy Mode** and switch it on. Workspace admins can find enforcement options under **Admin → Security**.

## Our commitment

AI can be useful, but it should be your choice. Privacy Mode is part of our promise that you stay in control of your data. We'll keep investing in more granular privacy controls, and we want to hear what you need next.

Questions or feedback? Reach out to our support team or share your thoughts in the community forum.

**The Team**

Introducing Privacy Mode: a version of your workspace with every AI feature switched off.

Starting today, any admin can turn on Privacy Mode from the Security settings page. When it is active, nothing in your account is sent to an AI model, whether ours or a third party's. Summaries, suggestions, auto-tagging, smart search, and drafting assistants are all disabled. Your content is never used to train or tune any model, and it is never passed to a model provider for processing.

We built this because many of you asked for it. Some teams work under strict compliance requirements. Others handle sensitive client material, legal records, or health information and want a clear boundary they can point to when someone asks where their data goes. A promise in a policy document is good, but a setting you can verify is better.

Here is how it works. Privacy Mode can be applied to your whole organization or to individual workspaces, so a legal team can stay fully AI-free while marketing keeps the tools it likes. Once enabled, AI processing is blocked at the infrastructure level rather than hidden in the interface, which means it cannot be bypassed by an integration or an API call. Your audit log records when the mode was turned on, who turned it on, and every attempt by a connected app to reach an AI feature while it was active.

Everything else in the product keeps working as before. Search still finds your files using standard keyword matching, templates and automations still run, and your reports and dashboards are unchanged. You simply lose the conveniences that depend on a model reading your content.

You can switch Privacy Mode on or off at any time. When you turn it off, AI features return only for the workspaces you choose, and nothing that was created while the mode was active gets retroactively processed.

Privacy Mode is available now on all paid plans at no extra cost. To get started, open Settings, choose Security, and select Privacy Mode. If you would like help planning a rollout across a large team, our support group is ready to walk you through it.

Your data, your rules. Now with a switch to prove it.

Battery life is about 35 minutes on standard mode, which covers my whole two-bedroom apartment with some to spare. Boost mode drains it fast, so I rarely use it.

★★☆☆☆ Great Premise, Lackluster Payoff

I wanted to love *The Glass Meridian*. The opening chapters promise so much: a mysterious lighthouse, a missing cartographer, and a coastline that seems to rearrange itself overnight. I was hooked.

Sadly, the middle third collapses under its own weight. Subplots multiply without resolving, and the protagonist, Elise, spends far too many pages brooding instead of investigating. Her motivations shift whenever the plot demands it, so I never felt invested in her choices.

The prose is often lovely, but it leans heavily on repeated imagery. If I read one more description of "salt-bitten light," I may scream.

Then there's the ending. After hundreds of pages of buildup, the central mystery is explained in a rushed, three-page monologue that raises more questions than it answers. Key characters simply vanish from the story.

It's a shame, because the author clearly has talent. Unfortunately, this book felt like a brilliant idea that never found its structure. I can't recommend it.
