Clock drift usually comes down to a few common causes, so here's what I'd check, roughly in order:

1. **Is time sync running at all?** Check `timedatectl` for "System clock synchronized: yes" and "NTP service: active." If you're using chrony, `chronyc tracking` and `chronyc sources` show offset and whether you have a reachable source. For ntpd, use `ntpq -p`.

2. **Only one sync daemon.** Running chrony, ntpd, and systemd-timesyncd together causes them to fight each other. Pick one and disable the rest.

3. **Firewall and network.** NTP needs outbound UDP 123. Make sure it isn't blocked, and that DNS resolves your pool servers.

4. **Virtualization.** On a VM, hypervisor time sync and guest NTP can conflict. Check whether VMware Tools, Hyper-V integration services, or the KVM clock source is adjusting time too. Also look at snapshots/suspend/resume, which often cause big jumps.

5. **Hardware clock and clocksource.** A failing CMOS battery or a flaky clocksource (check `/sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource`) can cause persistent drift. Compare `hwclock` against system time.

6. **Load and power management.** Heavy CPU contention or aggressive power-saving on older hardware can skew timekeeping.

7. **Logs.** Check `journalctl -u chronyd` (or your daemon) for "step" events, unreachable servers, or large offset warnings.

If you share whether this is a VM or bare metal and which daemon you use, people can narrow it down faster.

Lower your DNS TTL first. Do that a day or two before the move, drop it to 300 seconds or so, so that when you do flip the record, everyone picks up the change in minutes instead of hours.

Then set up the new host fully while the old one keeps serving traffic. Copy files, import the database, get the SSL cert sorted. You can test the new box by editing your local hosts file to point the domain at the new IP, so you see the real site without touching public DNS.

The part people forget is data that changes. If it's a WordPress site or anything with orders, comments, or signups, do a final sync right before cutover. Ideally put the old site in read-only mode for a few minutes, take the last DB dump, import it, then switch DNS.

After the switch, leave the old server running for at least a few days. Some resolvers ignore TTLs, so a few visitors will still hit the old IP. If you can, set up a proxy or redirect on the old host pointing at the new one so nobody lands on stale data.

Email is the other gotcha. If MX records are changing too, move those separately.

Usually it's one of a few things, so I'd work through them in this order:

**1. Distance and obstructions.** Concrete, brick, metal, mirrors, fish tanks, and even dense bookshelves absorb or reflect signal. If the room is behind a thick wall or on another floor, that's likely the culprit. Check signal strength (RSSI) there. Anything weaker than about -70 dBm will feel slow.

**2. Band and channel.** 5 GHz is fast but doesn't penetrate walls well. 2.4 GHz travels farther but is slower and crowded. If your device is clinging to a weak 5 GHz signal, or to a congested 2.4 GHz channel, speeds suffer. Use a Wi-Fi analyzer app to see neighboring networks and pick a less crowded channel.

**3. Local interference.** Microwaves, cordless phones, baby monitors, Bluetooth devices, and USB 3.0 hubs near the router or client can all hurt 2.4 GHz.

**4. Router placement.** Routers on the floor, in cabinets, or in a corner of the house cover poorly. Move it higher and more central.

**5. Fixes, cheapest first:**
- Reposition the router or its antennas
- Change channel or width (try 20/40 MHz on crowded 2.4 GHz)
- Add a mesh node or access point, ideally wired back via Ethernet
- Use powerline adapters or run Ethernet if possible

Avoid cheap range extenders, since they often halve throughput.

If you share your router model, the room's location relative to it, and the RSSI there, people can give more specific advice.

Start with two questions: how much data can you afford to lose (RPO), and how long can you afford to be down (RTO)? Everything else follows from those answers.

**Inventory what matters.** File shares, email, accounting software, databases, and laptops. Not everything needs the same protection, so tier it: critical (restore within hours), important (within a day), and nice-to-have.

**Follow 3-2-1 (or 3-2-1-1-0).** Keep 3 copies of the data, on 2 different media, with 1 offsite. Add 1 immutable or offline copy (protects against ransomware) and 0 errors, meaning verified restores.

**Typical small-office setup:**
- A NAS or local backup disk for fast restores
- Cloud backup (Backblaze B2, Wasabi, or similar) for offsite
- Backup software with versioning and encryption (Veeam, Restic, Duplicati, or Synology Hyper Backup)
- SaaS data (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) backed up separately, since the vendor's retention is not a backup

**Don't skip these:**
- Use separate credentials for backup storage, so a compromised domain admin can't delete it.
- Test restores on a schedule. Untested backups are just hopes.
- Set up failure alerts.
- Document the restore procedure so someone other than you can follow it.

Keep it simple enough that it will actually be maintained. A boring, tested setup beats a clever one that nobody checks.

Start with two questions: how much data can you afford to lose (an hour? a day?), and how long can you afford to be down? Those answers drive everything else.

For most small offices the old 3-2-1 rule still holds up fine: three copies of your data, on two different kinds of storage, with one offsite. In practice that's usually the live data, a local backup (a NAS or external drive), and a cloud copy (Backblaze, Wasabi, whatever fits your budget).

A few things I've seen bite people:

- Ransomware will happily encrypt any backup drive that's mounted or reachable with the same credentials. Make at least one copy immutable or offline, or use a cloud bucket with versioning/object lock.
- Backups you've never restored are just hopes. Pick a date every quarter and actually restore a few files, and one full machine if you can.
- Don't forget the stuff that isn't in the file share: email, SaaS data (365, Google Workspace), the accounting software, and the config for your router/firewall.
- Keep it boring. Tools like restic, Veeam Agent, or whatever your NAS vendor ships are fine. The one you'll actually monitor beats the clever one.

Set up alerts for failed jobs too, or you'll find out months later.

Without knowing your stack it's hard to say exactly, but ten-minute builds usually come down to a handful of common culprits. Here's how I'd narrow it down:

**1. Measure first.** Don't guess. Most build tools can produce timing output or a profile (Gradle build scans, `webpack --profile`, `cargo build --timings`, `-ftime-trace` for clang, and so on). Find out which step actually dominates.

**2. Dependency installation.** If you're downloading packages from scratch every run, that can eat minutes. Cache your dependency directory between runs, and use a lockfile so the cache stays valid.

**3. No incremental or cached builds.** If CI starts from a clean checkout each time, you're recompiling everything. Persist build caches, or use a remote cache like ccache, sccache, or Bazel/Gradle remote caching.

**4. Serial work.** Check that you're using all your cores (`make -j`, parallel test runners, etc.). Split independent stages into parallel jobs.

**5. Slow tests or linting.** Tests are often the biggest chunk. Run only affected tests on PRs, and save the full suite for merges.

**6. Resource limits.** Small CI runners or containers with little RAM/CPU, or a disk that's swapping, will drag everything down.

**7. Docker layers.** Order your Dockerfile so rarely changing steps come first and the cache stays effective.

If you share your language, build tool, and where it runs (local vs. CI), people here can give much more specific advice.

Usually it's a handful of boring things stacking up, not one culprit.

The big ones I've run into:

- **Push notifications and keepalive connections.** Chat or social apps hold a socket open and ping it every so often. Each ping is tiny, but it adds up over a month.
- **Background refresh.** iOS and Android both let apps fetch content while you're not looking. Feeds, maps, and email clients are the worst for this.
- **Analytics and ad SDKs.** A lot of apps phone home with telemetry every few minutes, and the dev often doesn't even know how chatty the bundled SDK is.
- **Auto-uploads and syncing.** Photos, cloud backup, podcast downloads, app updates queued up in the background.
- **Retry loops.** If the app has a bug or bad signal, it can hammer a failing request over and over.

To find the offender, check Settings > Cellular (iOS) or Settings > Network > Data usage (Android) and sort by usage. Then turn off background data or background app refresh for that app. If you're technical, run a proxy like mitmproxy or PCAPdroid and watch what it's actually sending. It's often eye-opening.

If it's your own app, look at your SDKs first.

Apps use data in the background for a handful of common reasons:

**1. Background refresh / sync.** Email, social, cloud storage, and messaging apps periodically poll servers for new content so it's ready when you open them. Photo backup (Google Photos, iCloud, OneDrive) can be a big one.

**2. Push notifications and keep-alive connections.** Chat apps hold a persistent connection open, which generates small but constant traffic.

**3. Ads, analytics, and telemetry.** Many free apps send usage data and fetch ads even when idle.

**4. Auto-updates and downloads.** The Play Store/App Store, game asset packs, and offline maps may fetch updates in the background.

**5. Media prefetching.** Streaming and social apps (TikTok, Instagram, Spotify) cache content ahead of time.

**6. Bugs or misbehaving apps.** Retry loops after failed requests, or a stuck sync, can burn data quickly.

**How to find and limit it:**
- **Android:** Settings → Network & internet → Data usage → pick the app → toggle "Background data" off, or enable Data Saver.
- **iOS:** Settings → Cellular → toggle individual apps off; also disable Background App Refresh under General.
- Check in-app settings for "sync over Wi-Fi only," video autoplay, and upload quality.
- Compare foreground vs. background usage in the data usage screen. If background is unusually high for one app, try clearing its cache, updating it, or reinstalling.

If you're on a network you manage, a DNS-level blocker or per-app firewall (e.g., NetGuard on Android) can show you exactly what each app is contacting.

Start by confirming it's actually a leak: graph the process's RSS over days. A sawtooth that returns to baseline is normal GC or caching behavior. A steady upward staircase that never comes down is a leak.

Next, narrow down the cause:

1. **Reproduce it under load in staging.** Replay realistic traffic and watch which endpoints or jobs make memory climb. Bisecting by feature is often the fastest win.

2. **Use a language-appropriate profiler.** Examples: heap snapshots in Node (Chrome DevTools), `tracemalloc` or `objgraph` in Python, `jmap`/Eclipse MAT or async-profiler in Java, pprof in Go, and Valgrind, heaptrack, or AddressSanitizer for C/C++.

3. **Compare snapshots over time.** Take one heap dump early and another after memory has grown, then diff them. The object types with the largest growth are your suspects. Then look at what's retaining them (the "path to GC root").

4. **Check the usual culprits:** unbounded caches or maps, event listeners or callbacks never removed, connections/file handles/threads not closed, per-request data stored in globals, and growing queues.

5. **Distinguish heap from native/off-heap growth.** If the heap looks stable but RSS grows, suspect native libraries, fragmentation (try jemalloc or tune `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` on glibc), or memory-mapped files.

As a stopgap, set memory limits and let the supervisor restart the service gracefully, while you track down the root cause.

This release adds first-class TypeScript support to the library. Type definitions are now bundled with the package, so there is no need to install a separate @types package. All public functions, classes, options objects, and return values are fully typed, and generic parameters have been added where inputs and outputs are related, which lets your editor infer types more accurately and catch mistakes earlier. The package manifest now includes a types entry and conditional exports, so both ESM and CommonJS consumers get correct typings automatically. Existing JavaScript usage is unaffected, and no runtime behavior has changed. If you previously relied on community-maintained typings, we recommend removing them to avoid conflicts. Please report any inaccurate or missing types by opening an issue.

Install it with `npm install -g sitewright`, then run `sitewright new mysite` to make a fresh project. Move into that folder and run `sitewright serve`. Your site will be up at localhost:4000, and it reloads whenever you save a file. Pages are just Markdown files in the `content` folder, so make a new one called `about.md`, type a few lines, and refresh the browser to see it. When you're happy with how things look, run `sitewright build` and the finished site lands in the `public` folder, ready to upload anywhere that serves static files.

Search results in our product are slow enough that users notice the delay and, increasingly, change their behavior because of it. Median query latency is acceptable, but the tail is poor: the slowest five percent of queries take several seconds to return, and the slowest one percent can exceed ten seconds. These slow queries are not rare edge cases. They disproportionately affect our most engaged users, who tend to have the largest datasets, run the most complex filters, and search most frequently. As a result, the people who depend on search the most are getting the worst experience.

The impact is visible in both product and engineering signals. Users abandon searches before results load, reissue the same query multiple times, or fall back to browsing manually, which raises load on other parts of the system and lowers task completion rates. Support tickets citing slow or unresponsive search have grown steadily over the past several quarters. Internally, teams building features on top of search have started adding their own caching and timeouts to work around the problem, which fragments behavior and makes results inconsistent across surfaces.

We do not yet have a complete picture of where the time goes. Early investigation points to several contributing factors, including unbounded result scanning for broad queries, index growth that has outpaced the original sharding strategy, expensive ranking computation applied to candidates that are later discarded, and contention during periods of heavy indexing. Because these factors interact, fixing any one of them in isolation may produce little visible improvement, and our current instrumentation makes it hard to attribute latency to a specific stage of the query path.

This document aims to define the problem precisely enough to guide a solution. The goal is to reduce tail latency for search so that the large majority of queries return within a target budget, without regressing result relevance or freshness. The work should begin by establishing per-stage latency measurement, then use that data to prioritize changes. Success will be measured by improvements in the 95th and 99th percentile latency, a reduction in search abandonment and repeated queries, and a decline in related support volume. Out of scope for this document are changes to the search user interface, major shifts in ranking strategy, and migration to a different search backend, though findings may inform those decisions later.

Git says your branch has diverged when your local branch and its remote counterpart each contain commits the other does not. In other words, history split at some shared ancestor, and both sides moved forward independently. Git cannot simply move your branch pointer forward (a fast-forward) or push without discarding someone's work, so it flags the split.

This usually happens in a few ways. You committed locally, and meanwhile a teammate pushed to the same branch. Or you amended, rebased, or reset commits that were already pushed, which rewrites them into new commits with different hashes. The old versions still exist on the remote, so both sides now have unique commits.

To see exactly what differs, run git log --oneline --graph --all, or compare with git log origin/main..main and git log main..origin/main.

To resolve it, you have two main options. Merge the remote changes into yours with git pull (or git pull --no-rebase), which creates a merge commit. Or replay your commits on top of the remote ones with git pull --rebase, which keeps history linear. Either way, resolve any conflicts and then push.

Only force push if you deliberately rewrote history and are sure nobody else's work will be lost. Prefer git push --force-with-lease for safety.

A script that slows down over time almost always has something that keeps growing. The usual culprits:

**1. Unbounded data structures.** Lists, dicts, or caches that you keep appending to but never trim. Memory climbs, lookups or copies get costlier, and the OS may start swapping. Check whether anything accumulates results, logs, or "seen" items forever.

**2. Quadratic operations.** Things like `x in some_list`, `list.insert(0, ...)`, or repeated string concatenation get slower as the collection grows. A loop that looked fine with 1,000 items becomes painful at 1,000,000. Switch to sets, dicts, `collections.deque`, or `"".join(...)`.

**3. Leaked resources.** Unclosed files, sockets, database connections, threads, or subprocesses pile up. Use `with` blocks and make sure you close what you open.

**4. Reference cycles and lingering references.** Objects held by globals, closures, or caches can't be garbage collected. Event handlers or callbacks that are registered repeatedly are a common source.

**5. External factors.** Growing log files, a database table without an index, or rate limiting and throttling by a remote service.

**How to find it:**
- Watch memory over time (`psutil`, or `tracemalloc` from the standard library). Rising memory points to a leak or accumulation.
- If memory is flat, profile early and late in the run with `cProfile` or `py-spy` and compare which functions dominate.

Start by profiling at two points in time. The difference between them usually reveals the culprit quickly.

It's not great, but "bad" depends on what you're protecting.

The issue is XSS. Anything in localStorage can be read by any JavaScript running on your page, so if an attacker gets a script injected (a compromised npm package, a sloppy third-party widget, an unescaped comment field), they can grab the token and use it from anywhere. Even after you patch the hole, the stolen token keeps working until it expires.

The usual alternative is an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. JS can't read it, so XSS can't steal it directly. The tradeoff is that cookies get sent automatically, so you have to think about CSRF. SameSite=Lax or Strict handles most of that, and a CSRF token covers the rest.

One caveat people forget: with XSS, an attacker can still make requests *as the user* from the page even if they can't read the cookie. httpOnly limits the damage (no token exfiltration, no long-lived access), but it doesn't make XSS harmless.

My take:
- Internal tool or low-stakes app with a strict CSP and short-lived tokens? localStorage is probably fine.
- Anything with money, personal data, or admin accounts? Use cookies.
- Either way, keep access tokens short-lived (like 15 minutes) and rotate refresh tokens.

Also, "JWT vs sessions" is a separate question. Plain server-side sessions in a cookie are often simpler.

Eventual consistency means that if you stop writing to a system, all copies of the data will *eventually* agree, but at any given moment they might not.

**In practice:** data is stored on multiple nodes (replicas) for speed and availability. When you write to one, the change propagates to the others in the background. During that window, a read from a different replica can return stale data.

**What you'll actually see:**

- You update your profile photo, refresh, and see the old one. A few seconds later it's the new one.
- You post a comment, and a friend on another server doesn't see it right away.
- Two users edit the same record on different replicas at the same time, and the system has to resolve the conflict afterward (last-write-wins, merging, or custom logic).

**Why systems accept this:** Strong consistency requires replicas to coordinate before acknowledging a write, which adds latency and can make the system unavailable during network partitions (the CAP theorem tradeoff). Eventual consistency favors availability and speed.

**What it means for you as a developer:**

- Don't assume a read immediately after a write returns that write (unless the system offers "read your writes" guarantees).
- Design operations to be idempotent, since retries and duplicates are common.
- Plan for conflict resolution.
- Use strong consistency selectively for things like payments or inventory, where stale data is costly.

"Eventually" usually means milliseconds to seconds, but there's typically no hard upper bound.

Examples: DynamoDB (default reads), Cassandra, DNS, and most CDN caches.

The most common cause is **React Strict Mode**. If your app is wrapped in `<React.StrictMode>` (the default in Create React App, Vite, and Next.js templates), React deliberately renders each component twice during development. It does this to help you catch bugs: if your render logic has side effects or isn't pure, the double render exposes the problem. Effects are also mounted, unmounted, and mounted again in development for the same reason.

This only happens in development. Production builds render once, so you can confirm by building and running the production version.

**Other possible causes:**

- **State updates on mount.** If an effect sets state right after the first render, you get a second render with the new value. That's normal, not a bug.
- **Parent re-renders.** When a parent's state or props change, children re-render too unless they're memoized.
- **Context changes.** Any component consuming a context re-renders when its value changes, including when a provider creates a new object on every render.
- **Unstable props.** Passing new objects or functions each render can trigger extra renders in memoized children.

**What to do:**

1. Don't remove Strict Mode just to silence it. It's helping you.
2. Make sure your render function is pure: no mutations, network calls, or subscriptions outside effects.
3. Put side effects in `useEffect` and return a cleanup function so the mount/unmount/mount cycle is harmless.
4. Use the React DevTools Profiler to see why each render happened.

If the double render also appears in production, look at parent state changes or effects that set state.

Most likely you're running in development with `<React.StrictMode>` wrapped around your app (Create React App, Vite, and Next all put it there by default). In dev, StrictMode deliberately renders every component twice to help you catch side effects that shouldn't be in render. It also mounts, unmounts, and remounts effects once, so your useEffect may fire twice on first load too. Production builds don't do any of this, so run a build and you'll see it only renders once.

Check index.js or main.jsx and see if StrictMode is in there. If you remove it, the double render goes away, but I'd leave it on and fix the cause instead.

What usually trips people up is something in the render body that isn't pure: mutating a variable declared outside the component, pushing to an array that lives outside, calling an API, or logging and assuming the log count means something. Move that stuff into useEffect, and give the effect a cleanup function so the mount/unmount/remount cycle doesn't cause duplicate subscriptions or fetches.

If StrictMode isn't there, then it's real re-rendering. Common causes are a parent re-rendering, setting state inside an effect with no dependency array, or state being updated right after mount (like from a fetch). React DevTools' Profiler will tell you what triggered each render.

Computers store numbers in binary, and 0.1 isn't representable exactly in binary, just like 1/3 isn't representable exactly in decimal. Write 1/3 as 0.3333... and you have to cut it off somewhere. Binary has the same problem with 0.1, except the repeating pattern shows up for numbers that look perfectly tidy in base 10.

In binary, 0.1 is 0.000110011001100... forever. A double only has 53 bits of precision, so it stores the nearest value it can, which is a hair over 0.1 (about 0.1000000000000000055). 0.2 gets rounded the same way, also slightly high. 0.3 gets rounded too, but to a different nearby value.

When you add the stored 0.1 and the stored 0.2, the exact sum lands between two representable numbers, and the result rounds to 0.30000000000000004. The stored 0.3 is one step below that. So they're two neighboring doubles, not the same one, and == says false.

Nothing is broken. This is how IEEE 754 works, and every language using it does the same thing (Python, JavaScript, Java, C, and so on).

What to do about it:

- Never compare floats with ==. Check whether they're within a small tolerance, like `abs(a - b) < 1e-9`, or use something like `math.isclose`.
- For money, use integers (cents) or a decimal type.
- Round only when displaying.

If you want to poke at the exact stored values, search for "float converter" and paste in 0.1.

This almost always means your CI environment differs from your machine in some way your tests quietly depend on. The most common culprits:

**1. Environment differences.** Runtime versions, OS (macOS vs. Linux), file-system case sensitivity, locale, and time zone can all change behavior. Pin versions in CI to match local, or better, run both in the same container.

**2. Dependencies.** Locally you may have stale or globally installed packages, while CI installs fresh from the lockfile. Make sure the lockfile is committed and CI installs from it strictly.

**3. Test order and shared state.** Tests that pass in one order may fail in another, or when run in parallel. Look for shared globals, leftover database rows, temp files, or cached data. Try running the suite in random order locally.

**4. Timing and flakiness.** CI machines are slower and busier. Hard-coded sleeps, tight timeouts, and race conditions show up there first. Replace sleeps with explicit waits or conditions.

**5. Missing configuration.** Environment variables, secrets, config files, or seed data that exist on your machine but not in CI. Also check for files that are git-ignored but needed.

**6. Hidden assumptions.** Hard-coded absolute paths, reliance on the current date or time, network access, or available ports.

**How to debug:** Read the CI failure output carefully first. Then reproduce it locally by using a clean clone, a fresh dependency install, and the same container image CI uses. If you can reproduce it, you can fix it.

If you share the failing test output and your CI config, people can narrow it down much faster.

Almost always it comes down to some difference between your machine and the CI box. A few things I'd check, roughly in order of how often they bite me:

**Test order and shared state.** Locally you might run one file or a single test; CI runs everything, maybe in parallel or random order. If one test leaves behind a global, a file, a DB row, or a mocked function, another one can break. Try running the whole suite locally, in random order if your runner supports it.

**Time and timezone.** CI is usually UTC. Anything touching dates, "today", or formatting can behave differently. Same goes for locale.

**Environment differences.** Different OS (case-sensitive filesystem on Linux vs. macOS/Windows is a classic), different language or dependency versions, missing env vars, or a lockfile that isn't actually being respected.

**Stale local state.** Cached builds, leftover files, a database you seeded months ago. A fresh clone in a clean directory often reproduces the failure.

**Timing and flakiness.** CI machines are slower and have fewer cores. Tests with sleeps, race conditions, or tight timeouts will fail there first.

**Network or services.** Something that works because you have a local database or internet access that CI doesn't.

Start by reading the actual CI error rather than guessing. Then reproduce it in a container matching the CI image.

The choice mostly comes down to which operations you do most often.

**Use a hash map when:**
- Your main operations are insert, delete, and exact-key lookup. These are O(1) on average.
- Keys arrive in no particular order and you don't need to traverse them in order.
- The data changes frequently. Inserting into a sorted array means shifting elements, which costs O(n).

**Use a sorted array when:**
- You need ordered operations: range queries, nearest-neighbor lookups, predecessor/successor, min/max, or iterating in sorted order. Binary search gives you O(log n) for these, and a hash map can't do them efficiently at all.
- The data is mostly static. Build it once, sort it, then query it many times.
- Memory and cache behavior matter. Contiguous arrays are compact and cache-friendly, while hash maps carry overhead for buckets, load-factor slack, and pointers. For small collections, a sorted array often beats a hash map in practice despite worse asymptotics.
- You need deterministic performance. Hash maps have rare worst-case O(n) behavior from collisions or resizing.

**Rule of thumb:** if you only ask "is X present, and what's its value?", pick a hash map. If you ask "what's the next value after X?" or "what falls between A and B?", pick a sorted array.

If you need both frequent updates and ordering, consider a balanced tree (like a `TreeMap` or `std::map`) instead of either.

This error means V8, the JavaScript engine inside Node, hit its heap size limit and couldn't allocate more memory. Node sets a default cap that depends on your version and system memory, so a process can die even when the machine has plenty of RAM free.

**Common causes**

1. **Memory leaks.** Objects stay reachable so the garbage collector can't free them. Typical culprits are unbounded caches, global arrays or maps that only grow, event listeners added repeatedly and never removed, and closures holding large references.
2. **Loading too much at once.** Reading a huge file or database result set fully into memory, or building giant strings or arrays, can exceed the limit quickly.
3. **Runaway work.** Infinite loops or recursion that keep allocating.
4. **A limit that's simply too low** for a legitimately memory-hungry workload.

**What to do**

- **Raise the limit as a stopgap** with `node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js` (value in MB). This buys time but doesn't fix a leak.
- **Find the real cause.** Monitor `process.memoryUsage()` over time. If heap usage climbs steadily and never drops, you have a leak. Take heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools (run with `--inspect`) and compare them to see which objects accumulate.
- **Stream instead of buffering.** Use streams or pagination for large files and queries.
- **Bound your caches.** Use an LRU cache with a max size, and remove listeners when done.

Start by confirming whether memory grows indefinitely (a leak) or spikes on specific requests (too much data at once).

HTTPS wraps your HTTP traffic in TLS, which gives you three protections that matter on public wifi: encryption, authentication, and integrity.

**Encryption.** When your browser connects, it and the server perform a handshake. Using key exchange (typically ephemeral Diffie-Hellman), they agree on a shared secret key without ever sending it over the network. All subsequent data is encrypted with that key. Someone sniffing the wifi sees only that you're talking to some IP address (and usually the domain name, via SNI), plus scrambled bytes. They can't read page contents, URLs beyond the domain, cookies, or form data like passwords.

**Authentication.** Encryption alone wouldn't help if you were encrypting to the attacker. So the server presents a certificate, signed by a certificate authority your device already trusts. It proves the server owns that domain. An attacker running a fake hotspot or intercepting traffic can't produce a valid certificate for, say, yourbank.com, so your browser shows a warning instead of connecting silently.

**Integrity.** Each record carries a cryptographic authentication tag, so any tampering in transit, such as injecting ads or malicious scripts, is detected and the connection fails.

**Limits.** HTTPS doesn't hide which domains you visit, and it won't help if you click through certificate warnings or install a malicious root certificate. HSTS helps prevent attackers from downgrading you to plain HTTP.

Most of the time, this is caching, not a failed change. DNS answers are stored at several levels, and each one can keep serving the old value until it expires.

**The usual causes:**

1. **TTL (time to live).** Each record carries a TTL, such as 3600 seconds. Resolvers that cached the old value keep it until that time runs out. If the old TTL was 24 hours, some users may see the old address for up to a day. Lowering the TTL *before* a planned change avoids this.

2. **Local caches.** Your operating system, browser, and router all cache lookups. Flush the OS cache (`ipconfig /flushdns` on Windows, `resolvectl flush-caches` on systemd Linux, `sudo dscacheutil -flushcache` on macOS) and restart the browser.

3. **ISP or public resolver caches.** Your resolver may still hold the old record. Query a different one, such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8, to compare.

4. **Wrong place edited.** Confirm the domain's nameservers actually point to the DNS host where you made the change. Editing zone records at a provider that isn't authoritative does nothing.

5. **Nameserver changes.** If you changed the nameservers at the registrar, the registry's NS records have their own TTL, often 24-48 hours.

6. **Record mistakes.** A conflicting record, such as a CNAME alongside other records on the same name, a typo, or a missing trailing dot in a zone file, can break things.

**How to check:** Use `dig yourdomain.com @ns1.yourhost.com` to query the authoritative server directly. If it shows the new value, your change is correct and you're only waiting on caches. If it shows the old value, the problem is on the DNS host's side.

A **race condition** happens when the correctness of your program depends on the timing or ordering of events that you don't control, usually threads, processes, or async tasks touching shared state. If two things "race" to read or write the same data and the outcome changes depending on who wins, you have one.

A classic example: two threads each read a counter (say, 5), add one, and write back. Both write 6, so one increment is lost. The read-modify-write sequence wasn't atomic.

**How to spot one:**

- **Intermittent bugs.** Failures that appear randomly, vanish when you add logging, or only show up under load or on certain machines.
- **Shared mutable state.** Look for variables, files, caches, or database rows accessed by multiple threads or requests without locks or other protection.
- **Check-then-act patterns.** "If the file doesn't exist, create it" or "if balance is sufficient, withdraw" can break when something changes between the check and the action.
- **Tools.** ThreadSanitizer, Go's `-race` flag, Java's concurrency analyzers, and Helgrind can detect unsynchronized access automatically.
- **Stress testing.** Run the suspect code with many threads and iterations to make rare interleavings likely.

**How to fix:** use locks or mutexes, atomic operations, immutable data, message passing, or database transactions. Better still, minimize shared state so there's nothing to race over.

The short version: HTML isn't a regular language, and regular expressions are built to describe regular languages.

HTML is nested. A `<div>` can contain another `<div>`, which can contain another, and so on. To match a closing tag with its correct opening tag, you have to keep track of how deep you are. Classic regexes have no memory for that kind of counting, so they can't do it reliably. Modern regex engines add extensions like recursion, but the patterns become unreadable and fragile.

Real-world HTML also makes things worse:

- Attributes can appear in any order, use single quotes, double quotes, or none.
- `>` can legally appear inside attribute values.
- Comments, `<script>` blocks, CDATA, and `<pre>` content can contain text that looks like tags.
- Browsers accept malformed markup, such as unclosed tags and bad nesting, and silently repair it.

A regex that works on your three sample pages will break on the fourth, often in ways you don't notice until bad data has spread.

The better approach is to use a real HTML parser (BeautifulSoup, lxml, jsoup, HtmlAgilityPack, your browser's DOM). It handles the messy cases the way browsers do, and lets you query by structure with CSS selectors or XPath.

Regex is fine for quick, throwaway tasks on a known, tiny, fixed snippet. For anything else, parse it properly.

Don't rename it in a single step. A direct rename breaks any code that still references the old name, and during a deploy old and new application versions run side by side. Use the expand/contract pattern instead:

1. **Add the new column.** Deploy a migration that creates it, nullable and without heavy defaults, so it doesn't lock the table.

2. **Keep both in sync.** Use dual writes in the application, or a database trigger, so every insert and update populates both columns.

3. **Backfill existing rows.** Copy old values into the new column in small batches (a few thousand rows at a time) with pauses between them. This avoids long locks, replication lag, and bloated transactions.

4. **Verify.** Compare the two columns to confirm they match. Add any constraints or indexes to the new column at this point, using concurrent or online index builds where your database supports them.

5. **Switch reads.** Deploy code that reads from the new column. Keep dual writes running so you can roll back safely.

6. **Stop writing to the old column.** Once you're confident, deploy code that only uses the new one.

7. **Drop the old column.** Do this in a later release, after a waiting period. Consider taking a backup first.

Alternatives: some databases let you create a view or computed alias under the old name, which can bridge the gap. If you have a maintenance window and a small table, a plain `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` is fine, but still test it on a staging copy first.

Every step should be a separate, independently reversible deploy.

Both commands integrate changes from one branch into another, but they produce different histories.

**Merge** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has both branches as parents. Existing commits are left untouched, so the history shows exactly what happened: that work diverged and later came back together. The downside is that a busy project can end up with a tangled history full of merge commits.

**Rebase** takes the commits from your branch and replays them, one by one, on top of the target branch. Each replayed commit is a brand-new commit with a new hash, even though its content is the same. The result is a clean, linear history, as if you had started your work from the latest point all along. The downside is that it rewrites history.

**When to use which:**

- Use **rebase** to tidy up your own local or feature branch before sharing it, or to pull in the latest changes from main without cluttering the log.
- Use **merge** when integrating a finished feature into a shared branch, or whenever you want to preserve the true record of how work happened.

**The golden rule:** never rebase commits that others have already pulled. Because rebase rewrites commits, teammates' copies will no longer match, which causes confusing conflicts and duplicated work. If you do rebase a branch you've already pushed, you'll need a force push, so make sure it's only your branch.

Neither is "better." Merge preserves history; rebase simplifies it.

Retries are configured through the `retry` option when you create a client. By default the client makes a single attempt and does not retry, so you must opt in by supplying a retry policy. The simplest approach is to set a maximum number of attempts, which tells the client how many times it may send a request before giving up and raising the final error.

```python
from httpclient import Client, RetryPolicy

client = Client(
    base_url="https://api.example.com",
    retry=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=4),
)
```

With this configuration the client sends the original request and then up to three more if the earlier attempts fail. The count includes the first attempt, so a value of 1 is the same as disabling retries.

Between attempts the client waits according to a backoff strategy. The default is exponential backoff, where the delay doubles after each failure, starting from `backoff_base` seconds and never exceeding `backoff_max`. You can adjust both values to suit your service. Setting `jitter=True` adds a random amount to each delay, which prevents many clients from retrying at the same instant after a shared outage.

```python
retry = RetryPolicy(
    max_attempts=5,
    backoff_base=0.5,
    backoff_max=30.0,
    jitter=True,
)
```

You also control which failures trigger a retry. The `retry_on_status` option takes a set of HTTP status codes, and the default is 429, 502, 503 and 504. Connection errors and timeouts are retried by default as well, and you can turn this off by setting `retry_on_network_error=False`. Responses with other status codes, such as 400 or 404, are returned immediately because repeating the same request is unlikely to change the result.

```python
retry = RetryPolicy(
    max_attempts=3,
    retry_on_status={429, 500, 503},
    retry_on_network_error=True,
)
```

Only idempotent methods are retried automatically. GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS qualify, while POST and PATCH do not, because resending them could create duplicate side effects. If your endpoint is safe to repeat, for example because it accepts an idempotency key, you can allow retries for those methods by listing them in `retry_methods`.

```python
retry = RetryPolicy(
    max_attempts=3,
    retry_methods={"GET", "PUT", "POST"},
)
```

When a server sends a `Retry-After` header, the client honors it and waits for the requested time instead of using the computed backoff delay, as long as the value does not exceed `backoff_max`. You can disable this behavior with `respect_retry_after=False`.

A policy set on the client applies to every request, but you can override it for a single call by passing the `retry` argument to the request method. Passing `retry=None` disables retries for that call only.

```python
response = client.post("/orders", json=payload, retry=None)
```

If every attempt fails, the client raises the error from the last attempt, and the exception carries an `attempts` attribute recording how many requests were sent. This makes it straightforward to log or report persistent failures after the policy has been exhausted.

# Runbook: Job Queue Backup

**Trigger:** Queue depth or oldest-job age exceeds alert threshold (e.g., depth > 10,000 or age > 15 min), or users report delayed processing.

**Severity:** SEV2 by default. Escalate to SEV1 if customer-facing jobs (payments, notifications, exports) are delayed beyond SLA.

## 1. Assess (first 5 minutes)
- Check queue dashboard: depth, enqueue rate, dequeue rate, oldest job age.
- Determine the pattern:
  - **Enqueue spike:** a traffic surge or a runaway producer.
  - **Consumer slowdown:** workers are up but throughput is low.
  - **Consumer outage:** workers are crashed, stuck, or not scaled.
- Check recent deploys, config changes, and cron schedules from the last 2 hours.

## 2. Diagnose
- **Workers:** Are they running? Check pod/process count, restarts, OOM kills, and CPU/memory.
- **Logs:** Look for repeated errors, retry storms, or a single failing job type.
- **Dependencies:** Check the database, cache, and third-party APIs for latency or outages.
- **Poison jobs:** Look for the same job ID retrying repeatedly or blocking a worker.
- **Locks:** Check for long-held DB locks or stuck distributed locks.

## 3. Mitigate
| Cause | Action |
|---|---|
| Too few workers | Scale out consumers (watch DB connection limits) |
| Runaway producer | Throttle or disable the producer; rate-limit enqueue |
| Poison job | Move to dead-letter queue; fix or discard after review |
| Bad deploy | Roll back the release |
| Slow dependency | Enable circuit breaker; reduce concurrency to avoid cascading failures |
| Low-priority flood | Pause low-priority queues so critical jobs drain first |

**Do not** purge the queue without approval from the service owner. Jobs may be unrecoverable.

## 4. Verify recovery
- Dequeue rate exceeds enqueue rate and depth is trending down.
- Oldest job age is returning to normal.
- Error rate and retry count are back to baseline.
- Spot-check that critical job types completed successfully.

## 5. Follow-up
- Scale workers back down once the backlog clears.
- Replay or reconcile any dead-lettered or dropped jobs.
- Post an update in the incident channel and close the alert.
- Write a postmortem if SLA was breached or customer impact occurred.
- Add or tune alerts, autoscaling rules, and rate limits as needed.

**Escalation:** If depth is still growing after 30 minutes of mitigation, page the service owner and the on-call engineer for the infrastructure team.

**Title:** App crashes on launch when device language is set to Turkish

**Severity:** Critical (P1). App is unusable for all Turkish-locale users.

**Environment**
- App version: 4.2.1 (build 2087)
- Platform: Android 14 (Pixel 7) and iOS 17.5 (iPhone 14); reproduced on both
- Device language/region: Türkçe (Türkiye), `tr-TR`
- Network: Wi-Fi and cellular; not network dependent

**Description**
The app crashes immediately after the splash screen when the device language is set to Turkish. With any other language (English, German, Spanish, French tested), the app works normally. The crash is deterministic, and the app cannot be opened until the device language is changed.

**Steps to Reproduce**
1. Go to device Settings > System > Languages and set the primary language to Türkçe (Türkiye).
2. Force-quit the app if it is running.
3. Launch the app.
4. Observe the splash screen, followed by an immediate crash to the home screen.

**Expected Result**
The app launches and displays the home screen, using Turkish strings or falling back to English if a translation is missing.

**Actual Result**
The app crashes within 1–2 seconds of launch. No error dialog is shown.

**Frequency:** 100% (10/10 attempts)

**Crash Log / Stack Trace (excerpt)**
```
FATAL EXCEPTION: main
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant com.example.app.model.Category.SETTİNGS
    at java.lang.Enum.valueOf(Enum.java:273)
    at com.example.app.model.Category.valueOf(Category.kt:12)
    at com.example.app.ui.HomeViewModel.loadTabs(HomeViewModel.kt:58)
    at com.example.app.ui.HomeActivity.onCreate(HomeActivity.kt:41)
```

**Suspected Root Cause**
This looks like the well-known Turkish "dotted/dotless I" locale bug. A string conversion such as `"settings".uppercase()` or `toUpperCase()` uses the default device locale. In Turkish, lowercase `i` uppercases to `İ` (dotted capital I), not `I`, so `"settings"` becomes `"SETTİNGS"`, which does not match the enum constant `SETTINGS`. The same issue occurs in reverse with `I`.lowercase() producing `ı`.

**Suggested Fix**
- Use a locale-insensitive conversion for programmatic identifiers, for example `str.uppercase(Locale.ROOT)` / `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` in Kotlin/Java, or `.uppercased(with: Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX"))` in Swift.
- Audit the codebase for other calls to `toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()`, `uppercase()`, `lowercase()`, `String.format()`, and case-insensitive comparisons that don't specify a locale.
- Add a lint rule (e.g., Android Lint `DefaultLocale`) to catch this in CI.

**Workaround**
Change the device language to a non-Turkish locale.

**Regression Testing Suggestions**
- Add an automated test that runs the startup path under `Locale("tr", "TR")`.
- Include Turkish in the pseudo-locale/QA device matrix before each release.

**Attachments**
- Full logcat output
- Screen recording of the crash
- Device bug report (`adb bugreport`)

**Postmortem: API outage from expired TLS certificate**

**Summary**
On Tuesday, our public API and dashboard were down for about 40 minutes because the TLS certificate on the edge load balancer expired. Clients saw handshake failures and browsers showed certificate warnings. No data was lost, but anything that depended on HTTPS calls to us failed during that window, including customer integrations and webhooks.

**Timeline (UTC)**
- 14:02 – Certificate expires. Error rates climb almost immediately.
- 14:05 – First customer report comes in through support chat.
- 14:09 – Monitoring alert fires. It was a generic "5xx rate high" alert, which didn't point at TLS, and the on-call engineer initially suspected a bad deploy.
- 14:16 – Deploy ruled out after a rollback made no difference.
- 14:24 – Someone ran `openssl s_client` against the endpoint and saw the expired cert.
- 14:29 – We found the renewal had been failing silently for weeks. Reissuing the cert required a DNS validation record that no longer existed.
- 14:37 – DNS record recreated, new cert issued.
- 14:42 – New cert installed on the load balancer. Traffic recovers.

**Root cause**
The auto-renewal job had been failing since a DNS cleanup a few weeks earlier removed the validation record it relied on. The job logged errors but didn't alert anyone. The expiry warning emails went to a shared mailbox that nobody had checked since the team reorganized.

**What went well**
- Once someone looked at the cert directly, diagnosis and fix took under 20 minutes.
- Support flagged the problem before our own alerting did.

**What went poorly**
- It took 22 minutes to even consider a certificate problem.
- We had no monitoring on certificate expiry.
- The rollback was a wasted detour, though a reasonable one given what we knew.

**Action items**
1. Add an expiry check that pages when any production cert has fewer than 14 days left. (Owner: infra, due next week)
2. Make renewal job failures alert the on-call channel. (Owner: infra, due next week)
3. Route cert expiry emails to a monitored group alias instead of the old shared mailbox. (Owner: IT, done)
4. Add a note to the DNS cleanup checklist: check for records used by ACME validation before deleting. (Owner: platform, due this week)
5. Add "check cert validity" to the on-call runbook for any sudden spike in connection or 5xx errors. (Owner: on-call lead, due this week)
6. Inventory all certs we manage and where each one is renewed. We found out we don't have a complete list. (Owner: infra, 30 days)

**Takeaway**
Nothing about this was exotic. The renewal broke quietly, and nothing was set up to tell us. We're fixing the alerting first and the process gaps right after.

## `--dry-run`

Shows what a command would do without doing it. Nothing gets written, deleted, moved, or sent. You get the same output you'd normally see, just prefixed so you know it's pretend.

```
$ mytool sync ./photos --dry-run
[dry-run] would copy  photos/IMG_0412.jpg -> backup/IMG_0412.jpg
[dry-run] would copy  photos/IMG_0413.jpg -> backup/IMG_0413.jpg
[dry-run] would delete backup/old_draft.jpg
[dry-run] 2 copied, 1 deleted (nothing was changed)
```

### When to use it

Run it first any time you're about to do something you can't easily undo: syncing over a directory, cleaning up old files, running a command with a wildcard, or trying a config you just edited. If the list looks right, run the same command again without the flag.

### What it does and doesn't do

- It reads files and checks state like normal, so it still needs read access to everything the real run would touch.
- It doesn't write to disk, change permissions, make network calls that modify anything, or run hooks.
- It exits with code 0 if the plan was built fine, even when changes are pending. If you want a nonzero exit when there's something to do (handy in CI), add `--exit-code`.
- Errors you'd hit anyway, like a bad path or invalid config, still show up and still fail the command.

### Caveats

The preview is based on what's there right now. If another process changes files between your dry run and the real run, the results can differ. Also, a few things can only be found out by actually doing them, like running out of disk space partway through. A clean dry run is a good sign, not a guarantee.

### Combining with other flags

`--dry-run` works with `--verbose` for more detail per item, and with `--json` if you want to pipe the plan into something else. With `--quiet` it prints only the final summary line.

```
$ mytool sync ./photos --dry-run --json
{"action":"copy","src":"photos/IMG_0412.jpg","dest":"backup/IMG_0412.jpg","dry_run":true}
```

# Release Notes: Connection Pooling

## Highlights

The database client now supports **connection pooling**. Instead of opening a new connection for every operation, the client maintains a managed pool of reusable connections. This reduces latency, lowers load on your database server, and improves throughput for concurrent workloads.

## What's New

- **Built-in connection pool.** Connections are created on demand, returned to the pool after use, and reused by later requests.
- **Configurable pool size.** Set minimum and maximum connection counts to match your workload and database limits.
- **Idle connection management.** Connections that sit unused beyond a configurable timeout are closed automatically, freeing server resources.
- **Acquisition timeout.** Requests wait for an available connection up to a set limit, then fail with a clear error rather than hanging indefinitely.
- **Health checks.** Connections are validated before being handed out, and broken ones are discarded and replaced transparently.
- **Graceful shutdown.** Closing the client drains in-flight operations and then closes all pooled connections.

## Configuration

```python
client = Client(
    host="db.example.com",
    pool_min=2,
    pool_max=20,
    pool_idle_timeout=300,      # seconds
    pool_acquire_timeout=30,    # seconds
)
```

Pooling is enabled by default with conservative settings. To restore the previous one-connection-per-operation behavior, set `pool_max=1` or `pooling=False`.

## Upgrade Notes

- **Default behavior change.** Applications that relied on session-level state (temporary tables, session variables, open transactions) persisting across separate calls should use explicit transactions or a dedicated connection, since consecutive calls may now use different pooled connections.
- **Server connection limits.** Ensure `pool_max`, multiplied by the number of client processes, stays below your database's maximum connection setting.
- **Resource cleanup.** Call `client.close()` (or use the client as a context manager) to release pooled connections on exit.

## Performance

Workloads with frequent short queries should see noticeably lower per-request latency, since connection setup and authentication costs are paid once rather than on every call. Results vary with network conditions and database configuration.

## Known Limitations

- Pool settings apply per client instance and are not shared across processes.
- Changing pool settings requires creating a new client.

Running the tests is pretty simple. Install the dev dependencies first with `pip install -e ".[dev]"`, ideally inside a virtualenv so you don't clutter your system Python. Then run `pytest` from the repo root and you should see everything pass in under a minute. If you only care about one area, point it at a file, like `pytest tests/test_parser.py`, or use `-k` with part of a test name to narrow it down. A few of the integration tests need a local Postgres running; if you don't have one handy, skip them with `pytest -m "not integration"`. If something fails on a fresh checkout and you haven't touched anything, that's worth an issue, so please let us know what OS and Python version you're on.

The application follows a layered architecture in which a stateless web tier handles incoming HTTP requests and routes them to a service layer containing the core business logic. PostgreSQL serves as the system of record, storing all durable relational data such as users, accounts, and transactions, with schema migrations, foreign-key constraints, and indexed queries ensuring integrity and performance. Redis sits alongside it as an in-memory cache and ephemeral data store, holding frequently read query results, session data, and rate-limiting counters to reduce database load and keep response times low. Reads typically follow a cache-aside pattern: the service checks Redis first, falls back to Postgres on a miss, and then populates the cache with a time-to-live, while writes go to Postgres first and then invalidate or update the relevant cache keys to prevent stale data. Because the application servers hold no local state, they can be scaled horizontally behind a load balancer, with Postgres scaled through connection pooling and read replicas and Redis through replication or clustering as traffic grows.

# Setting Up a Static Site with a Custom Domain

A static site is one of the simplest, fastest, and cheapest ways to get a presence on the web. With no servers to maintain and no databases to secure, you can publish a portfolio, blog, or documentation site using nothing more than HTML, CSS, and a bit of JavaScript, often for free.

But a URL like `yourname.github.io` or `yoursite.netlify.app` only goes so far. A custom domain, such as `yourname.com`, makes your site look professional, easier to remember, and fully yours, no matter where it's hosted.

In this tutorial, you'll learn how to:

1. **Build and deploy** a simple static site to a hosting provider
2. **Register or choose** a domain name
3. **Configure DNS records** (A, CNAME, and optionally AAAA) to point your domain to your host
4. **Enable HTTPS** so your site is served securely
5. **Verify and troubleshoot** your setup, including handling DNS propagation delays

**What you'll need:**

- A basic static site (even a single `index.html` file will do)
- An account with a static hosting provider, such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or Vercel
- A domain name, or a few dollars to register one
- About 30 minutes, plus some waiting time for DNS changes to take effect

By the end, your site will be live at your own domain, secured with HTTPS, and ready to grow. Let's get started.

I've set up a lot of static sites over the years, and the part that trips people up is almost never the site itself. Building a few HTML files is easy. The annoying bit is getting your own domain to point at it without spending an evening staring at DNS settings and wondering why nothing has changed yet.

So here's what we're going to do. We'll put a simple site up on a free host, buy or reuse a domain, and connect the two. By the end, typing your own address into a browser will bring up your page, with HTTPS working and no scary warnings.

You'll need three things before you start: a folder with an `index.html` in it (even a single line of text is fine), a free account on whichever host you pick (Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, and GitHub Pages all work well), and a domain name. If you don't have a domain yet, grab one from any registrar. Prices are mostly similar, so don't agonize over it.

One warning up front: DNS changes can take anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours to show up. If something looks broken after you've changed a setting, go make a coffee before you start undoing things. Nine times out of ten, it just needs time.

Let's start with getting the site online at the host's default address, since it's much easier to fix the domain once you know the site itself works.

## Rate Limits

The API enforces a limit of 100 requests per minute for each API key. Limits are tracked per key, so usage on one key does not affect the quota of another. The window is a rolling 60-second period, and each response includes headers showing your current status: `X-RateLimit-Limit` (the maximum number of requests allowed), `X-RateLimit-Remaining` (requests left in the current window), and `X-RateLimit-Reset` (the time, in Unix seconds, when the quota resets). If you exceed the limit, the API returns an HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` response with a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds to wait before sending another request. To avoid interruptions, we recommend implementing exponential backoff with jitter, caching responses where possible, and spreading requests evenly rather than sending them in bursts.

```
/*
 * Retry policy: exactly three attempts (initial try + two retries).
 *
 * Why three:
 *   - Most transient failures (network blips, brief service restarts,
 *     momentary lock contention) clear up within one or two retries.
 *     If a third attempt also fails, the problem is very likely not
 *     transient, and further retries only delay surfacing the error.
 *   - With exponential backoff (e.g., 200ms, 400ms), three attempts keep
 *     the worst-case added latency under about a second, which fits
 *     within our caller's timeout budget.
 *   - Limiting attempts prevents retry amplification: when a downstream
 *     service is struggling, many clients retrying aggressively can
 *     turn a partial outage into a full one.
 *
 * If you change this number, revisit the backoff schedule and the
 * upstream timeout together, since they are tuned as a set.
 */
```

Deploys here are designed to be boring, and that is intentional. Once your pull request is reviewed and merged into the main branch, our CI pipeline automatically builds the application, runs the full test suite, and publishes a versioned artifact. That artifact is first rolled out to the staging environment, where automated smoke tests verify that core flows still work. If staging looks healthy, the same artifact is promoted to production through a gradual rollout, starting with a small percentage of traffic and expanding as error rates and latency stay within normal bounds. You never rebuild for production, which means what you tested in staging is exactly what ships. If something goes wrong, the pipeline can automatically halt the rollout, and you can roll back to the previous version with a single command or button click in the deploy dashboard. Database migrations run as a separate step before the new code goes out, so write them to be backward compatible with the version currently running. As a rule, deploy small changes often, watch the dashboards for the first several minutes after your change reaches production, and post in the team channel so others know what is going out. If you are ever unsure, ask a teammate before you ship, because someone will always be glad to help.

**Why does the app need my location?**

We only use your location to show you things that are actually near you, like nearby results, local availability, and accurate distances. Without it, you'd have to type in an address or zip code every time, and that gets old fast.

We don't track you in the background, and we don't sell your location to anyone. The app only checks where you are while you're using it, and you can turn that off whenever you like.

If you'd rather not share it, the app still works. You'll just need to enter your location by hand. To change your setting, go to your phone's Settings, find the app, and tap Location.

Still have questions? Write to us and a real person will get back to you.

I don't think remote work itself makes juniors worse, but it does remove a lot of the accidental learning that used to happen for free. In an office, a junior overhears how seniors debug, sees how a tense code review gets resolved, and can lean over and ask a "dumb" question without scheduling anything. Remotely, all of that has to be deliberate, and many teams never build the habits to replace it. So juniors on those teams often do stall, but that's a failure of process, not of the medium.

The teams that make it work tend to do a few things: pair programming on a regular schedule, written-down reasoning in PRs and design docs, and an explicit norm that asking questions in public channels is encouraged. When those are in place, I've seen juniors ramp up just as fast as they would in person, and sometimes faster, since the knowledge is actually written down instead of living in someone's head. If a company is going fully remote and expects juniors to figure it out alone, yes, they'll struggle. But that would be true in an office too, just less visibly.

I get where you're coming from, especially with tuition being what it is. But "waste of money" is too broad a verdict. The answer depends heavily on the major, the school, and how much debt someone takes on. A degree in nursing, engineering, or accounting from a reasonably priced school has a very different return than an expensive degree with no clear career path. On average, graduates still earn significantly more over a lifetime and have lower unemployment, even after you account for the cost.

That said, you're right that college isn't the right move for everyone, and trades or apprenticeships are great options that get overlooked. I'd just say the real problem is going in without a plan or taking on unmanageable debt, not the idea of college itself. Treating it as an investment you have to evaluate, rather than a default or a scam, seems like the more useful way to look at it.

I get why it feels that way, especially with tuition where it is and so many people stuck with debt for degrees that didn't pay off. But "college" covers a huge range of outcomes. Someone who finishes an engineering or nursing degree at an in-state school is in a very different position than someone who takes on six figures of loans for a major with thin job prospects. The data consistently shows that bachelor's degree holders earn substantially more over a lifetime and face lower unemployment on average, so the question is less "is college worth it" and more "which college, which major, and at what price."

It's also worth saying that college isn't the only good path. Trades, apprenticeships, and community college transfer routes are great options and often a smarter financial move for plenty of people. But dismissing college entirely ignores that many careers simply require a degree, and that the cost can be managed with cheaper schools, scholarships, and working during school. Treating it as a calculated investment rather than a default or a scam probably gets you closer to the truth.

I once lost a full week to a bug where our nightly report job produced slightly wrong totals, but only on some days and never on my machine. I checked the queries, the rounding, the timezone handling, and the data itself, and everything looked fine. The numbers were off by a few cents in a handful of accounts, which made it easy to dismiss as noise until finance noticed the pattern.

The culprit turned out to be a floating point sum that depended on the order rows came back from the database. Without an explicit ORDER BY, the production replica returned rows in a different physical order after a vacuum, so the accumulated rounding error shifted. Switching to decimal types and summing in integer cents fixed it for good. The lesson I took away is that if a result is only wrong sometimes, suspect anything that quietly depends on ordering, and never use floats for money.

"The Psychology of Money" by Morgan Housel genuinely shifted how I think about this stuff. Someone who understands every spreadsheet trick but panics during a downturn will lose to someone who just stays calm and keeps investing for decades.

Wealth is the stuff you don't see, the money you chose not to spend, which gives you options and freedom. I'd lean toward waiting, but I think the real question is what kind of phone we're talking about. I built a meal-planning app for people with food allergies, and it died after about 14 months. The idea felt obvious: families managing multiple allergens spend hours cross-checking labels, so surely they'd pay to automate it. We spent eight months building a polished ingredient-matching engine before putting it in front of more than a handful of people. When we finally launched, users loved the demo but rarely came back. The real pain wasn't planning, it was the moment of uncertainty in a grocery aisle or restaurant, and our app didn't help with that.

The biggest lesson was that I'd confused "people say this is a problem" with "people will change their behavior to fix it." I should have sold a rough version, even a manual concierge service, in the first month and watched what people actually did. I also underestimated how much trust matters in health-adjacent products: one wrong ingredient flag and you've lost a family for good. If I did it again, I'd start with the narrowest, highest-stakes moment and earn trust there before building anything broader.

I spent two years building a scheduling tool for independent fitness instructors. I talked to maybe fifteen of them early on, they all said it sounded great, and I took that as validation. What I missed was that nobody had ever offered to pay or even to switch from the messy mix of spreadsheets and text messages they already used. Polite enthusiasm is not the same as a real problem, and I confused the two for far too long.

The biggest lesson was to ask for a commitment early, even a small one like a deposit, a signed letter of intent, or a week of using a crude prototype. If people won't give you something that costs them anything, you have your answer. I also wish I had launched an ugly version in month two instead of month fourteen. We ran out of money polishing features that no one had asked for, and the market told us what it thought about a week after we finally shipped.

Cue the stomach drop. My phone was at 22% and I had one bar of service, which was useless. I did what I should've done immediately: stopped, drank some water, and ate a granola bar instead of panicking.

Then I remembered I'd downloaded the offline map that morning (thank you, past me). The blue dot showed me maybe half a mile off the trail, uphill and east. And there it was. A faded orange blaze on a tree, about ten feet from where I'd crossed. I'd walked right past it.

Lesson learned: download offline maps, check your surroundings at every crossing, and snack when you're scared.

**I PAID OFF MY CREDIT CARD. ALL OF IT. I'm still shaking a little.**

Throwaway-ish account, but I had to tell someone who would actually get it.

Three years ago I was sitting on $14,820 in credit card debt across two cards, with an APR that made my stomach hurt every time I opened a statement. I was making minimum payments and watching the balance barely move. Some months it actually went *up*.

Here's what finally worked for me:

- **Wrote down every number.** Balance, APR, minimum. Seeing it all on one page was brutal but necessary.
- **Avalanche method.** Highest APR first, minimums on the rest.
- **Cut the boring stuff.** Cancelled three subscriptions I forgot about, cooked at home, and stopped "treating myself" every Friday.
- **Picked up weekend freelance work.** Every dollar of it went straight to the card. No exceptions.
- **Used windfalls wisely.** Tax refund, birthday cash, a small bonus. All of it went to debt.

There were months I wanted to quit. I watched friends go on trips and told myself "not yet."

Today I logged in, hit "pay full balance," and saw $0.00. I just stared at it for like five minutes.

I'm not rich, and I've got a long way to go with savings. But I'm free of that weight, and it feels unreal.

If you're in the thick of it right now: keep going. It really does end.

**Salt, Sand, and Slow Mornings**

I didn't realize how badly I needed the ocean until I was standing in front of it on Saturday morning, coffee in hand, wind tugging at my jacket.

We left the city early Friday evening, windows down, a questionable playlist at full volume. By the time we reached the little coastal town, the sky had gone that deep blue that comes just before dark, and the air smelled like salt and woodsmoke. Our rented cottage was small and creaky, with mismatched mugs and a porch swing that groaned with every push. I loved it immediately.

Saturday was all about doing very little. We walked the beach for hours, pockets filling with shells we'd inevitably forget about. The tide was out, leaving long mirrors of wet sand where the clouds reflected. I watched a kid chase seagulls with total commitment and zero success. Honestly, relatable.

For lunch we found a shack by the harbor selling fish tacos and sweet tea. We ate on an overturned crate, fingers sticky, watching the fishing boats come in. Nothing fancy, and probably the best meal I've had all year.

Sunday morning I woke before everyone else and walked down to the water alone. The beach was empty except for a few sandpipers darting at the edge of the waves. I sat there for a long time, not thinking about email or deadlines or anything at all.

Driving home, sandy and sunburned, I made a promise to go back sooner. The ocean has a way of resetting you. I'm already planning the next trip.

# Why I Left the Corner Office for a Classroom

Last June, I cleared out my desk after eleven years in corporate finance. My colleagues threw me a small party, and nearly everyone asked the same question: "Are you sure?"

I was. Though it took me a long time to get there.

The truth is, I was good at my job. I built models, hit targets, and earned promotions. But somewhere around year eight, I noticed that the work I felt proudest of wasn't on any spreadsheet. It was the Saturday mornings I spent tutoring at a community center, watching a kid finally understand fractions. That flash of recognition in their eyes beat any quarterly bonus.

I started doing the math, ironically. How many hours of my life was I trading for numbers that would be forgotten by next quarter? What would I want to say I'd done when I looked back?

So I went back to school at night, earned my teaching certification, and applied for a position teaching middle school math. The pay cut was real, and I won't pretend otherwise. My savings took a hit, and I've learned to cook a lot more beans.

But now I wake up eager to go to work. My days are loud, unpredictable, and exhausting. A thirteen-year-old told me last week that I was "the first teacher who made math make sense." I carried that sentence around for days.

I don't know if everyone should make a leap like this. But if a quiet voice keeps asking whether you're sure, it might be worth listening.

# The Winter I Learned to Make Bread

When the first real cold arrived this year, I did what I always do: I complained, wrapped myself in a blanket, and waited for spring. But somewhere around the second week of frost, I decided to try something different. I would learn to bake bread.

My first loaf was a disaster. It came out of the oven dense as a paving stone, pale and stubborn. I'd killed the yeast with water that was far too hot, and I knew it the moment I tried to slice it. The crust shattered, the middle was gluey, and my kitchen smelled faintly of defeat.

But the smell of the *second* attempt changed everything. Warm yeast, toasted flour, a hint of sweetness. The whole apartment felt softer. I started to understand why people have been doing this for thousands of years.

What surprised me most was the patience it demands. You can't rush dough. You mix it, knead it, and then you simply wait while the cold world outside goes on without you. I began planning my evenings around rises and rests. Folding dough became a quiet ritual, a way to slow down when everything else felt hurried.

By January, my loaves had golden crusts and open, airy crumbs. I brought one to a neighbor, still warm, wrapped in a dish towel. She smiled like I'd handed her sunshine.

Winter hasn't gotten any warmer. But my kitchen has, and that turns out to be enough.

**The Day the Motorway Went Quiet**

I remembered the advice: get out on the passenger side, climb over the barrier, stand well back. So there I stood, on a damp grass verge in November, hood up, watching traffic blur by and feeling oddly small.

The breakdown service said forty-five minutes. It took seventy. I spent that time texting my sister, eating a squashed cereal bar from my coat pocket, and noticing things I never see at speed: the hawthorn bushes, a crow patrolling the embankment, the sheer unbroken river of headlights.

The mechanic, a cheerful man named Dave, diagnosed a failed alternator within about ninety seconds. "Happens to the best of us," he said, which I chose to find comforting.

The repair bill stung, and I missed my meeting. But I also got an unplanned hour of stillness, which I rarely allow myself. Now I keep a blanket, a torch, and spare snacks in the boot. And I check the battery light a little sooner.

# What My Dead Side Project Taught Me

Last spring I spent four months building a recipe-planning app. It would take whatever was in your fridge, cross-reference your calendar, and generate a week of meals. I was sure it was brilliant. It had a landing page, a logo, and about nine hundred lines of code I was proud of. It had zero users.

The failure wasn't technical. The app worked fine. The failure was that I never asked anyone if they wanted it. I told myself I was "validating" by reading forum threads where people complained about meal planning, but complaints aren't commitments. Plenty of people grumble about dinner. Almost nobody will change their habits, let alone enter their fridge contents into a form every Sunday.

When I finally showed it to ten friends, the feedback was polite and lukewarm. Three tried it once. Nobody came back. One friend said, kindly, "I just use a note on my phone." That stung, because she was right. My competition wasn't another app. It was a lazy, free, good-enough habit.

Here's what I took away. First, talk to people before writing code, and ask what they currently do, not whether they'd use your idea. Second, build the ugliest possible version in a weekend. If nobody cares about that, polish won't save it. Third, separate your enjoyment of building from evidence of demand. I loved the work, and that fooled me into thinking the work mattered to anyone else.

I don't regret the months. I sharpened my skills and learned to spot my own wishful thinking. The next project starts with a conversation, not a repository.
